The closer you get to the **tropics of Cancer and Capricorn**, the closer together the two zenith positions come. Then only **one rainy season** remains, and the dry season gets longer. Often it is hottest shortly **before the start of the rainy season**, because the sun is already high but the sky is still short of clouds.

Typical of the tropical wet and dry climate is the **savanna**, a grassland with single trees or groups of trees. The geographers **Troll** and **Lauer** divided it up by the number of wet months. The **moist savanna** has about 7 to 9.5 humid months, the **dry savanna** about 4.5 to 7 and the **thorn savanna** about 2 to 4.5. The fewer the wet months, the sparser the vegetation becomes. There are large savannas in Africa, South America and Australia.

The Brazilian capital, **Brasília**, has a tropical wet and dry climate. The rainy season there lasts roughly from **October to April**. In the southern winter a pronounced dry season follows, in which it hardly rains. It is quite different in **Singapore**, where it is wet all year round. **Cairo** and **Lima**, on the other hand, have a desert climate with very little rain.

gewusst: The term “humid” means that more precipitation falls in a month than can evaporate.
In the savanna of Africa, many large herds of animals follow the rain.

teile.einleitung: The Tuareg are a people who live in the Sahara and the Sahel. In the past many of them travelled through the desert as nomads with camels and herds. They are known for their indigo-blue cloths and for the fact that among them the men cover their faces.
wichtigste: The Tuareg belong to the Berbers.
They live in the Sahara and the Sahel, mainly in Niger, Mali, Algeria and Libya.
Their language is called Tamasheq, and their old script is Tifinagh.
Among the Tuareg, traditionally the men wear the face veil.
Because of their indigo-blue cloths they are often called “blue men”.
The city of Agadez in Niger is regarded as a centre of the Tuareg.

abschnitte.text: The **Tuareg** are a **Berber people**. The Berbers lived in North Africa before the Arabs came there. The Tuareg live in the **Sahara** and the **Sahel**, mainly in **Niger**, **Mali**, **Algeria** and **Libya**. Their territory is spread across several countries. Many Tuareg call themselves **Kel Tamasheq**, which means “those who speak Tamasheq”.

In the past many Tuareg lived as **nomads**. Nomads have no fixed home but travel with their herds to pastures and water points. They take their tents with them. The Tuareg kept **camels**, goats and sheep. With **caravans** they carried goods such as **salt** across the desert. Today many Tuareg live in villages and towns, though some still move around.

Among the Tuareg, traditionally the **men** cover their faces with a veil, the **tagelmust**. The women usually show their faces openly. This is different from many other societies. Many of the cloths are dyed with **indigo**, a deep blue dye. The colour sometimes even rubs off onto the skin. That is why the Tuareg are often called “blue men”.

The Tuareg speak **Tamasheq**, a **Berber language**. There are different variants depending on the region. They have their own very old script: **Tifinagh**. This script consists of dots, lines and circles. Today it is also used for other Berber languages, for example in Morocco.

The city of **Agadez** in **Niger** is regarded as a centre of the Tuareg. It lies on the southern edge of the Sahara and was an important place for the caravans. It is famous for its **mud-brick mosque** with a minaret of mud about **27 metres** high. The old town of Agadez is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Tuareg are also known for their silver jewellery and their music.

gewusst: Among the Tuareg, the tent traditionally belongs to the woman.
The Tuareg band Tinariwen from Mali has become known all over the world for its desert music.

teile.einleitung: Overfishing means that more fish are caught than can grow back. Fish stocks then shrink, and some even collapse completely. It is one of the biggest problems for the oceans.
wichtigste: With overfishing, more fish are caught than can be replaced.
According to the 2026 FAO report, about 38 per cent of marine fish stocks are overfished.
The maximum sustainable yield (MSY) is the largest catch that is possible in the long term.
Ghost nets keep catching animals in the sea.
The blue MSC label marks fish from certified fisheries.
Since 2022 more aquatic animals have come from farming than from wild catch.

abschnitte.text: Fish breed and grow back. But if more are caught than are born, the **stock** shrinks. In the worst case it collapses completely. Experts speak of the **maximum sustainable yield**, or **MSY** for short. This is the largest catch that is possible in the long term without the stock getting smaller. According to the **FAO fisheries report** of 2026, about 62 per cent of the stocks studied are fished sustainably, while about **38 per cent** are overfished.

abschnitte.titel: The deep sea and the food chain
abschnitte.text: Fish that grow slowly are especially at risk. The **orange roughy** from the deep sea can live for over 100 years and only starts breeding late. Off New Zealand and Australia its stocks collapsed after just a few years of intensive fishing. The marine biologist **Daniel Pauly** described the trend in 1998 as **“Fishing down marine food webs”**. Once large predatory fish such as cod or tuna are overfished, people increasingly catch smaller species further down the **food chain**.

**Ghost nets** are fishing nets that have been lost or abandoned. They drift in the sea for years and keep catching fish, seals and turtles. **Bottom trawling** also does great damage. In it, heavy nets are dragged across the seabed and tear up **cold-water corals**, sponges and other living things. Such habitats need decades or longer to recover.

The **MSC label** was founded in 1997 by WWF and Unilever. Today the **Marine Stewardship Council** is an independent organisation whose blue label marks fish from certified fisheries. In September 2025 a **WTO agreement** came into force that bans state subsidies for illegal fishing and for overfished stocks. **Aquaculture**, that is fish farming, has also supplied more aquatic animals than wild catch since 2022. It only relieves the oceans, however, if the feed itself does not consist of wild fish.

gewusst: The WTO agreement on fisheries subsidies is the first WTO agreement with an environmental goal at its centre.
An orange roughy can live for over 100 years.

teile.einleitung: A watershed is a boundary line where it is decided in which direction water flows off. On one side it flows into one river, on the other into a quite different one, sometimes even into different seas.
wichtigste: In the mountains a watershed usually runs along the ridges.
The European Continental Divide separates the rivers flowing to the North Sea and the Atlantic from those flowing to the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
It also runs right across Switzerland.
Piz Lunghin near Maloja is a triple watershed.
The Gotthard Pass lies between the Reuss and the Ticino.
At the Witenwasserenstock water begins that flows to the Rhine, the Rhône and the Po.

abschnitte.text: When it rains on a **ridge**, the water runs down on both sides. The line between is called the **watershed**. It separates two **catchment areas**, that is, the areas from which a river gets its water. In the mountains, watersheds usually follow the highest **crests**. On flat land, on the other hand, they are often hardly recognisable.

Across Europe runs the **European Continental Divide**. North and west of it, the rivers flow into the North Sea and the Atlantic. South and east of it, they flow into the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. The line also runs through **Switzerland**, over many Alpine passes and the **Jura**.

A special place is **Piz Lunghin** near Maloja in the canton of Graubünden. From there water flows in three directions: via the **Rhine** into the North Sea, via the **Po** into the Adriatic, and via the **Inn** and the Danube into the Black Sea. That is why it is called a **triple watershed**. Very close by lies the **Maloja Pass**: on the Engadine side the water flows into the Inn, and on the steep Bregaglia side it flows via the Mera to Lake Como.

The **Gotthard Pass** lies on the watershed between the **Reuss** and the **Ticino**. To the north the water flows via the Reuss into the Rhine, to the south via the Ticino into the Po. Not far from there lies the **Witenwasserenstock**. From it water flows via the Reuss to the Rhine, via the **Rhône** to the Mediterranean and via the Ticino to the Po. It is an important watershed point in the Alps.

gewusst: A raindrop on Piz Lunghin can, depending on the side, end up in three different seas.
In American English, “watershed” can also mean the whole catchment area of a river.

teile.einleitung: Tokyo is the capital of Japan and lies on a bay of the Pacific Ocean. The Greater Tokyo area is one of the largest urban areas in the world. Modern skyscrapers, old temples and crowded stations meet here.
wichtigste: The name Tokyo means **“eastern capital”**.
The city used to be called **Edo**.
**Over 30 million** people live in Greater Tokyo.
At 634 metres the **Tokyo Skytree** is the tallest tower in Japan.
The Summer Olympics **“Tokyo 2020”** took place in 2021.
**Shinjuku** is regarded as the busiest station in the world.

abschnitte.text: The city used to be called **Edo**. It was the city of the powerful **shoguns**, the military rulers who governed Japan for a long time. In 1868 the emperor moved here, and the city was given the name **Tokyo**. “To” means east and “kyo” means capital, so Tokyo is the “eastern capital”. Before that, Kyoto had long been the imperial city.

**Well over 30 million people** live in Greater Tokyo. That is more than three times as many as in the whole of Switzerland. Tokyo lies on **Tokyo Bay**, which belongs to the **Pacific Ocean**. The **Tokyo Skytree** is 634 metres high and the tallest tower in Japan. At the **Shibuya Crossing** all the traffic lights turn green at the same time, and then thousands of people cross the street in every direction.

**Sensō-ji** in the Asakusa district is the oldest Buddhist temple in Tokyo. According to tradition it was founded in the 7th century. Visitors enter it through the great **Kaminarimon Gate** with a huge red lantern. In the middle of the city there is also the **Imperial Palace** with large gardens. Many festivals and old customs are still kept up in Tokyo today.

Millions of people get on, off and change trains at **Shinjuku** station every day. The Guinness Book of Records lists it as the busiest station in the world. The fish market at **Tsukiji** was also famous. Because it had become too small and out of date, it moved in October 2018 to the new wholesale market at **Toyosu**. Fish and seafood are traded there today.

Tokyo had already hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964. The next Games were called **“Tokyo 2020”**. Because of the **coronavirus pandemic** they were postponed and only took place in the summer of 2021. Most of the competitions were held without spectators. This made Tokyo the first Asian city to host the Summer Games twice.

gewusst: The height of 634 metres was chosen for the Tokyo Skytree because the numbers can be pronounced in Japanese like the old name of the area around Tokyo.
Even in 2021 the Games were still called “Tokyo 2020”.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower uses the force of flowing or falling water to produce electricity. In Switzerland, with its mountains, rivers and lakes, it is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: In 2024 about 60 per cent of Swiss electricity came from hydropower.
Water drives a turbine, which turns a generator.
Run-of-river power stations stand on rivers, and storage power stations use reservoirs in the mountains.
Pumped-storage power stations can pump water up and later produce electricity again.
Hydropower is renewable and gives off hardly any CO₂ in operation.

abschnitte.text: Flowing or falling water has **energy**. In a power station it flows through a **turbine**, a wheel with blades, and makes it turn. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electric current. The more water and the greater the drop, the more electricity is produced. In the past, hydropower was already used with mill wheels, for example to grind grain.

**Run-of-river power stations** stand on rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare. They use the water that is flowing past and supply electricity regularly. **Storage power stations** collect water in **reservoirs** behind big dams in the Alps. The water flows through pipes far down to the turbines. In this way electricity can be produced exactly when a lot is needed, for example in winter.

A **pumped-storage power station** has two lakes at different heights. When there is a lot of electricity, for example on sunny middays, it pumps water into the upper lake. When a lot of electricity is needed later, it lets the water flow back down through the turbines. In this way it works like a giant **battery**. For an electricity supply with sun and wind, such stores are becoming more and more important.

According to the **Federal Office of Energy**, hydropower supplied about 59.5 per cent of domestic electricity in 2024. In Switzerland there are hundreds of hydropower stations. One of the best-known installations is the **Grande Dixence** dam in Valais, the highest gravity dam in the world. The power stations pay the cantons and communes a **water fee** for using the water. For mountain cantons such as Valais or Graubünden this is an important income.

Hydropower is **renewable**, because rain and snow fill rivers and lakes again and again. In operation hardly any CO₂ is produced. Dams and power stations do change nature, however: valleys are flooded, and fish can no longer migrate freely. That is why **fish ladders** are built today and care is taken that enough **residual water** stays in the river.

gewusst: The largest hydropower station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam in China.
The Grande Dixence dam is about 285 m high.

teile.einleitung: The Tren Maya is a new railway line in the south of Mexico. It runs in a large loop across the Yucatán Peninsula and connects seaside resorts, cities and ancient Maya sites. The first sections opened at the end of 2023.
wichtigste: Tren Maya means “Maya Train” in English.
The line opens up the Yucatán Peninsula in a loop.
The first sections opened at the end of 2023.
The train is meant to promote tourism and development in the south of Mexico.
Critics point to damage to forest, caves and cenotes.

abschnitte.text: The **Tren Maya** runs across the **Yucatán Peninsula** in the south-east of Mexico. The line is about **1,500 kilometres** long and runs through several Mexican states. It connects well-known places such as the seaside resort of **Cancún**, the city of **Mérida** and the Maya site of **Palenque**. The project was built under President **Andrés Manuel López Obrador**. The first trains ran at the end of **2023**, and further sections followed afterwards.

On the peninsula there are many ruins of the ancient **Maya**, for example **Chichén Itzá**. That is how the train got its name. It is meant to take tourists from the beaches to these places. The government hopes that this will create jobs and that the poorer south of the country will catch up economically. The people who live there are also meant to be able to use the train.

The building work is **controversial**. Large areas of **forest** were cleared for the line. The ground of the peninsula consists of limestone with many **caves** and **cenotes**. Cenotes are natural limestone holes filled with water, which were sacred to the Maya. Environmental groups fear that pillars and building work will damage these caves and the groundwater. The government replied that it was taking protective measures.

gewusst: On the Yucatán Peninsula there are thousands of cenotes, and many are connected to each other by underground rivers.
The Yucatán Peninsula has almost no rivers on the surface, because rainwater seeps away into the limestone.

teile.einleitung: Wind is moving air. Sometimes it is a gentle breeze, sometimes a dangerous hurricane. It arises because the sun does not warm the Earth equally everywhere.
wichtigste: Wind is air that moves.
It arises from differences in air pressure.
A breeze is light, a gale strong, a hurricane the strongest.
When no wind blows at all, it is called a calm.
The bise is a cold wind from the north-east in Switzerland.
Wind turbines make electricity from wind.

abschnitte.text: The sun warms land and water to different degrees. Warm air is lighter and rises, while cold air sinks. In this way areas of high and low **air pressure** arise. The air flows from high to low pressure, and we feel this as **wind**. The greater the difference, the stronger the wind blows.

How strong the wind is is described by the **Beaufort scale**, with steps from 0 to 12. Step 0 is called a **calm**: smoke rises straight up. A **breeze** is a light, pleasant wind. A **gale** is very strong and can break off branches. The highest step is the **hurricane**. It can strip roofs and uproot trees.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the wind come from?
abschnitte.text: On many church towers there is a **weathercock**. It turns with the wind and shows which direction it comes from. Winds are named after where they come from: a west wind comes from the west. In Switzerland people especially know the **bise**, a cold, dry wind from the north-east that often blows across the Central Plateau. The **foehn**, on the other hand, is a warm downslope wind in the Alps.

In autumn many children fly a **kite**, which the wind carries high into the air. For thousands of years people have also used the wind for sailing ships and windmills. Today **wind turbines** make **electricity** from wind. The wind turns the big rotor blades, and a generator turns this movement into electrical energy.

gewusst: In a hurricane the wind blows at at least 118 kilometres per hour.
The bise can blow especially strongly on Lake Geneva and in winter cover everything with ice.

teile.einleitung: The World Trade Organization, the WTO for short, is an international organisation with its seat in Geneva. It sets rules for trade between countries and helps to settle trade disputes.
wichtigste: The WTO has existed since 1 January 1995 and has its seat in Geneva.
In 2025 it had 166 members.
Since 2021 Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala from Nigeria has been Director-General (as of 2026).
Important principles are most-favoured-nation treatment and national treatment.
The Doha Round of 2001 has still not been completed.
China joined the WTO in December 2001.

abschnitte.text: The **WTO** came into being on 1 January 1995 as the result of the so-called **Uruguay Round**, a long round of negotiations. It took over and extended the rules of the earlier **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade**, the GATT. Its seat is in **Geneva**, and Switzerland has been a member from the start. In 2024 the Comoros and Timor-Leste joined, so the number rose to 166 members. They account for the largest part of world trade.

Under the principle of **most-favoured-nation treatment**, a trade advantage that a country grants to one member must be granted to all members. Nobody may be treated worse than the best trading partner. Exceptions apply, for example, to **free trade agreements**. **National treatment** requires that imported goods are treated no worse than domestic ones once they have passed customs, for example with taxes or regulations.

Under the roof of the WTO there are several important agreements. The **GATT** governs trade in goods. The **GATS** governs trade in services. The **TRIPS** agreement sets minimum standards for the protection of **intellectual property**, that is, patents, trademarks and copyright. For Switzerland, with its pharmaceutical and watch industries, this protection is especially important.

The **Doha Round** began in 2001 in Qatar and was meant above all to bring advantages to developing countries. Disputes over farm subsidies and market access have so far prevented it from being concluded. In December 2001 **China** joined the WTO, and its exports then rose sharply. Since 2021 **Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**, an economist and former finance minister of Nigeria, has led the organisation (as of 2026). She is the first woman and the first person from Africa at the head, and in 2024 she was confirmed for a second term.

If members have a dispute over trade rules, they can call on the WTO's **dispute settlement**. A panel examines the case and makes a decision. Against this decision an appeal can be made to the **Appellate Body**. It needs at least three judges. Because the USA is blocking the appointment of new judges, it has been unable to take decisions since December 2019.

gewusst: The WTO building in Geneva is called the Centre William Rappard and lies right on Lake Geneva.
The WTO usually takes decisions by consensus, that is, only if no member objects.

teile.einleitung: Timbuktu is an old city in the north of Mali in West Africa. It lies close to the River Niger on the edge of the Sahara. In the Middle Ages Timbuktu was a rich trading city and a famous centre of learning.
wichtigste: Timbuktu lies in **Mali**, close to the Niger and on the edge of the **Sahara**.
The main goods traded were **salt and gold**.
The **Djinguereber Mosque** was built of mud around 1327.
In the 15th and 16th centuries Timbuktu was a centre of **learning**.
Since **1988** the city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
“To Timbuktu” means **very far away**.

abschnitte.text: Timbuktu lay in an important spot: between the **Sahara** in the north and the **River Niger** in the south. **Caravans** of camels brought salt from the desert, and **gold** came from the south. The goods were exchanged here. This is how Timbuktu became rich and well known far and wide. The city belonged in turn to great African empires such as the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire.

The famous **Djinguereber Mosque** was built of **mud** around 1327. Wooden beams stick out of the walls. They serve as scaffolding so that the walls can be re-plastered regularly, because rain slowly washes the mud away. The inhabitants do this work together. Other well-known mosques are the **Sankore Mosque** and the Sidi Yahia Mosque.

In the 15th and 16th centuries Timbuktu was a **centre of learning**. Many scholars taught religion, law, astronomy and medicine here, for example at the Sankore Mosque. To this day there are **tens of thousands of old manuscripts** in Timbuktu. Families have kept them for generations. They show how rich knowledge was in West Africa at that time.

For Europeans, Timbuktu was long considered a mysterious place that was hard to reach. That is why in German people say **“bis nach Timbuktu”** (“all the way to Timbuktu”) when something is very far away. The German explorer **Heinrich Barth** reached the city in 1853. He stayed for several months and described it in detail. His reports are still regarded as an important source.

Timbuktu was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in **1988**. Because of armed conflicts in the north of Mali, it has been on the **Red List** of endangered World Heritage since **2012**. At that time some old tombs were damaged, and they were later rebuilt. The desert also threatens the city, because sand covers the houses and streets.

gewusst: The walls of the mud mosques have to be re-plastered almost every year.
Many manuscripts from Timbuktu were hidden in chests to protect them.

teile.einleitung: The Western Schism was a split in the Catholic Church from 1378 to 1417. During this time there were two, and for a while even three, popes at once. Only the Council of Constance brought agreement.
wichtigste: The Schism lasted from 1378 to 1417.
It was triggered by the disputed election of Pope Urban VI in Rome.
The breakaway cardinals elected Clement VII, who resided in Avignon.
After the Council of Pisa in 1409 there were even three popes.
The Council of Constance ended the Schism in 1417.
The doctrine that a council stands above the pope is called conciliarism.

abschnitte.text: The word **schism** comes from Greek and means split. In the Western Schism, the Church in the west of Europe split. It was not about questions of faith but about the question of who the rightful pope was. The countries of Europe took one side or the other according to their political alliances.

In 1378 **Urban VI** was elected in Rome. The election took place under pressure from a Roman crowd. Because of his abrupt manner, most of the cardinals later declared the election invalid. In September 1378 they elected Robert of Geneva as **Clement VII**. He moved to **Avignon** in the south of France. Now there were two popes, and each had his followers.

France supported the pope in Avignon. **England** stayed loyal to the pope in Rome, partly because it was fighting France in the **Hundred Years' War**. A country's allegiance to a pope is called **obedience**. For believers this was confusing, because both popes claimed to be the right one.

To solve the problem, bishops met in 1409 at the **Council of Pisa**. They deposed both popes and elected Alexander V. But the other two did not step down. So now there were even **three popes**. The pope of the Avignon line, **Benedict XIII**, later withdrew to the castle of **Peñíscola** on the coast of Valencia and never accepted his deposition.

Only the **Council of Constance** on Lake Constance brought the solution. In 1415 **Gregory XII**, the pope of the Roman line, resigned. The others were deposed. In 1417 a new, generally recognised pope was elected. Because the popes could not agree among themselves, many theologians saw the council as the highest authority. This doctrine is called **conciliarism**.

gewusst: Constance lies right on the border with Switzerland, next to Kreuzlingen in the canton of Thurgau.
Benedict XIII held on to his claim until his death, although hardly anyone still recognised him.

teile.einleitung: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese navigator. He was the first European to find the sea route around Africa to India. In 1498 he reached the Indian port city of Calicut.
wichtigste: Vasco da Gama came from Portugal.
He was the first European to find the sea route to India.
On the way he sailed round the Cape of Good Hope.
In 1498 he arrived in Calicut in India.
Spices such as pepper made the sea route very valuable.
As early as 1488 Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the southern tip of Africa.

abschnitte.text: In the 15th century **Portugal** wanted to find a sea route to India. In Europe **spices** such as **pepper** were in great demand and expensive. Until then they had come by long overland routes and through many middlemen. Portuguese sailors therefore felt their way step by step south along the coast of Africa. In 1488 **Bartolomeu Dias** was the first to round the southern tip of Africa.

In 1497 **Vasco da Gama** set out from Lisbon with four ships. He sailed round the **Cape of Good Hope** and went north along the east coast of Africa. At Christmas he sighted a coast in present-day South Africa and named it **Natal**, after the Portuguese word for Christmas. In East Africa he found a pilot who knew the way across the Indian Ocean. In 1498 he reached **Calicut** on the west coast of India.

The voyage was long and dangerous, and many sailors died of illnesses such as **scurvy**. But the spices they brought back were worth a great deal. Portugal afterwards built trading posts in Africa and Asia and became a rich **sea power**. Vasco da Gama later travelled to India twice more. He died in India in 1524.

gewusst: The South African province of KwaZulu-Natal still bears the name that Vasco da Gama gave to a coast.
Vasco da Gama needed about two years for the voyage there and back.

teile.einleitung: Uzbekistan is a country in Central Asia. It is famous for old trading cities on the Silk Road with blue domes and minarets. Until 1991 it belonged to the Soviet Union.
wichtigste: The capital of Uzbekistan is called Tashkent.
Samarkand is a famous old trading city with blue domes.
Uzbekistan and Liechtenstein are surrounded only by landlocked countries.
The Aral Sea on the border has shrunk greatly.
A lot of cotton is grown in Uzbekistan.
The national dish, plov, is a rice dish.
Until 1991 Uzbekistan belonged to the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.text: Uzbekistan lies in **Central Asia**, between Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan and Turkmenistan. All of these neighbours themselves have no access to the open sea. Such a country is called **doubly landlocked**, and apart from Uzbekistan this now applies only to **Liechtenstein**. Large parts of the country are desert and steppe. The rivers **Amu Darya** and **Syr Darya** bring water from the mountains.

For many centuries the **Silk Road** ran through what is now Uzbekistan. Merchants brought silk, spices and other goods between China and Europe. That is why rich cities such as **Samarkand**, **Bukhara** and **Khiva** grew up. Their mosques and schools with blue domes and colourful tiles are famous to this day. The capital, **Tashkent**, is the largest city in the country.

Uzbekistan grows a lot of **cotton**. During the time of the **Soviet Union**, a great deal of water was diverted from the rivers for the fields. As a result, less and less water reached the **Aral Sea**. The lake, once one of the largest in the world, has shrunk greatly. Salt deserts were left behind, and the fishing industry collapsed.

Since 1991 Uzbekistan has been an independent state. The national language is **Uzbek**, and many people also speak Russian. Most of the inhabitants are Muslims. The national dish, **plov**, is a rice dish with meat, carrots and onions. It is often cooked in big pans for celebrations.

gewusst: On the former bed of the Aral Sea, old fishing boats now lie in the middle of the sand.
The city of Samarkand is over 2,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Wellington is the capital of New Zealand. The city lies at the southern end of the North Island on a windy strait and is known for its hills, its harbour basin and its culture.
wichtigste: Wellington has been the capital of New Zealand since 1865, before that it was Auckland.
The city lies at the southern end of the North Island on Cook Strait.
It is the southernmost capital of an independent country.
Because of the frequent wind it is called “Windy Wellington”.
The round government building is called “The Beehive”.
It is named after the Duke of Wellington, the victor of Waterloo.

abschnitte.text: Wellington is the **capital** of New Zealand, but not the largest city. The largest is **Auckland**, which was also the capital until 1865. Wellington was chosen because it lies more centrally between the North and South Islands. The **parliament** meets here. The round government building is called **The Beehive** because of its shape. The government and the ministers work in it.

Wellington lies at the southern tip of the **North Island**, on **Cook Strait**. This strait separates the North Island from the South Island. From Wellington **ferries** run to Picton on the South Island. Because the wind whistles through the strait, it is often very windy. That is why the city is called **Windy Wellington**. No other capital of an independent country lies so far south.

Wellington is very hilly. The red **Wellington Cable Car** is a **funicular railway**. It runs from the city centre up to the Botanic Garden. From the top there is a lovely view over the harbour. Many houses stand on steep slopes.

The national museum is called **Te Papa**. The name comes from the language of the **Maori**, the first inhabitants of New Zealand. In the museum you learn a lot about the nature, history and culture of the country. Wellington is also known for its film studios, in which, for example, parts of the “Lord of the Rings” films were made.

The city is named after **Arthur Wellesley**, the 1st **Duke of Wellington**. He was a British general and politician. In 1815 he defeated **Napoleon**, with his allies, at the Battle of **Waterloo**. New Zealand was a British colony at that time, so many places received British names.

gewusst: Because Wellington lies in an earthquake zone, many buildings were built to be especially earthquake-proof.
Because of its film studios, Wellington is sometimes jokingly called “Wellywood”.

teile.einleitung: Zebras are the striped wild horses of Africa. They live in herds in the savanna, and each animal has its very own stripe pattern.
wichtigste: Zebras are striped black and white.
They are closely related to the horse.
There are three species of zebra today.
Zebras eat mainly grass.
Every stripe pattern is unique.
A young zebra is called a foal.

abschnitte.text: **Zebras** belong to the **horse** family and are closely related to horses and donkeys. They live in Africa, mainly in savannas and grasslands. Today there are **three species**: the **plains zebra**, the **Grevy's zebra** and the **mountain zebra**. The plains zebra is the most common. The Grevy's zebra is the largest species and is regarded as severely endangered.

A zebra's coat is striped **black and white**. Under the coat the **skin is dark**. No zebra looks like another: **every pattern is unique**, like a fingerprint in us humans. What the stripes are for is still being researched. One well-supported explanation is that they keep off biting flies.

Zebras are plant-eaters and eat mainly **grass**. They live **in herds**, often together with wildebeest and antelopes. Many eyes see more, and so they notice dangers sooner. A **young zebra** is called a **foal**. It can walk soon after birth and recognises its mother by her pattern and her voice.

Zebras have many enemies, for example **lions**, hyenas and crocodiles. In an attack the herd **flees** quickly in a zigzag. If a zebra is cornered, it defends itself with powerful **kicks** and bites. A kick from the hard hooves can be dangerous even to a lion.

gewusst: Despite many attempts, zebras have never been properly tamed like horses.
When a herd of zebras runs together, the stripes blur and predators find it hard to pick out single animals.

teile.einleitung: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the envelope of air around the Earth. Almost all of the weather happens in it: clouds, rain, snow and thunderstorms form here. We humans live at the bottom of this layer.
wichtigste: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere.
It reaches about 8 to 17 kilometres high.
Almost all the water vapour is in it.
That is why almost all the weather happens there.
With increasing height it gets colder in the troposphere.

abschnitte.text: The **atmosphere** consists of several layers. The lowest is called the **troposphere**. It varies in thickness: at the **poles** it reaches about **8 kilometres** high, and at the **equator** about **17 kilometres**. Over Switzerland it usually ends at a height of about 11 to 12 kilometres. Its upper boundary is called the **tropopause**, and above it begins the **stratosphere** with the ozone layer.

abschnitte.titel: This is where the weather lives
abschnitte.text: Almost all the **water vapour** of the atmosphere is in the troposphere. That is why **clouds**, rain, snow and thunderstorms form here. The air is constantly in motion: it rises, sinks and is mixed. The name comes from the Greek word “tropos”, meaning turning. Large passenger aircraft often fly in the upper part of the troposphere or just above it.

In the troposphere it gets **colder** with increasing **height**, on average by about **6.5 degrees per kilometre**. You also notice this in the mountains. On the **Jungfraujoch** at about 3,450 metres, it is much colder than in Interlaken. At the tropopause the temperature can fall to **-50 °C** and below. Above that, in the stratosphere, it gets warmer again.

gewusst: Although the troposphere is so thin, it contains most of the total mass of air in the atmosphere.
Tall thundercloud towers can grow up to the tropopause and spread out there like an anvil.

teile.einleitung: The Mediterranean island of Cyprus has been divided since 1974. In the south live mainly Greek Cypriots, in the north mainly Turkish Cypriots. The Cyprus conflict has still not been resolved.
wichtigste: Cyprus became independent from Britain in 1960.
In 1974 Greek nationalists staged a coup, after which Turkey intervened militarily.
Since then the island has been divided, and a UN buffer zone separates the parts.
The buffer zone is called the Green Line and also divides the capital, Nicosia.
Only Turkey recognises the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.
In 2004 the Greek Cypriots clearly rejected the Annan Plan.

abschnitte.text: On **Cyprus**, **Greek Cypriots** and **Turkish Cypriots** have lived for centuries. The Greek Cypriots are the larger group. For a long time the island belonged to the Ottoman Empire, and later it was under British rule. In **1960** Cyprus became **independent from Britain**. Soon there were tensions and violence between the communities. That is why the UN sent peacekeeping troops in 1964.

In **July 1974**, **Greek nationalists**, with the support of the then military government of Greece, overthrew the Cypriot president. Their aim was the union of Cyprus with Greece. **Turkey** saw the Turkish Cypriots as threatened and intervened **militarily**. Turkish troops occupied the north of the island. Many people had to leave their homes and flee to the other side.

Since then a **UN buffer zone** has separated the island. It is called the **Green Line** and is monitored by UN troops. This border runs right through the capital, **Nicosia**, which has therefore been a divided city since 1974. Since 2003 there have been crossing points where people can pass from one side to the other.

In the south lies the **Republic of Cyprus**. It is internationally recognised and has been a member of the European Union since 2004. In the north the Turkish Cypriots proclaimed the **Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus** in 1983. It is recognised as a state **only by Turkey**. Both sides see the history and the solution of the conflict differently.

The UN tried several times to reunite the island. The best-known proposal was the **Annan Plan**, named after the then UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan. In **2004** both communities voted on it. The Turkish Cypriots voted mostly in favour, while the **Greek Cypriots clearly rejected it**. The plan therefore did not come into force. Later talks too, including in Switzerland, have so far brought no solution.

gewusst: The UN peacekeeping force on Cyprus is one of the oldest UN peace missions.
In the buffer zone in Nicosia stand houses and shops that have stood empty and almost unchanged since 1974.

teile.einleitung: Xochimilco is a district in the south of Mexico City. It is famous for its canals and for an ancient farming method of the Aztecs.
wichtigste: Xochimilco lies in the south of Mexico City.
It is known for a network of canals.
The chinampas are artificially made garden islands.
This farming method dates from the time of the Aztecs.
Xochimilco is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In the area of Mexico City there used to be a large lake district. In **Xochimilco**, many **canals** are left over from it. The name comes from the Nahuatl language and means roughly “place of the flower fields”. Today families and tourists travel through the canals in brightly painted boats, the **trajineras**. Together with the historic centre of Mexico City, Xochimilco is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The **chinampas** are artificially made **garden islands** in the canals. People piled up mud from the lake bed and plant remains and fixed the edges with willows and posts. In this way very fertile fields arose in the middle of the water. The **Aztecs** already grew maize, beans, vegetables and flowers in this way. Some farmers still use the method today.

The canals are the home of the **axolotl**, a special salamander that lives wild almost only here. The growing city, polluted water and alien fish threaten it greatly. Conservationists and farmers are working together to preserve the chinampas and the canals.

gewusst: The axolotl can regrow lost legs and even parts of its heart.

teile.einleitung: We speak of water stress when more water is used in an area than is available in the long term. Experts measure it with various indicators, and more and more regions around the world are affected.
wichtigste: Under the Falkenmark indicator, there is water stress below 1,700 cubic metres of renewable water per person per year.
Below 1,000 cubic metres it is called water scarcity, and below 500 absolute water scarcity.
Agriculture takes about 70 per cent of the world's fresh water.
The Aqueduct Atlas rates a withdrawal of over 80 per cent of the available water as “extremely high”.
The Middle East and North Africa are the most strongly affected.
Cape Town faced a “Day Zero” in 2018, and Chennai went through a severe water crisis in 2019.

abschnitte.text: The Swedish hydrologist **Malin Falkenmark** developed a simple indicator. It measures how much **renewable water** is available per person per year. Below 1,700 cubic metres we speak of **water stress**, below 1,000 of **water scarcity** and below 500 of **absolute water scarcity**. Then there is hardly enough water for basic needs and agriculture. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres.

Other indicators compare how much water is withdrawn and how much is there. Indicator 6.4.2 in **UN Sustainable Development Goal 6** puts fresh water withdrawal in relation to renewable resources, minus what nature itself needs. The **Aqueduct Atlas** of the World Resources Institute calls a withdrawal of over 80 per cent “extremely high”. Then there is hardly any reserve for drought years. The most strongly affected are the **Middle East** and **North Africa**, where there is little rain, a lot of evaporation and a growing population.

Worldwide about **70 per cent** of fresh water withdrawal goes to **agriculture**, mainly for irrigating fields. That is why sparing irrigation, for example with drip hoses, is an important key against water stress. The rest is used by industry and households. Sometimes, though, the water is not really lacking: with **economic water scarcity**, there is enough rainfall, but money, pipes, stores and treatment are lacking. This affects many regions in Africa south of the Sahara.

In **Cape Town** in South Africa the reservoirs were almost empty in 2018 after several drought years. The city announced a possible **Day Zero**, on which the taps would be turned off. Strict saving measures and rain prevented that day. In the Indian city of millions **Chennai**, the four main reservoirs were almost empty in 2019. After a weak monsoon and overuse of groundwater, water had to be brought by trains and tankers.

Switzerland is regarded as the **water tower of Europe** and, by comparison, has a great deal of water. Even so, hot, dry summers can lead to problems here too. Then the levels of rivers and lakes fall, and some communes call on people to save water. With climate change and melting glaciers, the subject is becoming more important in Switzerland too.

gewusst: One cubic metre of water is roughly the content of seven full bathtubs.
In Cape Town in 2018, for a time people were allowed to use only 50 litres of water per person per day.

teile.einleitung: Urbanisation means that more and more people live in cities. Cities grow, while fewer people live in the countryside. It is one of the big changes in the world.
wichtigste: Urbanisation means that more and more people live in cities.
The movement of people from the countryside to the city is called rural exodus.
Pull factors such as more jobs draw people to the city.
Push factors such as a lack of work drive people away from the countryside.
According to a UN forecast of 2018, about 68 per cent of people will live in cities in 2050.
When people move to the suburbs, it is called suburbanisation.
In Africa the smallest share of people live in cities.

abschnitte.text: In the past most people lived in the countryside and worked in farming. Today more than half of the world's population lives in cities. According to a **UN** forecast of 2018, in 2050 the figure will be about **68 per cent**. Cities are growing especially fast in Asia and Africa. In **Africa**, however, the smallest share of people has so far lived in cities.

Why do people move to the city? Experts distinguish two kinds of reasons. **Pull factors** attract, for example **more jobs**, schools, hospitals and leisure activities. **Push factors** drive people away, such as **a lack of work in the countryside** or poor services. The movement of people from the countryside to the cities is called **rural exodus**.

Many people move from the city centre to the **suburbs**, where it is quieter and there is more space. This is called **suburbanisation**. Often, though, they keep on working in the city. Someone who travels back and forth every day between home and workplace is a **commuter**. In Switzerland, trains are therefore often very full in the morning and in the evening.

When settlements spread out into the landscape without order, it is called **urban sprawl**. Meadows, fields and nature are lost in the process. More roads and pipes are also needed. In Switzerland, **spatial planning** is meant to make sure that land is used sparingly. Building is meant to take place mainly where settlements already exist.

gewusst: Some giant cities have more inhabitants than the whole of Switzerland.
Only since about 2007 have more people worldwide lived in cities than in the countryside.

teile.einleitung: Vaca Muerta is a huge layer of rock in the province of Neuquén in Argentina. It holds large amounts of oil and natural gas. They are extracted by a controversial method, fracking.
wichtigste: Vaca Muerta is Spanish and means “dead cow”.
The formation lies mainly in the province of Neuquén in Patagonia.
It consists of shale rock that contains oil and natural gas.
It is extracted by fracking.
Vaca Muerta is one of the largest deposits of this kind in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Vaca Muerta** means “dead cow” in Spanish. It is the name of a rock formation in the west of Argentina, mainly in the province of **Neuquén** in Patagonia. It formed a very long time ago from deposits on the floor of a sea. Today it is a dense **shale rock**, in whose tiny pores **oil** and **natural gas** are trapped. The deposits are among the largest of their kind in the world.

Because the rock is so dense, the oil does not flow out by itself. In **fracking**, water, sand and additives are therefore forced at high pressure into deep boreholes. This creates fine cracks through which oil and gas flow to the borehole. For Argentina, Vaca Muerta is very important economically. Critics warn of the high **water use**, of pollution and of the consequences for the climate and the local population.

gewusst: The formation is named after a mountain in the area, the Sierra de la Vaca Muerta.

teile.einleitung: The water on Earth is constantly on the move: it evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain or snow and flows back into the sea. This eternal journey is called the water cycle.
wichtigste: The energy of the sun drives the water cycle.
Most water evaporates over the oceans.
Oceans cover about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface.
Water vapour cools at height and forms clouds.
On average, water stays in the atmosphere for only about 9 days.
In groundwater or in the oceans, water can stay for hundreds to thousands of years.

abschnitte.text: The **sun** warms seas, lakes, soils and plants. In the process water **evaporates**: it turns into invisible **water vapour** and rises into the air. Without the sun's energy the cycle would stand still. Because the **oceans** cover about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface, most of the evaporated water comes from the sea. Plants also give off a lot of water into the air through their leaves.

The higher the air rises, the colder it gets. The water vapour then **condenses** into tiny droplets or ice crystals, and **clouds** form. When the drops become heavy enough, they fall to Earth as **precipitation**: as rain, snow or hail. On average a water molecule stays in the atmosphere for only about **9 days** before it falls down again.

Some of the rain flows straight into the sea via streams and rivers. Another part soaks into the ground and becomes **groundwater**. There water can often stay for hundreds or thousands of years. In the mountains water is stored as snow and in **glacier ice**. Only when it melts does it flow on.

In Switzerland a lot of rain and snow falls, because damp air rises at the **Alps** and rains out. That is why Switzerland is often called the **water tower of Europe**. Here great rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône and the Inn rise. Their water flows as far as the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. On the way it is used by people, animals and plants.

gewusst: The water you drink today may once have been part of a cloud over the Atlantic.
The total amount of water on Earth stays almost the same, it only keeps changing its place and state.

teile.einleitung: Tunisia is a country in the north of Africa on the Mediterranean. In ancient times the mighty city of Carthage lay here, and here in 2010 the “Arab Spring” began. Today Tunisia is also a popular holiday country.
wichtigste: The capital of Tunisia is Tunis.
The ancient city of Carthage lay near present-day Tunis.
Tunisia was a French protectorate from 1881 and became independent in 1956.
At the end of 2010 the protests of the “Arab Spring” began here.
Djerba is the large holiday island in the south.
In El Djem stands a huge Roman amphitheatre.

abschnitte.text: **Tunisia** lies in **North Africa** between Algeria and Libya. To the north and east it borders the **Mediterranean**. The capital, **Tunis**, is also the largest city, and the country bears its name. In Tunisia lies the **northernmost point** of the African mainland, a cape near **Bizerte**. From there it is not far to Sicily. The official language is **Arabic**, and many people also speak French.

Near present-day Tunis lay the ancient city of **Carthage**. It was founded by the **Phoenicians** and fought against Rome in the **Punic Wars**. Its most famous general was **Hannibal**, who crossed the Alps with elephants. Later the area belonged to the Roman Empire. The **amphitheatre of El Djem**, one of the largest in the Roman world, dates from this time. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

From **1881** Tunisia was a French **protectorate**. This means that France controlled the country. In **1956** Tunisia became independent, in the same year as its neighbour Morocco. Afterwards it became a republic.

In **December 2010** large protests against the government began in Tunisia. The people demanded more freedom and better living conditions. In **January 2011** President **Ben Ali** had to leave the country. The protests spread to other Arab countries. This movement is called the **Arab Spring**. In 2015 a Tunisian quartet of four organisations received the Nobel Peace Prize for its work for dialogue in the country.

In the south lies the holiday island of **Djerba** in the Gulf of Gabès. It is the largest island in North Africa and popular with tourists. Further inland the **Sahara** begins. There lies the **Chott el Djerid**, a huge **salt lake**. It is dried out for most of the year, and then a crust of salt glitters in the sun.

gewusst: Scenes for the “Star Wars” films were shot in the south of Tunisia, and a desert planet is named after the town of Tataouine.
In Matmata some people live in cave dwellings dug into the ground around deep pits.

teile.einleitung: The United Arab Emirates, or UAE for short, are a state on the Arabian Peninsula in Asia. They consist of seven emirates and were founded in 1971. They are known for desert, oil and modern cities such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi.
wichtigste: The UAE consist of seven emirates.
The capital is Abu Dhabi.
The state was founded in 1971.
The UAE lie mainly on the Persian Gulf in Asia.
The currency is called the dirham.
The falcon is an important national symbol.
The Palm Jumeirah is an artificial island in the shape of a palm tree.

abschnitte.text: The UAE lie in the east of the **Arabian Peninsula** and so in **Asia**. They consist of **seven emirates**: Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain, Ras al-Khaimah and **Fujairah**. Each emirate is led by a ruling family. The state was founded in **1971**. Most of the emirates lie on the **Persian Gulf**, whereas Fujairah lies almost entirely on the Gulf of Oman.

The capital is **Abu Dhabi**, and the best-known city is **Dubai**. There stands the **Burj Khalifa**, the tallest building in the world. Off the coast the **Palm Jumeirah** was built up, an artificial island in the shape of a palm tree. Since 2017 there has been a branch of the Paris **Louvre** in Abu Dhabi. Many of these buildings went up in only a few decades.

Before the discovery of **oil**, people lived mainly from fishing, trade and pearl diving. The oil brought great wealth. Today the emirates are also trying to earn money from trade, airports and **tourism**. The currency is called the **dirham**. A large part of the people in the country are workers from other countries.

The **falcon** is an important national symbol. Falconry, that is, hunting with trained falcons, has a long tradition. Camel racing is also popular. The national language is **Arabic**, and the state religion is Islam. In summer it often gets hotter than 40 degrees.

gewusst: In the UAE there is even a ski hall in the middle of the desert.
In the UAE falcons sometimes have their own passport for travelling.

teile.einleitung: An Advent calendar helps you count the days until Christmas. Most have 24 little doors, one for each day from 1 to 24 December. The custom comes from Germany and is popular all over the world today.
wichtigste: An Advent calendar usually has 24 little doors.
You open one door every day from 1 to 24 December.
Behind the doors there is often chocolate, pictures or small presents.
In the past people simply drew chalk lines on the door or wall.
The first Advent calendars appeared in Germany in the 19th century.
In many Swiss villages there are Advent windows.

abschnitte.text: For children, the wait for Christmas often seems long. The **Advent calendar** makes the wait shorter. Every day you may open a **little door**, from 1 to 24 December. In this way you can see exactly how many days are left until **Christmas Eve**. That is why an Advent calendar usually has **24 little doors**.

The first Advent calendars appeared in the **19th century** in **Germany**. At that time they were very simple. Some families drew a **chalk line** on the door or wall for each day until Christmas Eve. Every day the children were allowed to rub out one line. Others hung up a religious picture each day. Later, **printed** calendars became popular.

abschnitte.titel: What is behind the little doors?
abschnitte.text: In many shop-bought Advent calendars there is a piece of **chocolate** behind every door. Others show **pictures** or little stories. Many families also make their own calendar with little bags or boxes, filled with **small presents**. Today there are also calendars with toys, tea or puzzles.

In many **Swiss villages** there is a special custom: the **Advent windows**. Different families each decorate one window. On a particular day in December this window lights up for the first time. In this way an **Advent calendar for the whole village** comes about. Often there is tea or punch as well, and the neighbours meet in the evening.

gewusst: Some towns turn the windows of a large building into a giant Advent calendar.
There are also Advent calendars with only 4 little doors, one for each Sunday in Advent.

teile.einleitung: The UNHCR is the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. It protects and supports people who have had to flee war and persecution, and it stands up for stateless people. Its headquarters are in Geneva.
wichtigste: The UNHCR was founded by the UN General Assembly in 1950.
The basis of its work is the Geneva Refugee Convention of 1951.
Besides refugees, it also protects stateless people.
It received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
It is financed mainly by voluntary contributions.
World Refugee Day is on 20 June.

abschnitte.text: The **UN General Assembly** decided to found the **UNHCR** in December **1950**, and its work began in January 1951. Originally it was only meant to help the many refugees in Europe after the Second World War for a few years. But there were always new crises, and so the UNHCR became a permanent organisation. Its headquarters are in **Geneva**. Besides refugees, it also has the task of protecting **stateless people**, that is, people who are not recognised as citizens by any state.

The basis of the work is the **Geneva Refugee Convention**. It was adopted in Geneva on **28 July 1951**. It sets out who counts as a **refugee** and what rights they have. Originally it applied only to events before 1951 and could be limited to Europe. The **New York Protocol** of **1967** lifted this limit in time and place. Since then the convention has applied worldwide.

A core part of refugee protection is the principle of **non-refoulement**. This is French and means roughly “not to send back”. Refugees must not be sent back to a country where they face **persecution**. This principle is set out in **Article 33** of the Geneva Refugee Convention. The UNHCR makes sure that states keep to it.

The UNHCR helps people on the run with **shelter**, water, food and medical care. It supports states with asylum procedures and looks for lasting solutions, such as returning to the home country or a new home. According to the “Global Trends” report, at the end of **2024** about **123 million** people worldwide had been forcibly displaced. They include refugees, asylum seekers and people who had to flee within their own country. For **Palestine refugees** in the Middle East, a separate relief agency, **UNRWA**, has been responsible since 1949.

Only a very small part of the budget comes from the regular UN budget. Almost all of it is **voluntary contributions** from governments, the EU, companies and private individuals. Switzerland also supports the UNHCR. For its work the UNHCR twice received the **Nobel Peace Prize**, in **1954** and **1981**. Every year on **20 June**, the UN's **World Refugee Day** draws attention to the situation of refugees. It was first held in 2001.

gewusst: Prisoners of war are looked after not by the UNHCR but by the International Committee of the Red Cross, which is also based in Geneva.
The UNHCR is one of a few organisations that have received the Nobel Peace Prize more than once.

teile.einleitung: The tourism balance shows how much money a country earns from foreign visitors and how much its own inhabitants spend on trips abroad. It is part of a country's balance of payments. This shows whether a country gains or loses money through tourism.
wichtigste: Tourism balance: **income** from foreign visitors minus **spending** by locals abroad.
It belongs to the **services balance**, a part of the current account.
Visitors' spending in the country counts like an **export of services**.
**Spain** has a large surplus, and **Germany** traditionally a large deficit.
A **strong franc** worsens Switzerland's tourism balance.
Chinese travellers spent the most in the world on foreign travel in 2023.

abschnitte.text: The tourism balance compares two amounts: what **foreign visitors** spend in the country and what **locals** spend on trips abroad. You calculate income minus spending. An example: a country earns 18 billion francs from visitors, and its inhabitants spend 21 billion abroad. Then the balance is 18 minus 21, which is **minus 3 billion francs**. The balance is negative, so it is a **deficit**.

abschnitte.titel: Part of the balance of payments
abschnitte.text: The **balance of payments** shows all of a country's economic transactions with the rest of the world. Travel counts as a cross-border **service**. That is why the tourism balance belongs to the **services balance**, and this is part of the **current account**. When American tourists spend money in Switzerland, they are buying Swiss services. Economically this counts like an **export**, because foreign currency comes into the country.

**Spain** receives dozens of millions of foreign visitors every year. The income far exceeds what Spaniards spend on travel, and the balance is strongly **positive**. **Germany**, on the other hand, traditionally has one of the largest **deficits** in the world. Germans travel abroad a great deal, but the country attracts fewer foreign holidaymakers. According to the World Tourism Organization, travellers from **China** spent the most on foreign travel in 2023, ahead of those from the USA.

The **exchange rate** has a big influence on the tourism balance. When the **Swiss franc** is strong, holidays in Switzerland become more expensive for foreign visitors when they convert their money. At the same time, trips abroad become cheaper for people in Switzerland. So fewer visitors tend to come, and locals tend to travel abroad more. That is why the tourism balance gets **worse** when the franc is strong.

gewusst: Even a coffee that a visitor from Japan buys in Lucerne counts in the statistics as a Swiss export.
Countries with many visitors and little foreign travel by their inhabitants often have large surpluses.

teile.einleitung: Toronto is the largest city in Canada and lies on the shore of Lake Ontario. It is the capital of the province of Ontario, but not the capital of the country. Toronto is regarded as one of the most diverse cities in the world.
wichtigste: Toronto is the capital of the **province of Ontario**, and the national capital is Ottawa.
Its landmark is the **CN Tower**, about 553 metres high.
About half of the inhabitants were **born outside Canada**.
The **Toronto Raptors** became NBA champions in 2019.
The **Hockey Hall of Fame** is in Toronto.
**Niagara Falls** is only about 130 kilometres away.

abschnitte.text: Toronto lies on the north shore of **Lake Ontario**, one of the five Great Lakes of North America. The city is the capital of the **province of Ontario**, and the provincial parliament meets here. The capital of Canada as a whole, however, is **Ottawa**. Off the city centre lie the **Toronto Islands**, a car-free group of islands with parks and beaches. You can reach them in a few minutes by ferry.

The landmark of Toronto is the **CN Tower**, about 553 metres high. The television tower opened in 1976. For over 30 years it was the tallest free-standing structure in the world. From the viewing platform you can see far across Lake Ontario. Part of the floor is made of glass, so you can look straight down.

Toronto is regarded as one of the most **multicultural cities** in the world. About half of the inhabitants were born outside Canada. Over **150 languages** are spoken in the city. There are districts such as Chinatown, Little Italy or Greektown with their own shops and restaurants. Besides English, you hear many other languages in everyday life.

In 2019 the **Toronto Raptors** became the first team from outside the USA to win the **NBA championship**. They are the only Canadian team in the North American professional basketball league. Ice hockey is especially popular in Canada. The **Hockey Hall of Fame**, the museum of ice hockey, is in Toronto. The famous **Stanley Cup** is also displayed there when it is not with the winning team.

Only about 130 kilometres from Toronto lies **Niagara Falls**. It is on the border between Canada and the USA, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. By car you can reach it in about an hour and a half. Millions of people visit the waterfalls every year.

gewusst: The CN Tower is sometimes struck by lightning, but it is well protected against it.
Toronto has a long underground network of pedestrian walkways with shops, called PATH.

teile.einleitung: Western Sahara is a desert region on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa. Since Spain withdrew in the 1970s, it has been disputed who the territory belongs to.
wichtigste: Until 1975/76 the territory was the Spanish colony of Spanish Sahara.
In the Green March in November 1975, about 350,000 Moroccans moved into Western Sahara.
The Polisario proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic in 1976.
Mauritania withdrew from its part in 1979.
In the 1980s Morocco built a sand wall over 2,000 km long.
Since 1991 the UN mission MINURSO has monitored the ceasefire.

abschnitte.text: Until the 1970s the territory was called **Spanish Sahara** and was a colony of Spain. The native population are called **Sahrawis**. In the **Madrid Accords** of 1975, Spain handed over the administration to **Morocco** and **Mauritania**. In 1975/76 Spain withdrew. Since then it has been disputed who Western Sahara belongs to.

abschnitte.titel: The Green March and the Polisario
abschnitte.text: In November 1975 King **Hassan II** called for the **Green March**. About 350,000 Moroccans moved into Western Sahara to underline Morocco's claim. Green stands here for Islam. The liberation movement **Frente Polisario**, on the other hand, fights for the independence of the Sahrawis. On 27 February 1976 it proclaimed the **Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic**.

After Spain's withdrawal, fighting broke out. **Mauritania** made peace in 1979 after attacks by the Polisario and gave up its part. Morocco then took over this area as well. In the 1980s Morocco built a **sand wall** over 2,000 kilometres long, also called a berm. It is secured with mines and separates the Moroccan-controlled area from the part that the Polisario controls.

Since **1991** the UN mission **MINURSO** has monitored the ceasefire. Originally it was also supposed to organise a **referendum**, a vote of the population on the future of the territory. This vote has still not taken place. Morocco regards Western Sahara as part of its country and proposes autonomy. The Polisario demands independence instead. Many countries are working for a solution, but the positions are far apart.

Since the fighting after 1975, many Sahrawis have lived in **refugee camps** near **Tindouf** in the south-west of Algeria. Some families have lived there for decades. They depend heavily on help from outside, for example for food. **Algeria** supports the Polisario.

gewusst: The sand wall in Western Sahara is one of the longest fortifications in the world.
Western Sahara is very thinly populated, and most of it is desert.

teile.einleitung: “On the Origin of Species” is a book by the English naturalist Charles Darwin. It appeared in 1859 and explained how living things change over a long time. It is regarded as one of the most important books in science.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin published the book in 1859.
In it he explains evolution through natural selection.
Darwin made important observations on his voyage on the “Beagle”.
The Galápagos Islands also gave him important clues.
Darwin worked on his ideas for over 20 years.

abschnitte.text: As a young man, **Charles Darwin** travelled around the world from 1831 to 1836 on the ship **“Beagle”**. He collected plants, animals and fossils. His observations on the **Galápagos Islands** are especially well known. There he saw that animals on different islands differ slightly, for example finches and tortoises. Back in England he thought about these observations for over 20 years.

Darwin recognised that living things of one species are never quite identical. Those that are better adapted to their surroundings are more likely to survive and have more offspring. These characteristics are passed on. In this way species change over a very long time. Darwin called this **natural selection**. From it came the **theory of evolution**.

Almost at the same time, the researcher **Alfred Russel Wallace** came up with a similar idea. That is why Darwin published his book in **1859**. It was widely read straight away and fiercely discussed. At that time many people believed that all species were unchangeable. Today evolution is one of the most important foundations of **biology**.

gewusst: The first edition of the book was sold out on the very first day of sale.
Darwin had originally studied medicine and theology before he became a naturalist.

teile.einleitung: A waterfall forms where a river or stream plunges over a step of rock into the depths. There are waterfalls all over the world, from small mountain streams to enormous falls that you can hear for kilometres.
wichtigste: A waterfall often forms where hard rock lies over softer rock.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest waterfall on Earth, at about 980 m.
The Tugela Falls in South Africa are often regarded as the second highest.
The Horseshoe Falls are the largest of the three Niagara Falls and lie mostly in Canada.
The Khone Falls of the Mekong in Laos are regarded as the widest waterfalls in the world.
The Trümmelbach Falls in the Lauterbrunnen valley plunge down inside a mountain.

abschnitte.text: Often a **hard layer of rock** lies over **softer rock**. The water wears away the soft rock below faster, which is called **erosion**. The hard edge is left standing as a step, and the water plunges over it. In time the edge breaks off again and again, and the waterfall slowly moves upstream. In the Alps, glaciers too have created many steep valley walls over which streams fall.

The highest waterfall on Earth is **Angel Falls** in Venezuela. It plunges about 979 m from a table mountain, of which over 800 m is in free fall. The **Tugela Falls** in the Drakensberg in South Africa are often regarded as the second highest. They fall in several steps for about 950 m. With falls this high, part of the water turns into fine spray on the way.

The **Niagara Falls** on the border between Canada and the USA consist of three falls. The horseshoe-shaped **Horseshoe Falls** lies for the most part on the Canadian side and carries the most water. The **Khone Falls** of the Mekong in Laos are spread over many steps and islands across a width of over 10 km. They are regarded as the widest waterfalls in the world and prevent ships from travelling the whole river.

In the **Lauterbrunnen valley** in the Bernese Oberland there are numerous waterfalls. Special among them are the **Trümmelbach Falls**: the stream has eaten a gorge into the rock and plunges down in several steps inside the mountain. It carries meltwater from the **Eiger**, **Mönch** and **Jungfrau**. The **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen are also well known, one of the largest waterfalls in Europe.

In Iceland **Gullfoss** is very famous. Its name means “golden waterfall”. It plunges in two steps into a deep gorge of the river **Hvítá**. In sunshine rainbows often form in the spray. Gullfoss is one of the best-known sights of Iceland.

gewusst: Angel Falls is named after the American pilot Jimmie Angel, who made it known from the air in the 1930s.
The Trümmelbach Falls can only be visited by a tunnel lift in the mountain.

teile.einleitung: The tundra is a treeless, cold landscape in the far north, near the polar regions. Only low plants such as mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs grow there. Despite the cold, many animals live in the tundra, for example reindeer, lemmings and Arctic foxes.
wichtigste: The tundra lies in the far north, near the polar regions.
Mainly mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs grow there.
It is too cold for trees for almost the whole year.
Deeper down, the ground always stays frozen, which is called permafrost.
The summer is short and cool.
Reindeer travel through the tundra in large herds.

abschnitte.text: The **tundra** lies in the far north of Europe, Asia and North America, right next to the permanent ice. It is **cold** there most of the time. The **summer** is short and cool and lasts only a few weeks. Trees need enough warmth to grow, and for that it is too cold in the tundra. That is why the landscape is wide and **treeless**.

In the tundra the ground thaws only a little at the top in summer. Below that it stays frozen all year round. This permanently frozen ground is called **permafrost**. The meltwater cannot seep away. That is why many **pools** and swamps form in summer. Countless mosquitoes then hatch there.

Mainly **mosses**, **lichens** and **dwarf shrubs** grow in the tundra. They stay close to the ground and so duck down out of the wind and the cold. In the short summer many colourful flowers bloom. The plants have to hurry, because it will soon be cold again. Berries such as bilberries also grow in the tundra.

The **reindeer** travels through the tundra in large herds and eats lichens and mosses. The **lemming** is a small rodent whose numbers vary greatly. In some years lemmings multiply in huge numbers, after which their numbers collapse again. Many predators and birds of prey live on them, such as the snowy owl. The **Arctic fox** usually has a brown-grey coat in summer, and in winter it turns **white** and very thick. This makes it well camouflaged in the snow.

In Switzerland too there is a landscape that resembles the tundra: **high up in the Alps**. Above the **tree line** it is too cold for trees. There only low plants, mosses and lichens grow. That is why people also speak of **alpine tundra**. There is permafrost, too, in the Swiss Alps at high altitudes.

gewusst: Reindeer lichen is not a true plant but a partnership between a fungus and an alga.
In summer many migratory birds fly thousands of kilometres to the tundra to raise their young there.

teile.einleitung: Under Yellowstone National Park in the USA lies a huge volcano. Its caldera is an enormous collapse basin that formed in an eruption about 630,000 years ago.
wichtigste: A caldera is a large basin that collapses after an eruption.
In about 2.1 million years Yellowstone has had three big caldera-forming eruptions.
The biggest was the Huckleberry Ridge eruption with about 2,500 km³ of material.
The present caldera formed about 630,000 years ago.
The magma reservoir today is mostly solid.
A hydrothermal explosion is much more likely than a supervolcano eruption.

abschnitte.text: In a very large volcanic eruption, so much magma is thrown out of the depths that the ground above it collapses. A huge basin forms, the **caldera**. The **Yellowstone Caldera** is about 70 by 45 kilometres in size. Because it is so huge, you can hardly recognise it from the ground, and it only becomes clearly visible on maps and aerial photographs. Beneath it lies a **hotspot**, a place with especially hot rock in the Earth's mantle.

In the last about **2.1 million years**, Yellowstone has had **three** big caldera-forming eruptions. The first and **largest** was the **Huckleberry Ridge eruption** about 2.1 million years ago, with about **2,500 km³** of material. About 1.3 million years ago the Mesa Falls eruption followed. The last, the Lava Creek eruption, formed the present caldera **about 630,000 years ago**. In between and afterwards there were many smaller lava flows.

The hotspot stays in place while the North American plate slowly slides over it. In this way a chain of old volcanic centres arose over millions of years. This track can be seen today as the **Snake River Plain** in **Idaho**, a broad, flat plain. The youngest centres lie in the north-east, at present-day Yellowstone.

The **Yellowstone Volcano Observatory** of the United States Geological Survey (**USGS**) monitors the volcano with instruments for earthquakes and ground movements. In the caldera there are two domes, **Sour Creek** and **Mallard Lake**, which measurably rise and fall. According to present measurements, the **magma reservoir is mostly solid** and contains only a little melt.

You often read that Yellowstone is “overdue” for a major eruption. Experts consider this wrong, because **eruptions do not follow a fixed rhythm**. Much more likely are smaller events. These include a **hydrothermal explosion**: hot water underground suddenly turns to steam and throws rock and mud into the air. Such explosions have already left several craters in the park.

gewusst: Ash from the Huckleberry Ridge eruption was found in far-off parts of the USA.
The many geysers and hot springs in the park are driven by the heat of the volcano.

teile.einleitung: Clouds look like cotton wool, feathers or grey blankets. They consist of tiny water droplets or ice crystals and bring us rain and snow.
wichtigste: Clouds consist of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Cumulus clouds look like puffs of cotton wool.
Cirrus clouds are thin and float very high up.
Stratus clouds cover the whole sky with grey.
When the droplets become too heavy, precipitation falls.
The wind moves the clouds across the sky.

abschnitte.text: The sun makes water evaporate from seas, lakes and plants. The invisible **water vapour** rises with warm air. At height it is colder, and the vapour turns into tiny **droplets** or **ice crystals**. Many billions of them together form a **cloud**. Because the **wind** moves the air, the clouds drift across the sky.

**Cumulus clouds** look like white puffs of cotton wool and often form on fine summer days. **Cirrus clouds** are thin and feathery and float very high up, where they consist of ice crystals. **Stratus clouds** cover the whole sky like a grey blanket. Clouds that bring a lot of rain are mostly **dark grey**. Huge, towering clouds can bring thunderstorms.

In a cloud the droplets collide and grow bigger. When they become **too heavy**, the air can no longer carry them, and it **rains**. If it is cold enough, snow falls. In thunderclouds hailstones can also form. Rain, snow and hail together are called **precipitation**.

The white streaks that aircraft leave high in the sky are called **contrails**. The engines give off hot, damp exhaust gases. In the icy cold at great height, the water vapour freezes at once into ice crystals. Sometimes the streaks vanish quickly, and sometimes they stay for a long time and spread out like cirrus clouds.

gewusst: A single large cumulus cloud can contain many tonnes of water.
Fog is really a cloud that lies directly on the ground.

teile.einleitung: The world population is the number of all the people who live on Earth. In 2025 it was about 8 billion, which is more than eight hundred times as many as Switzerland has inhabitants. Only a good 200 years ago, only about one billion people lived on Earth.
wichtigste: About 8 billion people live on Earth (as of 2025).
About 60 per cent of people live in Asia.
India and China are the countries with the most inhabitants.
Monaco is the most densely populated state in the world.
Population density is calculated as inhabitants divided by area.
The world population is growing more slowly today than 50 years ago.
About 9 million people live in Switzerland (as of 2024).

abschnitte.text: For a long time the number of people grew only very slowly. Only around the year 1800 did about one billion people live on Earth.
