Thanks to better food, hygiene and medicine, fewer children died after that, and the population grew faster and faster. According to the UN, the mark of **8 billion** was passed in November 2022. Experts also call the rapid growth since the 20th century the **population explosion**.

Most people live in **Asia**, about 60 per cent. The most populous countries are **India** and China, which each have over 1.4 billion inhabitants. India overtook China in 2023. After them, a long way behind, come the USA, Indonesia and Pakistan. In Africa the population is growing fastest today, whereas in Europe it is hardly growing at all.

**Population density** shows how many people live on average on one square kilometre. It is calculated as the number of inhabitants divided by the area. A country with 1,000,000 inhabitants and 5,000 square kilometres therefore has 200 inhabitants per square kilometre. The most densely populated is **Monaco**, where almost 40,000 people live on about 2 square kilometres. Mongolia, Australia and Canada, on the other hand, are very thinly populated.

Today women have fewer children on average worldwide than in the past, so the population is growing more slowly. The UN estimates that the world population will reach its peak in the 2080s, at a good 10 billion people. In many rich countries people are getting older and older on average, which is called **population ageing**. In many African countries, on the other hand, a large part of the population is still very young.

In Switzerland live about **9 million people** (as of 2024). The population grows mainly because people immigrate from other countries. Because the Alps are hardly inhabited, most people crowd onto the Central Plateau. There the population density is much higher than the average for the whole country, which lies at a good 200 inhabitants per square kilometre.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many people live on average on one square kilometre.
How many children are born in relation to the population.
How old people become on average.
The share of older people in a country keeps growing.

gewusst: Every year on 11 July is the UN's World Population Day.
Going from 1 billion to 2 billion people took over 100 years, whereas going from 7 to 8 billion took only about 11 years.
In Monaco almost 20,000 people live on one square kilometre, in Switzerland a good 200.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a kingdom in South-East Asia with Bangkok as its capital. The country is known for golden temples, elephants, beaches and fine food. Many people from Switzerland spend their holidays there.
wichtigste: The national animal of Thailand is the **Asian elephant**.
The currency is called the **baht**.
People greet each other with the **wai**: put your hands together in front of your chest and bow your head.
Most people are **Buddhists**.
Thailand was the only country in South-East Asia that was **never a European colony**.
King **Bhumibol** studied in Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: The **Asian elephant** is the national animal of Thailand. In the past, elephants worked in the forest and carried heavy tree trunks. Today many live in protected areas and elephant camps. In the north there are mountains and forests, and in the south long beaches and islands. The climate is warm, with a rainy season and a dry season.

Most people in Thailand are **Buddhists**. All over the country there are thousands of temples with golden Buddha figures. Many young men live for a time as monks in a monastery. To greet someone, you make the **wai**: you put your palms together in front of your chest and bow your head. The lower you bow, the more respect you show.

All the neighbouring countries used to be ruled by Europeans, but Thailand remained the only country in South-East Asia that was **always independent**. The country used to be called **Siam**. The old royal city of **Ayutthaya**, north of Bangkok, was the capital from 1351 to 1767, and its temple ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. King **Bhumibol Adulyadej** grew up partly in Switzerland and studied at the University of Lausanne. Later he reigned for a very long time.

People pay with the **baht**, and the banknotes show the king. In the cities many **tuk-tuks** are on the road: small, open taxis with three wheels. Their name comes from the sound of the engine. Thai food is also well known, with rice, noodles, coconut milk and hot spices. At markets you can buy many things right on the street.

On 26 December 2004 a powerful undersea earthquake off Sumatra set off a huge **tsunami**. The waves hit many coasts on the Indian Ocean, including the holiday island of **Phuket** and other places in Thailand. Many people died, among them people from Switzerland. Since then there have been warning systems and escape routes on many coasts.

gewusst: The full name of Bangkok in Thai is regarded as one of the longest place names in the world.
Thailand stayed independent even though Britain and France ruled the neighbouring countries.

teile.einleitung: All the oceans and seas of the Earth are connected with one another and form a single great body of water: the World Ocean. It covers the largest part of our planet.
wichtigste: About 71 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered by sea.
Usually five oceans are distinguished.
The Pacific is the largest ocean, the Arctic Ocean the smallest.
The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia and is the warmest.
Ferdinand Magellan gave the Pacific its name in 1520.

abschnitte.text: About **71 per cent** of the Earth's surface is sea. That is why the Earth is also called the **Blue Planet**. All the oceans are connected with one another and form the **World Ocean**. Usually five oceans are distinguished: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and the Arctic Ocean. In addition there are many marginal seas such as the Mediterranean or the North Sea.

The **Pacific Ocean** is the largest and deepest ocean. It stretches from the west coast of North and South America to Asia and Australia. It was named by **Ferdinand Magellan**. On his voyage round the world in 1520 he experienced calm weather on the new ocean and called it “Mar Pacífico”, the peaceful sea. In the Pacific also lies the **Mariana Trench**, the deepest point on Earth at almost 11,000 m.

abschnitte.titel: The Atlantic and the Indian Ocean
abschnitte.text: The **Atlantic** lies between America in the west and Europe and Africa in the east. It is the second largest ocean. The **Indian Ocean** is the third largest. It is bounded by Africa in the west, Asia in the north and Australia in the east. Because it lies for the most part in the **tropics** and does not reach into cold regions in the north, it is the **warmest** ocean.

The **Arctic Ocean** around the North Pole is the smallest ocean. It is also the shallowest on average, and large parts of it are covered with sea ice. Around Antarctica lies the **Southern Ocean**. There strong westerly winds blow, and a mighty ocean current circles the continent.

gewusst: Sea water contains on average about 3.5 per cent salt.
The Mariana Trench is so deep that Mount Everest would disappear in it completely.

teile.einleitung: A wildfire is a fire that spreads uncontrolled in forests, bushes or grassland. Such fires can destroy huge areas, but in some landscapes they also belong to the natural cycle.
wichtigste: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat, which is called the fire triangle.
The most common natural cause of wildfires is lightning.
Most wildfires, however, are caused by people.
In Ticino the wildfire risk is often already high in winter and spring when the dry north foehn blows.
In summer 2003 about 300 hectares of forest burned above Leuk in Valais.
In the Swiss mountains, wildfires are often put out with helicopters.
Some plants need fire for their seeds to germinate.

abschnitte.text: For something to burn, three things are needed: **fuel** such as wood, leaves or grass, **oxygen** from the air and enough **heat**. These three conditions are called the **fire triangle**. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out. That is why the fire brigade tries to take the heat from the fire with water or to remove its fuel. It is especially dangerous when it has not rained for a long time and the wind is strong.

The most common natural cause is **lightning**: a bolt can set dry wood or grass alight. Far more often, though, people are to blame. A discarded cigarette end, a careless barbecue or sparks from machines are often enough. That is why, in great dryness, many cantons impose **fire bans** in forests and near them. The authorities then warn with danger levels.

In **Ticino** there are especially many wildfires. On the southern side of the Alps the **north foehn** dries out leaves and soil strongly, so the risk there is often already high in winter and spring. In Valais, in August 2003, about 300 hectares of forest burned above **Leuk**. The fire came in a very hot and dry summer. To this day you can see on the slopes how slowly the forest grows back.

On the steep terrain of the mountains, fire engines can hardly get there. That is why **helicopters** are often used, which fetch water in large containers from lakes or rivers and drop it precisely over the fire. A **firebreak** is a strip without trees and bushes. Because nothing can burn there, the fire is stopped. After the fire is out, firefighters often keep watch over the site for days, because embers can go on smouldering in the ground.

In some **ecosystems** fires are part of the natural order. Some plants, such as certain pines or eucalyptus species, only open their seed capsules through heat. After the fire the seedlings find plenty of light and ash as fertiliser. In Australia, in the **Black Summer** of 2019 and 2020, huge bushfires raged after a long drought. Countless wild animals such as koalas died in them.

gewusst: A nest of embers in the ground can flare up again days after the fire is put out.
The Australian fires of 2019 and 2020 were so big that their smoke travelled as far as South America.

teile.einleitung: Tehran is the capital and largest city of Iran. The huge city lies at the foot of the Alborz mountains.
wichtigste: Tehran is the capital of Iran.
The city lies on the southern slope of the Alborz mountains.
The Azadi Tower of 1971 is a well-known landmark.
At 435 metres, the Milad Tower is the tallest tower in Iran.
Tehran has been the capital since the end of the 18th century.

abschnitte.titel: At the foot of the Alborz
abschnitte.text: Tehran lies in the north of **Iran** on the southern slope of the **Alborz mountains**. The mountains border the city to the north, and in winter their peaks are often covered in snow. Not far away stands **Damavand**, a volcano and the highest mountain in Iran. In the north of the city it is cooler, because it lies higher up. Tehran is one of the largest cities in Western Asia, with many millions of inhabitants. The people speak **Persian**.

The **Azadi Tower**, which in English means Freedom Tower, was built in **1971**. It stands on a large square in the west of the city and is a well-known **landmark**. The **Milad Tower** is a tall **television tower** and, at **435 metres**, the tallest tower in the country. It shapes the skyline of Tehran, and there is a viewing platform at the top.

Tehran has been the **capital** since the end of the 18th century. The **Golestan Palace** from that time is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the great **bazaar** you can buy carpets, spices and much more. The city has many museums, for example with old Persian art treasures. Problems are the heavy traffic and the poor air.

gewusst: Damavand is over 5,600 metres high and can be seen from Tehran on clear days.
Tehran has an underground railway with several lines.

t30bgh1.t: Territorial disputes in the South China Sea

teile.einleitung: The South China Sea lies between China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Several states are arguing there over small islands, reefs and areas of sea. It is about fishing grounds, natural resources, important shipping routes and power in the region.
wichtigste: With the **nine-dash line**, China claims about 90 per cent of the sea.
Six parties are arguing over the **Spratly Islands**.
China has controlled the **Paracel Islands** since a clash with South Vietnam in 1974.
The **Scarborough Shoal** off Luzon has been under de facto Chinese control since 2012.
In 2016 a tribunal in The Hague ruled against China's historic claims, and China does not accept the ruling.
Since about 2013 China has been building **artificial islands** on reefs.

abschnitte.text: China bases its claims on the **nine-dash line**. It goes back to a map of the Republic of China from 1947, on which eleven dashes were still drawn at the time. The line covers about 90 per cent of the sea and reaches far to the south, close to the coasts of other countries. China speaks of **historic rights**, because Chinese fishermen and sailors have long travelled in this area. The neighbouring states reject this line.

The **Spratly Islands** are many small islands, reefs and sandbanks. China, Taiwan and Vietnam claim them in full, and the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei claim parts of them. The **Paracel Islands** further north were brought completely under Chinese control in January 1974 after a clash with South Vietnamese troops, and Vietnam and Taiwan still claim them today. The **Scarborough Shoal** lies about 220 kilometres west of the Philippine island of Luzon. After a stand-off between ships of both states, China has remained present there since 2012.

The Philippines brought a case against China under the United Nations **Convention on the Law of the Sea**. The tribunal sat under the auspices of the **Permanent Court of Arbitration** in The Hague. In July 2016 it ruled that China cannot claim historic rights inside its line, because the law of the sea offers no basis for this. China did not take part in the proceedings and does not accept the ruling. For the Philippines and many other states, on the other hand, it is an important signal.

Since about 2013 China has been piling sand and rock onto reefs in the Spratly Islands. In this way more than 10 square kilometres of new land were created. On it China built **runways**, harbours and radar installations. The neighbouring countries and other states criticise this **militarisation**, while China describes the structures as part of its own territory. Other coastal states have also built facilities on their islands, but on a much smaller scale.

abschnitte.titel: Why the sea matters so much
abschnitte.text: A great many merchant ships sail through the South China Sea. The **Strait of Malacca** between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra connects it with the Indian Ocean and is one of the busiest straits in the world. Goods that come to Switzerland are also often transported this way. Each country also uses its own names: since 2012 the Philippines have officially spoken of the **West Philippine Sea**, and Vietnam calls it the **East Sea** (Biển Đông).

gewusst: The first version of the line on the Chinese map of 1947 had eleven dashes, and later it became nine.
At high tide, many of the disputed reefs lie almost completely under water.
Vietnam calls the sea the East Sea because, seen from Vietnam, it lies to the east.

teile.einleitung: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa. It lies in East Africa and is shared by three countries: Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya. The White Nile begins at Lake Victoria.
wichtigste: Lake Victoria is the largest lake in Africa.
It is named after the British Queen Victoria.
Three countries share the lake: Tanzania, Uganda and Kenya.
Tanzania has the largest share.
It is the second largest freshwater lake in the world.
The Nile begins at Lake Victoria.
Many people on the shore live from fishing.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Victoria** is so big that from one shore you cannot see the other. It is the **largest lake in Africa** and, by area, the **second largest freshwater lake** in the world. Only Lake Superior in North America is bigger. Lake Victoria is quite shallow, though. Three countries share the lake: **Tanzania** with the largest share, **Uganda** and **Kenya**.

On the north shore in Uganda the **White Nile** flows out of the lake. It later joins the Blue Nile and finally reaches the Mediterranean. For a long time it was unclear in Europe where the Nile begins. The British explorer **John Hanning Speke** came to the lake in 1858 and took it to be the source of the Nile. He named it after **Queen Victoria**.

abschnitte.titel: Animals on and in the lake
abschnitte.text: On the shore live **hippos**, which stay in the water by day and go onto land at night to feed. In the lake live **Nile crocodiles** and many kinds of birds. The lake was famous for hundreds of kinds of colourful fish, the **cichlids**. Many of them have disappeared since people put the big **Nile perch** into the lake. This predatory fish eats other fish.

Millions of people live around the lake. Many of them live from **fishing**. The Nile perch is caught and also sold abroad. Problems are caused by sewage, overfishing and a water plant, the **water hyacinth**, which sometimes spreads strongly. The countries on the lake are trying together to protect it.

gewusst: Lake Victoria is more than one and a half times as big as the whole of Switzerland.
There are many islands in the lake, and some of them are inhabited.

teile.einleitung: The Teatro Colón is the famous opera house of Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina. It is regarded as one of the best opera houses in the world, above all because of its sound.
wichtigste: The Teatro Colón stands in Buenos Aires in Argentina.
It opened in 1908.
It is famous for its outstanding acoustics.
Its name recalls Christopher Columbus, called Colón in Spanish.
The main hall has the shape of a horseshoe.

abschnitte.text: The **Teatro Colón** stands in **Buenos Aires**. It opened in **1908**, after a building period of about 20 years in which several architects worked on it one after another. Its name recalls the navigator **Christopher Columbus**, who is called **Colón** in Spanish. It is one of the largest and best-known opera houses in the world, like La Scala in Milan.

The Teatro Colón is famous above all for its **acoustics**. This is the word for how well you can hear music and voices in a room. Many experts count it among the concert halls with the best sound in the world. The main hall has the shape of a **horseshoe** and offers about 2,500 seats, plus standing places. Many tiers rise above one another up to the dome.

At the Teatro Colón there are **operas**, **ballet** and **concerts**. The house has its own orchestra, a choir and a ballet company. Famous singers and conductors from all over the world have performed here. After a long renovation, the house reopened in 2010.

gewusst: Under the stage and the streets there are many workshops where costumes and stage sets are made.
Today's Teatro Colón is already the second house with this name in Buenos Aires.

teile.einleitung: A waterhole is a spot in the savanna where water collects. Many different animals meet here to drink, to cool off or to lie in wait for prey.
wichtigste: A waterhole is a place with drinking water for animals.
In the savanna the rainy season and the dry season alternate.
In the dry season waterholes are especially important.
Lions wait nearby, because prey animals come there.
Zebras and wildebeest like to drink in groups, because many eyes spot enemies sooner.
Elephants suck water into their trunks and dig for water in dry river beds.

abschnitte.text: In the **savanna**, instead of summer and winter there are two other seasons: the **rainy season** and the **dry season**. In the rainy season a lot of grass grows, and there are puddles and ponds everywhere. In the dry season, on the other hand, it hardly rains for months. Then many waters dry up, and often water is left only at a few **waterholes**. All the animals of the area therefore come to these places.

An **elephant** sucks water into its **trunk** and then squirts it into its mouth. In this way it can drink a lot of water at once. When there is no waterhole left, elephants dig with their feet, trunk and tusks in the **dried-up river bed**. In this way they reach water in the ground. Other animals then profit from these holes too.

All animals have to drink. That is why **predators** such as lions often lie in wait for prey near waterholes. When drinking, animals lower their heads and are not attentive. **Zebras** and **wildebeest** therefore like to drink in big groups. In a group, almost always one animal notices when a predator comes and warns the others.

Some animals **wallow** in the mud at the waterhole, for example **warthogs** and **buffalo**. The mud cools the skin and protects against the hot sun. When it dries, it forms a crust that also keeps off annoying insects. So the waterhole is not only a place to drink but also a bathing place.

gewusst: In some national parks artificial waterholes are made so that the animals can get through the dry season.
A fully grown elephant can drink over a hundred litres of water in a day.

teile.einleitung: In the late Middle Ages an indulgence was a promise by the Church that punishments for sins would be shortened or remitted. Many people paid money for it and received a letter of indulgence. The trade in indulgences set off the Reformation.
wichtigste: An indulgence was meant to remit temporal punishments for sin, for example in purgatory.
Johann Tetzel was a well-known preacher of indulgences around 1517.
With the indulgence of 1517, money was collected for St Peter's Basilica in Rome.
Archbishop Albrecht of Brandenburg received half of the income.
The pope at the time was Leo X of the Medici family.
In Switzerland, Zwingli criticised the indulgence preacher Bernhardin Samson.

abschnitte.text: According to the Church's teaching in the Middle Ages, a sin also had a **punishment** as a consequence. This punishment had to be served on earth or after death in **purgatory**. The **indulgence** was meant to shorten these punishments or remit them completely. Originally you had to do good works, pray or go on pilgrimage for it. In the late Middle Ages, however, you could increasingly buy an indulgence with money.

The Dominican monk **Johann Tetzel** travelled through Germany around 1517 as a preacher of indulgences. He preached on behalf of the Archbishop of Mainz. The saying attributed to the trade in indulgences around Tetzel is: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs.” Tetzel's sermons angered **Martin Luther** greatly.

Pope **Leo X** of the **Medici** family was pope from 1513 to 1521. He proclaimed the indulgence for the rebuilding of **St Peter's Basilica** in Rome. The archbishop **Albrecht of Brandenburg** was Archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg. He had gone deeply into debt for his offices. So he had the indulgence preached in his territory and received half of the income.

Luther thought that you cannot buy yourself out of sins with money. True **repentance** must come from the heart. In 1517 he wrote his **95 Theses** against the indulgence. They spread quickly and set off the **Reformation**. The Protestant churches reject indulgences to this day.

In the **Confederation**, too, indulgences were sold. From 1518 the Franciscan **Bernhardin Samson** travelled through the country. **Huldrych Zwingli** preached against him in Zurich. In 1519 Samson was recalled to Rome. The Catholic Church still knows indulgences today, but has not sold them since the 16th century.

gewusst: The sale of indulgences for money was forbidden by the Catholic Church itself in 1567.
St Peter's Basilica in Rome was only finished more than a hundred years after building began.

teile.einleitung: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the IPCC, summarises what science knows about climate change. Its reports are an important basis for governments all over the world.
wichtigste: The IPCC was founded in 1988 by the WMO and UNEP.
Its secretariat has its seat in Geneva.
The IPCC does not do research itself but assesses published research.
It has three working groups with different tasks.
According to the Sixth Assessment Report, 2011 to 2020 was about 1.1 °C warmer than 1850 to 1900.
The Bernese climate physicist Thomas Stocker led Working Group I in the Fifth Assessment Report.

abschnitte.text: The **IPCC** was founded in **1988**. The founders were two UN organisations: the **World Meteorological Organization** (WMO) and the **United Nations Environment Programme** (UNEP). The UN General Assembly confirmed the founding. The secretariat is at the WMO in **Geneva**. The First Assessment Report appeared in 1990.

The IPCC does not do research itself. Hundreds of **scientists** from all over the world read the published specialist literature, summarise it and assess it. In this way large **assessment reports** are produced. For each report there is a short **Summary for Policymakers**. The delegates of the governments approve it together with the authors, line by line. The content must agree with the scientific report.

**Working Group I** assesses the scientific basis of climate change. **Working Group II** deals with impacts, adaptation and vulnerability. **Working Group III** examines how climate change can be slowed down, which is called mitigation. In the **Fifth Assessment Report** of 2013, the climate physicist **Thomas Stocker** of the University of Bern led Working Group I, together with Qin Dahe from China. Bern has long been an important centre of climate research and of research on ice cores.

The **Sixth Assessment Report** states that the global surface temperature in the decade 2011 to 2020 was about **1.1 °C** higher than in 1850 to 1900. It describes the human influence on warming as **unequivocal**. For uncertainties the IPCC uses fixed terms: “likely” means 66 to 100 per cent, “very likely” 90 to 100 per cent and “virtually certain” 99 to 100 per cent.

gewusst: In 2007 the IPCC received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.
The secretariat of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is based not in Geneva but in Bonn.

teile.einleitung: Villarrica is an active volcano in the south of Chile. In its crater there is often a lake of glowing lava. It is one of the most active volcanoes in South America.
wichtigste: Villarrica lies in the south of Chile.
It is an active volcano.
In its crater there is often a lava lake.
Its summit is covered with snow and ice.
At the foot of the volcano lies the town of Pucón.

abschnitte.text: **Villarrica** is a cone-shaped **stratovolcano** in the Andes in the south of Chile. It is about 2,800 metres high, and its summit is covered with snow and a **glacier**. In its crater there is often a **lava lake**, that is, glowing liquid rock. Such lava lakes exist at only a few volcanoes in the world. Villarrica erupts again and again, most recently with a strong eruption in 2015.

At the foot of the volcano lie a lake of the same name and the town of **Pucón**. Many tourists climb Villarrica when it is quiet. In an eruption the ice at the summit can melt. This creates dangerous **mudflows** that race down into the valley. That is why the volcano is constantly monitored.

gewusst: Anyone standing on the crater rim can sometimes see the glowing lava far below.

teile.einleitung: Transpiration is the release of water vapour through the leaves of plants. Plants take up water with their roots and let a large part of it evaporate again. This process is important for the plant itself and for the Earth's water cycle.
wichtigste: **Transpiration** is the release of water vapour through the leaves.
The water escapes through tiny openings called **stomata**.
The evaporation pulls water from the **roots** up into the leaves.
A large tree can release **hundreds of litres** of water on a summer day.
Transpiration **cools** the leaves and is part of the **water cycle**.

abschnitte.text: Plants take up water from the soil with their **roots**. Through fine channels in the stem or trunk it reaches the **leaves**. There a large part of it evaporates and escapes into the air as **water vapour**. This evaporation creates a **suction** that keeps pulling new water up from below. This is how water even reaches the top of tall trees.

The water escapes mainly through tiny openings on the underside of the leaf, the **stomata**. You can only see them under a microscope. Each opening is surrounded by two **guard cells** that can open or close it. When it is very dry, the openings close so that the plant does not lose too much water. Through the same openings the plant also takes in the gas **carbon dioxide** for photosynthesis.

Transpiration **cools** the leaves, rather like sweating in people. With the water, **nutrients** from the soil also reach all parts of the plant. How strongly a plant transpires depends on sun, warmth, wind and humidity. On hot, windy days much more water evaporates than on cool, damp days. A large tree can in this way release **hundreds of litres** of water on a summer day.

The evaporated water rises into the air, forms clouds and later falls again as rain. Transpiration is therefore an important part of the **water cycle**. Forests release especially large amounts of water into the air and so influence the climate around them. Together with evaporation from the ground, this is called **evapotranspiration**. In Switzerland too, where about a third of the land is covered by forest, this plays a big role.

gewusst: The rainforest in the Amazon region produces a large part of its own rain through transpiration.
If you put a transparent bag around a twig, after a short time you will see droplets of water inside it.

teile.einleitung: Tuvalu is a tiny island state in the Pacific. It consists only of flat atolls and reef islands and is one of the flattest countries on Earth. That is why Tuvalu is especially threatened by rising sea levels.
wichtigste: Tuvalu consists of nine atolls and reef islands with about 26 km² of land.
The highest natural point is only about 4.6 metres above the sea.
The capital is the atoll of Funafuti.
The islands used to be called the Ellice Islands and were a British colony.
Tuvalu earns money from the internet ending .tv.
In 2023 Tuvalu recorded in its constitution that the state continues to exist even without land.

abschnitte.text: **Tuvalu** lies in **Polynesia** in the Pacific, roughly halfway between Hawaii and Australia. The state consists of **nine atolls** and reef islands with a combined land area of only about **26 km²**. An **atoll** is a ring-shaped coral reef with small islands that encloses a lagoon. The name Tuvalu means roughly “eight together”, because originally eight islands were inhabited. The capital is the atoll of **Funafuti**, where about 60 per cent of the people live.

As a British colony the islands were called the **Ellice Islands**. Together with the Gilbert Islands, now **Kiribati**, they formed the Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony. In **1978** Tuvalu became independent. It belongs to the **Commonwealth**, and the head of state is the British king or queen. Tuvalu is one of the smallest states in the world.

The highest natural point of Tuvalu is only about **4.6 metres** above the sea. On the atolls a thin **lens of fresh water** floats on the salt water in the ground. If the sea level rises or storm surges come, **salt** gets into the groundwater and into the pits in which the root crop **pulaka** is grown. A study from **2018** showed that the land area had in total increased slightly since the 1970s, because waves move sand and coral rubble around. The risk from flooding and salinisation remains, however.

Every country has its own **internet country code**, Switzerland for example .ch. Tuvalu has the ending **.tv**. Because this abbreviation recalls television, it is popular with television and streaming companies. Tuvalu sells the rights to it. The **licence fees** are an important part of the state budget.

In **2023** Tuvalu changed its **constitution**. It now says that the state and its sea boundaries remain permanently in place. This is meant to apply even if the islands one day sink into the sea or become uninhabitable. In the same year Tuvalu agreed with **Australia** that people from Tuvalu can live and work there.

gewusst: On some days the runway of the airport on Funafuti also serves as a football pitch and meeting place.
By land area, Tuvalu is one of the four smallest states in the world.

teile.einleitung: Uranium is a heavy, weakly radioactive metal found in many rocks. It is mined because nuclear power stations need it as fuel. Uranium mining takes place in only a few countries and brings special dangers.
wichtigste: Since 2009 Kazakhstan has been the world's largest uranium producer.
In Kazakhstan uranium is mainly obtained by in-situ leaching underground.
The deposits with the richest ore lie in Saskatchewan in Canada.
Australia has the largest known uranium resources in the world.
The yellow concentrate called yellowcake is made from the ore.
Natural uranium contains only about 0.7 per cent uranium-235.
In a mine, the radioactive gas radon is a great danger.

abschnitte.text: Since 2009 **Kazakhstan** has produced the most uranium, about 40 per cent of world production. Behind it come **Canada**, **Namibia** and **Australia**, among others. In the Canadian province of **Saskatchewan** lie the Cigar Lake and McArthur River mines, whose ore sometimes contains over ten per cent uranium. Australia has the largest known reserves, with deposits such as **Olympic Dam**. In the desert town of **Arlit** in Niger, uranium has been mined since the 1970s.

Uranium is obtained by **open-cast mining**, in **underground** mines or by **in-situ leaching**. In leaching, a liquid is pumped through boreholes into the deposit. It dissolves the uranium out of the rock and is then pumped back up. In processing plants the ore is turned into a yellow powder called **yellowcake**. It consists mostly of uranium oxide and is the product the mines sell.

Natural uranium consists of over 99 per cent **uranium-238**. Only about 0.7 per cent is **uranium-235**, which can be split. For most nuclear power stations this share is raised to about 3 to 5 per cent, which is called **enrichment**. Switzerland has no uranium mine of its own, and the fuel for its nuclear power stations comes from abroad. Uranium does not count as a fossil fuel, because it did not come from living things.

When uranium decays, the radioactive gas **radon** is produced. It collects in tunnels and, when breathed in, raises the risk of lung cancer. That is why mines have to be strongly ventilated. What is left behind is often **spoil heaps** and sludge ponds with weakly radioactive residues. In East Germany, **Wismut** mined uranium for the Soviet Union in the Ore Mountains and Thuringia from 1946 to 1990, and the clean-up later cost billions.

gewusst: The richest ore in Saskatchewan contains many times more uranium than the world average.
Uranium is older than the Earth itself: it was formed in stars and was already part of the material our planet is made of.

teile.einleitung: The walrus is a large marine mammal from the Arctic. With its long tusks and thick moustache it is easy to recognise.
wichtigste: Walruses live in the north, in the Arctic.
Despite the name, the walrus is not a whale but a seal.
Males and females have two long tusks, which are lengthened canine teeth.
With their tusks walruses pull themselves onto the ice.
They like best to eat clams from the sea floor.
With their stiff whiskers they feel for their food.

abschnitte.text: The walrus is called by that name, but it is neither a whale nor a horse. It belongs to the **seals**. Walruses are very large and heavy, and males grow clearly bigger than females. Under the thick skin lies a layer of **blubber** that protects against the cold. On land they move rather clumsily, but in the water they are good swimmers.

The most striking things are the two long **tusks**. They are lengthened **canine teeth** that grow from the upper jaw. Males and females both have them, and in males they are usually longer. Walruses hook their tusks into the ice and haul themselves out of the water with them. The males also use their tusks to show who is the stronger.

Walruses like best to eat **clams**. To find them they dive down to the sea floor, where it is dark. With their many stiff **whiskers** they feel for the clams in the mud. Then they suck the soft inside out of the shell. In this way a walrus can eat a great many clams in one meal.

Walruses live in the **Arctic**, around the North Pole. There are no walruses in the Antarctic at the South Pole. They are sociable animals and often lie close together in big groups on the beach or on the **pack ice**. When the sea ice melts in summer, they have to rest on land more often.

gewusst: The scientific name of the walrus means roughly “tooth walker”.
When a walrus comes out of the cold water it often looks pale, and in the sun its skin turns reddish.

teile.einleitung: Communion, also called the Lord's Supper, is a celebration in Christian worship. The faithful share bread and wine and remember the last meal of Jesus with his disciples. In the Reformation, the reformers argued fiercely about what exactly happens in it.
wichtigste: At communion the faithful receive bread and wine or grape juice.
Zwingli understood communion as a memorial meal that recalls Jesus.
Luther taught that Christ is really present in bread and wine.
In 1529 Luther and Zwingli argued about it at the Marburg Colloquy.
In 1525 communion was celebrated for the first time in the Reformed way in the Grossmünster in Zurich.
The reformers also gave the cup to all the faithful.

abschnitte.text: According to the Bible, Jesus ate a last meal with his disciples on the evening before his death. He broke the bread and passed round the cup of wine. Christians therefore celebrate **communion**. In the Catholic Church the celebration is called the **Eucharist**. The faithful remember Jesus' death and his fellowship with people.

In the **late Middle Ages**, ordinary believers, the **laity**, usually received only the host, that is, the bread. Only the priests drank from the cup. The reformers thought it important that all the faithful should receive bread and cup. In Reformed congregations today **grape juice** is often offered as well, so that children and people who do not drink alcohol can take part.

**Martin Luther** taught that Christ is really present “in, with and under” bread and wine. He did not take over the Catholic doctrine of transformation, however. **Huldrych Zwingli** of Zurich saw it differently. He interpreted the word “is” in the sentence “This is my body” as “means”. For him bread and wine are **signs** that recall Jesus' death. For him communion is a **memorial meal**.

In 1529 Luther and Zwingli met in **Marburg** in Germany. They wanted to agree in order to be stronger together. On many questions they were in agreement. On communion, however, they found no common solution. That is why the Lutheran and the Reformed churches went separate ways for a long time.

In the spring of **1525**, communion was celebrated for the first time in Reformed form in the **Grossmünster** in Zurich. The Mass was abolished. Zwingli wanted **simplicity** instead of splendour. So plain **wooden cups** and wooden plates were used instead of golden chalices. In many Reformed churches in Switzerland communion is celebrated simply to this day.

gewusst: Some of the old Zurich wooden cups for communion have survived to this day.
Only in 1973 did Lutheran and Reformed churches in Europe agree on a shared communion service with the Leuenberg Agreement.

teile.einleitung: The thermohaline circulation is a huge loop of ocean currents that connects all the oceans. It is driven by differences in the temperature and salt content of the water. It spreads heat across the whole Earth and so also influences the climate in Europe.
wichtigste: “Thermo” stands for **temperature**, and “haline” for **salt**.
Cold, salty water is denser and sinks.
The loop is also called the **global conveyor belt**.
One complete circuit takes about **1,000 years**.
The **AMOC** is the Atlantic part of this loop.
A lot of meltwater from Greenland could weaken the circulation.

abschnitte.text: The name gives away what drives it: “thermo” stands for temperature, and “haline” for salt. Both determine the **density** of seawater. Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than less salty water. Denser water is heavier and **sinks**. These differences set huge masses of water in motion, even in the depths.

In the **Greenland Sea** and the **Labrador Sea**, salty surface water cools strongly, becomes heavy and sinks into the depths. This is how **North Atlantic Deep Water** forms. The formation of sea ice also helps: when water freezes, most of the salt is pushed out, and the ice consists mostly of fresh water. The water left behind becomes saltier and heavier. Off Antarctica, in the **Weddell Sea** and the **Ross Sea**, this forms **Antarctic Bottom Water**, the densest water mass in the world's oceans.

The oceanographer **Wallace Broecker** made the image of the **global conveyor belt** well known. It connects all the ocean basins into a loop of surface and deep currents. The deep water moves very slowly, and a whole circuit is reckoned to take about **1,000 years**. Currents like these are measured in **sverdrups**, named after the Norwegian oceanographer Harald Sverdrup. One sverdrup corresponds to a million cubic metres of water per second.

In the Atlantic this part of the loop is called the **AMOC**, short for “Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation”. It carries warm water northwards and cold deep water southwards. This includes the Gulf Stream, which gives Western Europe a milder climate. Researchers fear that strong **melting of the Greenland ice** could weaken the AMOC. The fresh water dilutes the salty surface water, which becomes lighter and sinks less easily.

gewusst: All the rivers of the Earth together bring about one sverdrup of water into the sea, and large ocean currents move many times that.
Water that sinks in the North Atlantic today only returns to the surface after centuries.

teile.einleitung: In a voyage round the world, you sail once around the Earth in a sailing ship and arrive back at the start. In the past it was a dangerous adventure into the unknown, and today it is a great sporting challenge.
wichtigste: The first voyage around the Earth began in 1519 with the fleet of Ferdinand Magellan.
After Magellan's death, Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship back in 1522.
Joshua Slocum was the first to sail alone around the world, from 1895 to 1898.
Laura Dekker was 16 years old when she finished her solo circumnavigation in 2012.
The Vendée Globe is a race alone and non-stop around the world.
Cape Horn is regarded as one of the most dangerous places for sailors.

abschnitte.text: In **1519** the fleet of **Ferdinand Magellan** put to sea from Spain. It wanted to find a sea route west to the Spice Islands. Magellan died in **1521** in the Philippines. **Juan Sebastián Elcano** led the last remaining ship, the **Victoria**, back to Spain in 1522. Of several ships, only this one made it. The voyage proved that you can sail right around the Earth.

On the open sea you often see no land for days. That is why sailors need aids to find their way. The **compass** shows the direction, because its needle points north. In the past, position was also worked out from stars, the sun and sea charts. Today **satellites** and GPS help. Even so, many sailors still learn the old methods.

The first to sail all alone around the Earth was **Joshua Slocum**. He was under way from 1895 to 1898 with his boat **Spray**. Later many people followed. The Dutch sailor **Laura Dekker** finished her solo circumnavigation in January 2012. When she arrived she was only **16 years** old.

The **Vendée Globe** is a famous sailing race. The competitors sail **alone** and **without a port stop** around the Earth. The start and finish are in France, and the race lasts several months. On the way they have to do repairs themselves and sleep only briefly. Swiss sailors such as **Alan Roura** from Geneva have also taken part.

**Cape Horn** lies at the southern tip of South America. Many round-the-world sailors pass it. There are often **storms** and very high waves, because the westerly winds blow almost unchecked around the Earth. It is regarded as one of the most dangerous places for sailors. Anyone who rounds the cape is especially proud of it in the sailing world.

gewusst: Of Magellan's fleet, only a small part of the crew returned to Spain.
Joshua Slocum wrote a book about his voyage that is still read today.

teile.einleitung: The Paris Agreement is a worldwide treaty to protect the climate. Almost all states have committed in it to limiting global warming. Switzerland is taking part too and has set itself its own targets.
wichtigste: The agreement was adopted in Paris in December 2015.
It came into force on 4 November 2016.
Warming is to stay well below 2 °C, ideally at 1.5 °C.
Each state sets its own climate targets, the NDCs.
New targets have to be submitted every five years.
Switzerland ratified the agreement in 2017.
Switzerland wants to halve its emissions by 2030 compared with 1990.

abschnitte.text: In December **2015** the states of the world met at the climate conference in **Paris**. There almost all countries agreed on a common goal. **Global warming** is to stay well below **2 °C**, compared with the time before industrialisation. The aim is for **1.5 °C** if possible. Before that there had been the **Kyoto Protocol** of 1997, but under it only industrialised countries had fixed targets. The Paris Agreement includes all states.

For the agreement to apply, a **double threshold** had to be reached. At least **55 states**, which together produce at least **55 per cent** of the world's greenhouse gases, had to **ratify** it, which means officially accept it. This was achieved in October 2016. On **4 November 2016** the agreement came into force. For a UN treaty this was unusually fast.

Each state sets its own climate targets itself. They are called **Nationally Determined Contributions**, or **NDCs** for short. Every **five years**, each country must submit a new target that is as ambitious as possible. This is called the **ambition mechanism**. In a **global stocktake** it is checked whether the world is on course. The first was completed in 2023 at the COP28 conference in **Dubai** and found that more needs to be done.

Switzerland **ratified** the agreement on 6 October **2017**. It has committed to cutting its greenhouse gases by **50 per cent** by **2030** compared with 1990. Part of this may be achieved through climate projects abroad. For this, in October 2020, Switzerland concluded with **Peru** the world's first agreement under **Article 6** of the Paris treaty. It allows savings from projects in Peru to be counted towards the Swiss target.

gewusst: The agreement came into force less than a year after it was adopted.
Switzerland was the first country in the world to conclude a climate agreement under Article 6.

teile.einleitung: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place. People of many religions go on pilgrimage to pray, to give thanks, to ask for help or simply to experience their faith.
wichtigste: The Hajj to Mecca is one of the five pillars of Islam and takes place in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah.
The smaller pilgrimage, Umrah, is possible all year round.
On the Camino de Santiago to Santiago de Compostela you must walk at least 100 kilometres to receive the certificate “Compostela”.
Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz is the most important place of pilgrimage in Switzerland.
The Swiss Way of St James, ViaJacobi, leads from Lake Constance to Geneva.
Lourdes in France became famous after apparitions of Mary in 1858.
At the Kumbh Mela, Hindus bathe at the meeting of the Ganges and the Yamuna.

abschnitte.text: For Muslims the **Hajj** to Mecca is one of the five pillars of Islam. Anyone who is healthy and can afford it should make it once in a lifetime. It takes place every year in the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar, **Dhu al-Hijjah**. Because the lunar year is shorter than our solar year, the date shifts every year. The smaller pilgrimage, **Umrah**, is voluntary and possible all year round.

Since the Middle Ages, Christian pilgrims have been going to **Santiago de Compostela** in Spain, to the tomb of the apostle James. Anyone who covers at least the last 100 kilometres on foot or 200 kilometres by bicycle receives the certificate **Compostela**. The stages are recorded with stamps in the pilgrim's passport. If 25 July, the feast day of James, falls on a Sunday, a **Holy Year** applies. In 2024 the pilgrim office registered almost half a million pilgrims, more than ever before.

The most important place of pilgrimage in Switzerland is **Einsiedeln** in the canton of Schwyz. In the Benedictine monastery stands the famous **Black Madonna**, a figure of Mary. Pilgrims have been coming here since the Middle Ages. Einsiedeln also lies on the Swiss Way of St James, the **ViaJacobi**. It leads from Lake Constance via Einsiedeln, Schwyz, the Brünig Pass, Fribourg and Lausanne to **Geneva** and continues in France towards Spain.

In **1858** the girl **Bernadette Soubirous** is said to have had apparitions of Mary in a grotto near Lourdes in the south of France. After that the small town developed into one of the largest places of pilgrimage in the world. Many sick people travel there in the hope of healing. They pray in the grotto and fetch water from the spring.

The **Kumbh Mela** in India is regarded as one of the largest religious festivals in the world. In 2025 it took place in **Prayagraj**, where the rivers **Ganges** and **Yamuna** meet. Devout Hindus bathe there to cleanse themselves of sins. According to the Indian authorities, several hundred million people came. For so many visitors, a whole tent city is set up on the river bank each time.

gewusst: The scallop shell is the sign of the pilgrims of St James, and you can see it on many signposts.
The Hajj lasts only a few days, yet people come from all over the world to Mecca for it every year.

teile.einleitung: UNESCO World Heritage covers the most valuable places of humankind: old cities, buildings and unique landscapes. The states of the world have committed themselves to protecting these sites. There are several World Heritage Sites in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The World Heritage Convention was adopted in Paris in 1972.
There are cultural sites, natural sites and mixed sites.
The rescue of the temples of Abu Simbel gave an important push.
Threatened sites are put on the list of World Heritage in Danger.
The Dresden Elbe Valley lost its title in 2009 because of a bridge.
In Switzerland they include the Jungfrau-Aletsch region, the castles of Bellinzona and the pile dwellings.

abschnitte.text: In the 1960s Egypt built the **Aswan Dam**. The temples of **Abu Simbel** would have sunk in the reservoir. With international help they were taken apart and rebuilt higher up. This rescue showed that some places matter to all of humankind. In **1972** UNESCO adopted the **World Heritage Convention** in **Paris**. Almost all states of the world have signed it.

UNESCO distinguishes three kinds of sites. **Cultural heritage** includes buildings, cities or archaeological sites. **Natural heritage** includes special landscapes, mountains or habitats. **Mixed sites** combine both. In 2023 the list included more than 1,100 sites around the world.

Some World Heritage Sites are threatened, for example by **war**, **building projects** or **natural disasters**. They are put on the **List of World Heritage in Danger**, which is often called the “red list”. If a site is badly damaged, it can lose its title. In **2009**, for example, UNESCO removed the **Dresden Elbe Valley** in Germany from the list. The reason was the **Waldschlösschen Bridge**, which spoiled the protected landscape.

The region **Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch** became World Heritage in **2001** as the first natural site in the Alps. It includes the **Aletsch Glacier**, the largest glacier in the Alps. The three castles of **Bellinzona**, Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro, have been World Heritage since **2000**. In the Middle Ages they guarded the way to the Alpine passes. Other sites include the **Old City of Bern**, the Convent of **St Gall** and the vineyards of **Lavaux** on Lake Geneva.

Some World Heritage Sites lie in several countries. The **prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps** have been World Heritage since **2011**. Their sites lie in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. Thousands of years ago people built houses on stilts there, on lake shores and in bogs. The **Rhaetian Railway** on the Albula and Bernina lines is also a World Heritage Site that Switzerland shares with Italy.

gewusst: The temples of Abu Simbel were sawn into over 1,000 blocks and put back together about 65 metres higher up.
In the canton of Ticino, Monte San Giorgio is World Heritage because of its many fossils.

teile.einleitung: The von Thünen rings are a model from geography and economics. It explains why farmers around a city grow different things. What matters most is the distance to the market, and with it the cost of transport.
wichtigste: The model comes from **Johann Heinrich von Thünen**.
He presented it in 1826 in his work **“The Isolated State”**.
As the distance from the city grows, the **location rent** falls.
In the innermost ring lie market gardening and dairy farming, and in the second, forestry.
In the outermost ring lies **livestock farming**.
A navigable river stretches the rings out lengthways.

abschnitte.text: **Johann Heinrich von Thünen** was an estate owner and economist in Mecklenburg in northern Germany. In 1826 the first volume of his work **“The Isolated State”** appeared. In it he imagined a single city in a **uniform plain**, with equally fertile soil everywhere, no rivers or mountains and no foreign trade. That way only the distance to the market decides what is grown where. This strong simplification makes the model easy to understand.

In the innermost ring, the **“free economy”**, lie market gardening and dairy farming. Vegetables and milk spoil quickly and had to get to market fast. In the second ring lies **forestry**: wood was used as fuel and building material, but in relation to its value it was very heavy. Long journeys by horse and cart would not have paid off. Further out comes arable farming, and in the outermost ring, before the wilderness, **livestock farming**, because animals can walk to market themselves and need a lot of land.

The **location rent** is the profit per area that is left over after the costs of production and transport are deducted. The further away, the higher the transport costs and the lower the location rent. An example: yield 10 tonnes per hectare, price 200 francs, costs 120 francs per tonne, freight 2 francs per tonne per kilometre. At 20 kilometres the location rent is 10 times 80 minus 10 times 2 times 20, which is **400 francs per hectare**. At **40 kilometres** it becomes zero, because 800 divided by 20 gives exactly 40.

Von Thünen also considered what happens if a **navigable river** leads to the city. By boat, transport is much cheaper. That is why intensive use along the river pays off even further from the city. The rings are therefore **stretched out lengthways along the river**. Today transport costs are much lower thanks to lorries and the railway, but the basic principle still helps us understand how land is used.

gewusst: Von Thünen tested his ideas with exact figures from his own estate, Tellow.
The Thünen Institute in Germany, which does research on agriculture, is named after him.

teile.einleitung: Virtual water is the water that was used to make a product. You cannot see it in the product, but it is, so to speak, inside it. With this term we can show how much water we use with our food and our goods.
wichtigste: Virtual water was used to make a product.
The term was coined by John Anthony Allan in the 1990s.
A kilogram of beef contains on average about 15,000 litres.
Arjen Hoekstra developed the water footprint around 2002.
A distinction is made between green, blue and grey water.
About 80 per cent of Switzerland's water footprint arises abroad.

abschnitte.text: Almost everything we eat or use needs water. Grain has to grow, animals have to drink and eat, and factories need water for cooling and cleaning. This water is called **virtual water**. The term was coined by the British geographer **John Anthony Allan** in the 1990s. On a worldwide average, for example, a kilogram of **beef** contains about **15,000 litres**.

Around 2002 the researcher **Arjen Hoekstra** developed the **water footprint**. It measures how much water a person, a company or a country uses in total. Three colours are distinguished. **Green water** is rainwater in the soil that plants take up. **Blue water** is surface water and groundwater that is taken out and used up. **Grey water** is the amount that would be needed to dilute pollution.

Switzerland is regarded as the water tower of Europe, because it has a lot of rain, lakes and glaciers. Even so, according to a study of 2012, about **80 per cent** of its water footprint arises **abroad**. This is because many foods, clothes and other goods are imported. Some of them come from regions where water is scarce. So our shopping has consequences for other countries.

For a very **dry country** it can make sense to **import** grain instead of growing it itself. In this way it saves its own scarce water. With the grain it buys virtual water, in a sense. This is exactly the idea that John Anthony Allan described. It helps us understand how water “travels” around the world through trade.

gewusst: John Anthony Allan received the Stockholm Water Prize in 2008.
A single cup of coffee needs over a hundred litres of water, from the bush to the cup.

teile.einleitung: A thematic map does not simply show mountains, rivers and roads, but a particular theme. This can be the climate, the population, languages or the result of a vote. With maps like these you can see at a glance how something is spread out across space.
wichtigste: A thematic map shows a particular **subject**.
A **topographic map**, by contrast, shows terrain, waters, settlements and paths in general.
**Isobars** connect places with the same air pressure, and **isotherms** connect places with the same temperature.
**Isohyets** connect places with the same amount of precipitation.
In a **choropleth map**, areas are coloured differently according to their value.
A **diagram map** shows small diagrams directly in the areas.

abschnitte.text: A **topographic map**, like the national map of Switzerland, shows terrain, waters, settlements and transport routes. A **thematic map**, on the other hand, shows a particular theme, such as precipitation, population density, the economy or election results. A good example is a map of the **national languages of Switzerland**. It shows where German, French, Italian and Romansh are spoken. A simplified map often serves as the base.

Many thematic maps use lines that connect places with the same value. The prefix **“iso”** means equal. **Isobars** connect places with the same air pressure, and with them you can recognise areas of high and low pressure on weather maps. **Isotherms** connect places with the same temperature, because “therm” means heat. **Isohyets** show where the same amount of rain or snow falls.

In a **choropleth map** each area is given a colour according to its value. Usually darker colours show higher values, for example a greater population density. In Switzerland you know maps like this from **votes**: each canton or municipality is coloured according to its share of “yes” votes. A clear, easy-to-read **key** is important, explaining which colour means which value.

In a **diagram map**, small diagrams stand directly in the individual areas. Often they are **pie charts**, which show shares of a whole. In this way you can show, for example, the language shares of each canton or the breakdown of a country's economy. This makes it possible to compare several values per area at the same time. Bars or circles of different sizes are also used.

gewusst: “Isohyet” comes from the Greek word for rain.
Weather maps on television are thematic maps, even if we rarely think of it.

teile.einleitung: The Warao are an Indigenous people in the Orinoco Delta in Venezuela. Their life is closely tied to the water, and they have always been skilful canoeists.
wichtigste: The Warao live mainly in the Orinoco Delta in the east of Venezuela.
Smaller groups also live in Guyana and Suriname.
The name Warao means roughly “boat people”.
Many live in stilt houses above the water.
The canoe is their most important means of transport.

abschnitte.text: The **Orinoco Delta** is a huge area of river branches, swamps and islands where the Orinoco flows into the Atlantic. The **Warao** live here. Their name means roughly “boat people”. Almost all routes lead across the water, so the **canoe** is their most important means of transport. Even small children learn to steer a canoe.

Many Warao live in **stilt houses** that stand above the water or the swampy bank. In this way they stay dry even in floods. The houses are often open and roofed with palm leaves. An important plant is the **moriche palm**: it provides food, fibres for hammocks and material for building. Besides that, the Warao live from fishing.

The Warao have their own **language**, which is not definitely related to any other known language. Today many of them live in difficult conditions, with little access to doctors and schools. Because of the crisis in Venezuela, many Warao have also emigrated in recent years to neighbouring countries such as Brazil.

gewusst: The language of the Warao is regarded as a language isolate, so it has no definitely known relatives.

teile.einleitung: A tsunami is a huge wave that is usually caused by an undersea earthquake. On the open sea it is hardly visible, but at the coast it piles up high. Anyone who knows the warning signs can get to safety in time.
wichtigste: Tsunami is a Japanese word meaning “harbour wave”.
The most common cause is an undersea earthquake.
In the deep ocean a tsunami can travel at about 800 km/h.
Only at the coast does the wave become high.
If the sea suddenly withdraws, you must get away from the beach at once.
On 26 December 2004 a huge tsunami hit the coasts around the Indian Ocean.

abschnitte.text: A **tsunami** is a wave that sets a huge amount of water in motion. The word is **Japanese** and is made up of the words for **harbour** and **wave**. Fishermen on the open sea often did not notice the wave at all. Only when they came back did they see that their harbour had been devastated. A tsunami usually consists of several waves, and the first is not always the biggest.

The most common cause is an **undersea earthquake**. The sea floor suddenly rises or drops, and the water above it is moved along with it. **Landslides**, underwater slides or **volcanic eruptions** can also set off a tsunami. Such a wave can even arise in lakes. In the year **563**, for example, a mountain collapsed at the eastern end of **Lake Geneva**. The wave reached as far as Geneva.

In the deep ocean a tsunami is very fast, about **800 km/h**. That is roughly as fast as a passenger aeroplane. There, however, the wave is low and hardly visible. When it reaches the **shallow water** at the coast, it slows down. But it piles up high and floods the land far inland.

An important **warning sign** is when the sea suddenly **withdraws** a long way. A strong earthquake at the coast is also an alarm signal. Then you must get away from the beach at once and **climb high**, onto a hill or into a tall, solid building. Many countries now have **warning systems** with measuring buoys in the sea. They warn the people on the coasts before the wave arrives.

On **26 December 2004**, the day after Christmas, a powerful undersea earthquake off **Indonesia** set off a tsunami. It hit many countries around the **Indian Ocean**, for example Thailand, Sri Lanka and India. In **2011** a huge tsunami hit the coast of north-eastern **Japan**. After disasters like these, the warning systems were expanded further.

gewusst: A tsunami can cross a whole ocean and still cause damage thousands of kilometres away.
On the open sea, tsunami waves often lift a ship only gently, so the people on board notice nothing.

teile.einleitung: Tropical rainforest grows around the equator, where it is warm all year round and rains almost every day. No other habitat on land is home to so many different species of animals and plants. The largest rainforest lies along the Amazon in South America.
wichtigste: Tropical rainforests lie near the equator.
It is almost always about 25 degrees, and there is no winter.
It rains almost every day, often in the afternoon.
The humidity is high, and the air feels muggy.
Many leaves have a drip tip.
Most species on land live in the rainforest.

abschnitte.text: Tropical rainforests grow in the **permanently wet tropics** around the **equator**. The largest lies in the area of the **Amazon** in South America. Other large rainforests are found in the **Congo Basin** in Africa and in South-East Asia, for example on Borneo. There the sun shines strongly all year round. There is no cold winter with snow as in Switzerland.

The temperature is almost always about **25 degrees** and changes only little over the year. It rains **almost every day**. In the morning the sun often shines, and a lot of water evaporates. In the **afternoon** tall clouds form, and there are heavy downpours. Part of this rain comes from water that the plants themselves **evaporate** through their leaves. Because the air contains a lot of invisible water vapour, the **humidity** is high and it feels muggy.

The rainforest is divided into **layers**. At the very top, individual **emergent giants** stick out. Below them, the tree crowns form a dense **canopy** in which many animals live. Further down grow smaller trees and shrubs. On the **forest floor** it is dark, because only little light gets through the canopy. Many leaves have a long **drip tip**, which lets the rainwater run off quickly.

No other habitat on land has as many different **species** as the tropical rainforest. Monkeys, parrots, frogs, snakes and countless insects live here. Many species have not yet been discovered and described at all. Many plants from which medicines are obtained also come from the rainforest. This great variety is called **biodiversity**.

Every year large areas of rainforest are **cut down** or burned. On the land, pastures for cattle, fields for soya or plantations for **palm oil** are created. Timber and mineral resources are also extracted. Because the soil of the rainforest is often **poor in nutrients**, the forest grows back only with difficulty afterwards. With the forest, the habitats of many animals and plants disappear too.

gewusst: In the rainforest most of the nutrients are not in the soil but in the plants themselves.
Hundreds of different species of insects can live on a single tree in the rainforest.

teile.einleitung: The Welland Canal is a shipping canal in the Canadian province of Ontario. It connects Lake Erie with Lake Ontario and takes ships around Niagara Falls.
wichtigste: The Welland Canal connects Lake Erie and Lake Ontario.
It bypasses Niagara Falls, which ships cannot pass.
With locks it overcomes a height difference of about 100 m.
It is a core part of the St Lawrence Seaway.
A first canal was already opened in 1829.

abschnitte.text: Between **Lake Erie** and **Lake Ontario** flows the Niagara River. It plunges over **Niagara Falls** and through rapids. For ships this route is impossible. So in Canada the **Welland Canal** was built, which runs across the Niagara Peninsula. In this way large cargo ships can travel from one lake to the other.

Lake Erie lies about **100 m** higher than Lake Ontario. Ships overcome this difference in height in **locks**. A lock is a chamber with gates: the ship sails in, and then the water is raised or lowered. The canal has eight locks. Over time it was rebuilt several times, and a first canal was already opened in **1829**.

The Welland Canal is a core part of the **St Lawrence Seaway**. This seaway connects the Great Lakes via the St Lawrence River with the **Atlantic**. In this way ships reach deep into the interior of North America from the sea. They carry mainly grain, ore and other bulk goods.

gewusst: A ship usually needs about half a day to travel through the whole Welland Canal.

teile.einleitung: The Templo Mayor was the main temple of the Aztecs in their capital, Tenochtitlan. Its remains now lie right in the middle of Mexico City.
wichtigste: The Templo Mayor was the most important temple of Tenochtitlan.
Tenochtitlan lies beneath present-day Mexico City.
In 1978 workers found a huge stone of the goddess Coyolxauhqui.
The temple was excavated afterwards.
The temple was dedicated to two gods: Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc.

abschnitte.text: In **1978** workers from an electricity company were digging in the centre of **Mexico City**. They came across a huge, round **stone relief**. It shows the moon goddess **Coyolxauhqui**. After this find, archaeologists began large excavations. Next to the cathedral they uncovered the **Templo Mayor**, the main temple of the Aztecs.

The Templo Mayor was a large stepped pyramid with **two shrines** at the top. One was dedicated to **Huitzilopochtli**, the god of the sun and of war. The other belonged to **Tlaloc**, the god of rain. The Aztecs made the temple bigger several times by placing new layers over the old ones. So today several building phases lie inside one another like the layers of an onion.

**Tenochtitlan** was the capital of the **Aztecs** and lay on an island in a lake. After the conquest by the Spanish under **Hernán Cortés** in 1521, the temple was destroyed. The Spanish built their new city on the ruins. Today a **museum** next to the excavations shows many of the finds. The historic centre of Mexico City is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: The stone of Coyolxauhqui has a diameter of more than three metres.
During the excavations, thousands of objects were found, including jewellery, masks and shells.

teile.einleitung: In a volcanic eruption, glowing rock, ash and gas burst up from inside the Earth. Some eruptions are calm, others very violent. They can bury whole cities and even change the weather around the world.
wichtigste: Molten rock that flows on the surface is called lava.
In an eruption, ash flies high into the sky.
In the year 79 Vesuvius buried the city of Pompeii.
In 2010 Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland brought many flights in Europe to a standstill.
In 1816 there was a year without a summer in Switzerland.
Someone who studies volcanoes is called a volcanologist.
In an eruption you should follow instructions and leave.

abschnitte.text: In the volcano, **magma** rises, with a lot of gas dissolved in it. If the pressure becomes too great, the volcano erupts. Liquid rock flows down the mountain as **lava**. In violent eruptions, **ash** is thrown kilometres high into the sky. Larger lumps of lava that fly through the air are called **volcanic bombs**.

In the year 79 **Vesuvius** buried the Roman city of **Pompeii** under a thick layer of ash. **Stromboli** in Italy erupts almost constantly with small explosions. Because it glows at night, it is called the “lighthouse of the Mediterranean”. In 2010 **Eyjafjallajökull** in Iceland sent out a huge cloud of ash. Many flights in Europe were therefore cancelled for days.

In 1815 the volcano **Tambora** in Indonesia erupted with enormous force. Its ash and gases spread high in the air around the Earth. As a result it became colder in many regions. In Switzerland 1816 was a **year without a summer**: it rained and snowed a lot, and the harvest was poor. Many people went hungry.

Researchers who study volcanoes are called **volcanologists**. They measure earthquakes, gases and the shape of the mountain in order to recognise eruptions early. If a volcano nearby erupts, you should **follow the instructions of the authorities** and leave the area. Despite the danger, many people like living near volcanoes. **Volcanic ash makes the soil fertile**, so good plants grow there.

gewusst: Lava can be over 1,000 degrees hot.
Volcanic eruptions also happen under the sea, and sometimes a new island is formed.

teile.einleitung: The compass rose is a kind of star showing the compass points. It helps to give wind directions and directions on maps exactly.
wichtigste: A compass rose shows the compass points as a star.
The four cardinal points are north, east, south and west.
With the intercardinal points there are 8 directions.
With 8 directions there are 45 degrees between two neighbouring directions.
A west wind comes from the west.
The cold bise in Switzerland comes from the north-east.

abschnitte.titel: How the compass rose is built
abschnitte.text: A **compass rose** looks like a star with points. The four **cardinal points** are **north, east, south and west**. Between them lie the **intercardinal points**: north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west. Together these make **8 directions**. You find compass roses on maps, sea charts and compasses.

A full circle has 360 degrees. North is at 0 degrees, east at 90, south at 180 and west at 270 degrees. With 8 directions, there are **45 degrees** between two neighbours: north-east is therefore 45 degrees, south-east 135 degrees and **south-west 225 degrees**. The exact opposite direction is always 180 degrees away. The opposite of south-west is therefore **north-east**.

For more precise information, the compass rose is divided further, for example into 16 directions. Then there are only 22.5 degrees between two neighbours. The new directions get compound names. Between north and north-east lies **north-north-east**, and between east and north-east lies east-north-east. Sailors in the past even used compass roses with 32 directions.

In meteorology the compass rose shows **where** the wind comes from. The statement “west wind” means that the wind comes from the west. In Switzerland people know the **bise**, a cold wind from the **north-east**, and many damp west winds. Weather stations also record how often the wind blows from each direction. The result is likewise shown as a compass rose.

gewusst: The name “wind rose” comes from the fact that the many points recall the petals of a rose.
On old sea charts, compass roses were often splendidly decorated and painted in colour.

teile.einleitung: Urbanisation means that more and more people live in cities and cities grow. Since about 2007, for the first time more than half of the world's population has lived in cities. This brings opportunities such as work and schools, but also problems such as traffic, heat and poor districts.
wichtigste: Urbanisation means the growth of towns and cities.
According to the UN, more than half of all people have lived in cities since about 2007.
Under the UN definition, a megacity has at least 10 million inhabitants.
In suburbanisation, housing and businesses move to the surrounding area.
Gentrification means that a district is upgraded and poorer residents are pushed out.
Informal settlements in Brazilian cities are called favelas.
Cities are often warmer, because sealed surfaces store heat.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin urbs, the city. **Urbanisation** means that the share of the city population rises and cities spread out. In Europe it began strongly in the 19th century with **industrialisation**, when people moved from the countryside to the factory towns. Today cities are growing very fast above all in Asia and Africa. The UN expects that around 2050 about two thirds of all people will live in cities.

A **megacity** has at least 10 million inhabitants. Examples are Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, São Paulo and Mexico City. The Greater Tokyo area is regarded as the largest urban area in the world. A **primate city** is far bigger and more important than all the other cities in a country. Examples are Paris in France or Bangkok in Thailand.

In **suburbanisation**, families and firms move from the city to the surrounding area, where there is more space. This creates urban sprawl and a lot of commuter traffic. The other way round, some old city districts are renovated and become popular. If rents then rise sharply, people with little money have to move away, which is called **gentrification**.

abschnitte.titel: Poverty on the edge of the city
abschnitte.text: Many people move to the city because they hope to find work, schools and hospitals there. If they cannot find an affordable home, they build simple huts on the edge of the city. Such **informal settlements** are called **favelas** in Brazil and slums in other countries. Often they lack clean water, electricity and sewers.

Asphalt, concrete and roofs store the sun's heat during the day and give it off at night. This creates an **urban heat island**, where it can be several degrees warmer than in the surrounding area. Trees, parks, stretches of water and green roofs help to cool cities down. Cities also need a lot of energy and cause traffic and waste.

In Switzerland too the great majority of the population lives in cities and urban areas, especially on the **Central Plateau**. The largest city is Zurich, followed by Geneva, Basel, Lausanne and Bern. Because settlements keep growing further into the countryside, people speak of **urban sprawl**. With the Spatial Planning Act, which the people tightened in 2013, more building is meant to take place within existing settlements, and farmland is to be protected.

begriffe.erklaerung: A city together with the surrounding communities that are closely linked to it.
A city or urban area with at least 10 million people.
A district becomes smarter and more expensive, and poorer residents have to move away.
Ground is covered with asphalt or concrete, so that no rain can soak away any more.
Houses and roads spread further and further into the landscape.

gewusst: Around 1800 only a few per cent of people worldwide lived in cities.
On a summer night it can be several degrees warmer in a big city than in the countryside next to it.
More people live in the Greater Tokyo area than in the whole of Switzerland, Austria and Belgium put together.

teile.einleitung: Abraham is an important figure in the Bible. He is regarded as the forefather of the people of Israel and is honoured in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The Bible tells how, at God's call, he left his homeland.
wichtigste: According to the Bible, Abraham came from the city of Ur in Mesopotamia.
God sent him to the land of Canaan.
At first he was called Abram, then God gave him the name Abraham.
God promised him as many descendants as there are stars in the sky.
The son of Abraham and Sarah was called Isaac.
