According to the Bible, Abraham was 100 years old when Isaac was born.

abschnitte.text: According to the Bible, Abraham's family first lived in the city of **Ur** in **Mesopotamia**, in present-day Iraq. From there it moved on north. Then God told Abraham to leave his homeland and go to a new land. This land was called **Canaan**. Abraham trusted God and set out with his wife Sarah and his herds.

God promised Abraham that he would be the father of a great people. One night he led Abraham outside and told him to count the **stars**. His descendants would be that many. At first Abraham was still called **Abram**. God gave him the new name Abraham, which is interpreted as “father of many nations”.

One day **three men** came to Abraham's tent at **Mamre**. Abraham was very hospitable and served them bread, butter, milk and meat. The visitors said that Sarah would soon have a son. Sarah was already old and could hardly believe it. So she **laughed** secretly in the tent.

God kept his promise. Abraham and Sarah had a son and called him **Isaac**. According to the Bible, Abraham was **100 years** old at that time. So the birth of his son was a great miracle. The name Isaac is often linked with the word “laugh”, because Sarah had laughed.

Abraham is important to **Jews**, **Christians** and **Muslims**. That is why these three religions are also called the **Abrahamic religions**. In Islam Abraham is called **Ibrahim**. For all three he is a model of trust in God. Many people therefore see Abraham as a sign of the link between the religions.

gewusst: Abraham's tomb is honoured in the city of Hebron, by both Jews and Muslims.
The story of Abraham is in the first book of the Bible, the Book of Genesis.

teile.einleitung: On 11 March 2011 a huge earthquake shook the north-east of Japan. It set off a giant tsunami that destroyed whole coastal towns and badly damaged the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. In Japan the disaster is called the “Great East Japan Earthquake”.
wichtigste: The earthquake happened on 11 March 2011 at 2:46 pm local time.
Its magnitude was 9.0 to 9.1, and it was the strongest earthquake ever measured in Japan.
It arose at the Japan Trench, where the Pacific Plate dives beneath Japan.
In places the tsunami reached a run-up height of about 40 metres.
About 20,000 people died or are missing, most of them because of the tsunami.
At the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant, the cooling of the reactors failed.

abschnitte.text: The **Tōhoku earthquake** began on **11 March 2011** at 2:46 pm local time off the coast of Miyagi Prefecture. The Japan Meteorological Agency gives a **magnitude** of 9.0, and the US Geological Survey 9.1. It was the **strongest earthquake ever measured in Japan** and one of the strongest in the world. Two days earlier, on **9 March**, there had been an earthquake of magnitude 7.2 about 40 kilometres away. Only afterwards was it recognised as a **foreshock**.

The earthquake arose at the **Japan Trench**, a deep-sea trench in the Pacific. There the **Pacific Plate** dives beneath north-eastern Japan at about 8 centimetres per year. In the process the plates catch on each other, and strain builds up over a long time. In 2011 this strain was suddenly released. Parts of the main island of **Honshū** were shifted about **2.4 metres** to the east, and in places the coast sank.

The earthquake lifted the sea floor and set off a huge **tsunami**. Within minutes the waves reached the coast. In the city of **Miyako** in Iwate Prefecture, a **run-up height** of about **40.5 metres** was measured, the highest value ever measured in Japan. Officially, about 19,800 dead and a good 2,500 missing are counted (as of 2021). Most of the victims were claimed by the tsunami.

At the **Fukushima Daiichi** nuclear power plant the wave reached about **14 to 15 metres**. It flooded the **emergency generators** that were supposed to keep the cooling going in a power cut. As a result the **cooling of the reactors** failed, and meltdowns occurred in several reactors. Radioactive substances got into the environment, and many people had to leave their homes. In **Switzerland** too this set off a debate: in 2011 the Federal Council decided that no new nuclear power plants would be built.

The earthquake was so strong that it affected the whole Earth. Because mass was shifted, the Earth turns minimally faster. By calculation, one day became about **1.8 microseconds** shorter. A microsecond is a millionth of a second. The effect can be measured but is meaningless in everyday life. The tsunami could still be felt on coasts on the other side of the Pacific.

gewusst: Japan has one of the best earthquake warning systems in the world: many people received a warning on their mobile phones seconds before the strong shaking.
The name Tōhoku means “north-east” and refers to the region in the north-east of the island of Honshū.

teile.einleitung: Advent is the time of preparation for Christmas. It covers the four Sundays before the Christmas festival. In this time Christians wait for the coming of Jesus and light candles on the Advent wreath.
wichtigste: The word “Advent” comes from Latin and means arrival.
There are four Sundays in Advent before Christmas.
The first Sunday in Advent is at the end of November or the start of December.
The Advent wreath is usually made of fir branches.
On each Sunday in Advent, one more candle is lit.
With Advent the new church year begins.

abschnitte.text: The word **Advent** comes from the Latin “adventus” and means **arrival**. In Advent Christians await the coming of Jesus, which is celebrated at Christmas. Advent is a time of **waiting** and of looking forward. In the past it was also a time of fasting, similar to Lent before Easter.

The season of Advent has **four Sundays**. The first Sunday in Advent falls at the end of November or the start of December. The fourth Sunday in Advent is the last Sunday before 25 December. With the first Sunday in Advent the new **church year** also begins in the churches. That is why Advent is a kind of new beginning for Christians.

An **Advent wreath** is usually made of green **fir branches**. Green is a sign of hope and life, even in the middle of winter. On the wreath stand four candles. On each Sunday in Advent **one more candle** is lit. In this way you can see that Christmas is coming ever closer and it is getting ever brighter.

In Advent there are many customs. Children open a little door every day on the **Advent calendar**. In many Swiss villages there are **Advent windows**, which light up anew every evening. People bake **Christmas biscuits**, sing songs and visit Christmas markets. On 6 December in Switzerland the **Samichlaus**, St Nicholas, comes to the children.

gewusst: The first Advent wreath is said to have been made in 1839 in Hamburg. It still had over 20 candles, one for each day.
In the Orthodox Church the time before Christmas lasts longer, about 40 days.

teile.einleitung: Waves are movements on the surface of seas and lakes. They can lap quite gently or thunder onto the coast as huge breakers.
wichtigste: Most waves at sea are caused by wind.
The stronger and longer the wind blows, the higher the waves become.
The highest point of a wave is called the crest, the lowest the trough.
When a wave breaks on the coast, it is called surf.
In surfing you ride on a board on the waves.
On a boat a life jacket protects you in high waves.

abschnitte.text: When **wind** blows over the water, it pushes the surface and **waves** form. The stronger the wind and the longer it blows over a large stretch of water, the higher they become. That is why waves on the open sea are much bigger than on a small pond. Moving ships also make waves. Very rarely, huge waves are caused by an earthquake under the sea, and they are called a **tsunami**.

The top part of a wave is called the **crest**. Often it is covered with white foam, which are called white horses. The lowest point between two waves is called the **trough**. It is surprising that the water itself hardly travels along. It moves mainly up and down while the wave travels on. You can see this with a ball that bobs on the waves.

When a wave comes into the **shallow water** near the coast, it is slowed at the bottom. At the top it carries on, becomes steeper and finally **breaks**. It tumbles over with a lot of foam. This is called **surf**. Strong surf can be dangerous, so at bathing beaches you should pay attention to warning flags.

In **surfing** you stand on a board and let a wave carry you. This takes a lot of practice and good balance. On a boat you should always wear a **life jacket** in high waves. It keeps your head above water if you fall in. On Swiss lakes too, such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva, a storm can bring high waves.

gewusst: In Nazaré in Portugal, professionals surf waves that are higher than a house with several storeys.
Waves can travel thousands of kilometres across the ocean before they break on a coast.

teile.einleitung: Bangladesh is one of the most important countries in the world for making clothes. Millions of people, mostly women, sew T-shirts, trousers and jumpers there for shops in Europe and America. The industry has brought the country jobs, but it is criticised for low wages and accidents.
wichtigste: After China, Bangladesh is the second-largest exporter of clothing (as of 2024).
Clothing makes up over 80 per cent of the country's goods exports.
Most of the workers in the factories are **women**.
When **Rana Plaza** collapsed in 2013, more than 1,100 people died.
Afterwards, fashion companies and trade unions agreed a binding accord on fire protection and building safety.
The most important export port is **Chittagong** on the Bay of Bengal.

abschnitte.text: In Bangladesh there are thousands of **clothing factories**, especially around the capital, Dhaka. As a single country, Bangladesh is the second-largest exporter of clothing after China, and in many statistics Vietnam comes just behind. Clothing brings in over 80 per cent of export earnings. This strong dependence on a single industry makes the economy **vulnerable**, for example when demand in Europe falls. Many well-known fashion brands have their goods made here.

Until the end of 2004 the **Multi-Fibre Arrangement** regulated world trade in textiles. It set quotas for many countries, which means maximum amounts for exports. After it expired in 2005, low-cost producers such as China and Bangladesh were able to grow strongly. There is also the EU rule **“Everything But Arms”**: the poorest countries may supply almost all goods to the EU free of customs duty. For Bangladesh this is a big advantage over other countries.

Most of the people who sew are **women**, often from rural areas. The work gave many of them an income of their own, but it is often badly paid and tiring. After protests, the **minimum wage** rose from 8,000 to 12,500 taka a month from December 2023. At the time that was about 100 francs. Trade unions had demanded much more, and the factory owners point to the tough competition with other countries.

On 24 April 2013 the factory building **Rana Plaza** collapsed in Savar, near Dhaka. More than 1,100 people died, mostly textile workers. Cracks in the building had already been known about the day before. Afterwards, fashion companies and trade unions agreed the **Accord on Fire and Building Safety**, called the Accord for short. It was legally binding and obliged the companies to carry out independent inspections and repairs of the factories.

Most of the clothing leaves the country through the port of **Chittagong** (Chattogram) on the Bay of Bengal. It is the most important seaport of Bangladesh. From there the containers travel by ship to Europe, North America and other parts of the world. In Swiss shops, too, you can find many clothes with the label “Made in Bangladesh”.

gewusst: The English name of the EU rule is “Everything But Arms”.
Rana Plaza is regarded as one of the worst disasters in the history of the textile industry.

teile.einleitung: Skyscrapers are very tall buildings that seem to reach into the sky. They are found mainly in big cities, where space is scarce.
wichtigste: A skyscraper is a very tall building with many storeys.
Its frame is made of steel and concrete.
Lifts take people quickly to the top.
People build upwards because there is little space in big cities.
The tallest high-rise in Switzerland stands in Basel (as of 2025).
In Kuala Lumpur stand the Petronas Twin Towers.

abschnitte.text: In **big cities** there is little space, and building land is expensive. So people build not outwards but upwards. In this way many offices and flats fit on a small area. The first skyscrapers appeared at the end of the 19th century in the USA, mainly in **Chicago** and **New York**. Today most very tall buildings stand in Asia and the Middle East.

A skyscraper needs a strong **frame of steel and concrete**. It carries the whole weight and must also withstand strong wind and earthquakes. The outer walls of many modern high-rises consist of **a lot of glass**. Without the **lift**, skyscrapers would hardly be imaginable: nobody wants to climb 50 floors on foot. Only the invention of safe lifts in the 19th century made such tall buildings possible.

The tallest building in the world is the **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai at 828 metres. The **Petronas Twin Towers** in **Kuala Lumpur** in Malaysia are also very well known, two identical towers joined by a bridge. **Hong Kong** was a British colony for a long time and has especially many skyscrapers, standing close together by the harbour. In New York the Empire State Building is world famous.

There are high-rises in Switzerland too, though smaller ones than in Asia. The **Prime Tower** in **Zurich** is about 126 metres high. The tallest high-rise in Switzerland stands in **Basel** (as of 2025): it is a tower of the pharmaceutical firm Roche, over 200 metres high. In Switzerland there is often discussion about where tall buildings fit into the townscape.

gewusst: Tall skyscrapers sway very slightly back and forth in strong wind, which is intended and safe.
The Burj Khalifa is about four times as tall as the Roche Tower in Basel.

teile.einleitung: Yellowstone National Park in the USA is regarded as the first national park in the world. It is famous for geysers, colourful hot springs and wild animals such as bison, wolves and grizzly bears.
wichtigste: Yellowstone was founded in 1872 as the first national park in the world.
Most of it lies in the state of Wyoming.
Under the park lies a huge volcano.
From geysers, hot water shoots into the air.
The Grand Prismatic Spring glows so colourfully because of microorganisms.
In 1995 the wolf was reintroduced.

abschnitte.text: **Yellowstone National Park** was founded in **1872** and is regarded as the **first national park in the world**. Most of it lies in the state of **Wyoming**, and small parts reach into Montana and Idaho. The name **Yellowstone** means **“Yellow Stone”**. It refers to yellowish rocks on the Yellowstone River. Millions of people visit the park every year.

Deep under the park lies a **huge volcano**. Its heat warms the water underground. In a **geyser**, water collects in narrow channels until it becomes so hot that it **shoots up** with steam. The best-known geyser is **Old Faithful**, which erupts fairly regularly. In Yellowstone there are more geysers than anywhere else on Earth.

The **Grand Prismatic Spring** is the largest hot spring in the park. From above it looks like a huge rainbow: deep blue in the middle, and yellow, orange and red at the edge. The colours come from **microorganisms**, tiny living things that live in the warm water. Different species live at different temperatures, and each has its own colour.

In the park live large herds of **bison** with thick fur. Yellowstone is one of the few places where bison have lived free for a very long time. **Grizzly bears** and black bears also roam about. The **wolf** had been wiped out in the park. In **1995** it was reintroduced. Since then the balance in nature has changed, because the wolves hunt deer.

gewusst: Switzerland founded its Swiss National Park in the Engadine in 1914, as one of the first in Europe.
Despite their weight, bison can run faster than a human.

teile.einleitung: The World Tourism Organization is a specialised agency of the United Nations for tourism. Since 2024 it has operated under the name “UN Tourism” and has its headquarters in Madrid.
wichtigste: The headquarters of the World Tourism Organization are in Madrid.
Since 2024 it has officially been called “UN Tourism”.
Since 2003 it has been a specialised agency of the UN.
World Tourism Day is on 27 September every year.
A tourist is someone who stays at least one night at the destination.
In the record year 2019 there were about 1.5 billion international arrivals.

abschnitte.text: The World Tourism Organization came into being in **1975** from an association of national tourism organisations. Since 1976 it has had its seat in **Madrid**, the capital of Spain. Spain is one of the most important tourist countries in the world. Only in **2003** was it taken into the system of **UN specialised agencies**. In January 2024 it changed its brand name to **UN Tourism**.

The organisation lays down how travellers are counted. A **tourist** is someone who stays at least one night outside their usual surroundings. Someone who goes home again without staying overnight is a **day visitor**. These rules help to compare the figures of different countries. In Switzerland, too, the Federal Statistical Office counts overnight stays in hotels.

In the record year **2019** the organisation counted about 1.46 billion international arrivals. In 2020 they collapsed by about three quarters because of the **Covid pandemic**. After that, tourism gradually recovered. For many countries, including Switzerland with its mountains and lakes, tourism is an important branch of the economy.

Every year on **27 September**, **World Tourism Day** is celebrated. It recalls the adoption of the organisation's statutes on 27 September 1970 and has been observed since 1980. In 1999 the organisation adopted the **Global Code of Ethics for Tourism** in Santiago de Chile. It contains principles for responsible and sustainable tourism. Since the start of 2026, **Shaikha Al Nowais** of the Emirates has led the organisation as its first woman, succeeding Zurab Pololikashvili.

gewusst: Every year World Tourism Day has a different motto, for example sustainability.
The collapse of 2020 was the sharpest fall in the history of international tourism.

teile.einleitung: The Yaghan are an Indigenous people in the far south of South America, on the islands of Tierra del Fuego. For thousands of years they lived in one of the coldest and roughest regions on Earth.
wichtigste: The Yaghan, also called the Yámana, live in the south of Tierra del Fuego.
Their territory today lies in Chile and Argentina.
In the past they were sea nomads and travelled by canoe.
Cristina Calderón was the last native speaker of the Yaghan language.
She died in 2022.

abschnitte.titel: Life at the end of the world
abschnitte.text: The **Yaghan**, also called the **Yámana**, lived on the islands and along the channels around the **Beagle Channel** and Cape Horn. They were **sea nomads**: they travelled from bay to bay in canoes made of bark. They lived on mussels, fish, seals and sea birds. In the canoes a small fire often burned to warm them. European sailors saw many such fires on the coast, hence the name **Tierra del Fuego**, “Land of Fire”.

In the 19th century missionaries, settlers, gold seekers and seal hunters came to Tierra del Fuego. They brought diseases such as measles, against which the Yaghan had no protection. Many people died, and the old way of life was lost. Today descendants of the Yaghan live mainly in **Chile**, for example in the settlement of Villa Ukika near **Puerto Williams** on Navarino Island.

**Cristina Calderón** was the last person who spoke the **Yaghan language** as her mother tongue. She died in **2022**. Before that she helped to write down words and stories so that they would not be forgotten. Chile honoured her as a “living human treasure”. Her family is working to pass on the language and culture.

gewusst: Charles Darwin met Yaghan people on his voyage on the “Beagle” and wrote about them.

teile.einleitung: Tea is one of the most popular drinks in the world. Real tea is made from the leaves of the tea plant, which originally comes from China.
wichtigste: Black tea and green tea come from the same plant.
The leaves are used, preferably the young leaves at the top.
China grows the most tea today (as of 2024).
Darjeeling is a well-known tea from India.
In Japan there is a famous tea ceremony with green tea.
Peppermint tea is a herbal tea and not real tea.

abschnitte.text: Real tea is made from the **leaves** of the **tea plant**. It is an evergreen shrub that grows in warm, damp regions, often on mountain slopes. The preferred pickings are the **young leaves at the top** of the twigs, usually two leaves and a bud. These are especially tender and aromatic. Tea contains **caffeine**, which keeps you awake.

**Green tea** and **black tea** come **from the same plant**. The difference lies in the processing. For green tea the leaves are heated shortly after picking so that they stay green. For black tea the rolled leaves are left to **oxidise** in the air. In the process they turn dark and get a stronger taste.

Tea originally comes from **China**, where people drank it thousands of years ago. China is still the country that grows **the most tea** (as of 2024), followed by **India**. Well-known varieties come from India, such as **Darjeeling** from the slopes of the Himalayas and **Assam**. Sri Lanka, formerly Ceylon, and Kenya also grow a lot of tea.

In **Japan** there is a famous **tea ceremony**. In it, green tea is prepared according to strict rules and drunk in peace and quiet. People often use **matcha**, green tea as a fine powder. In **England** afternoon **teatime** is an old tradition. In Morocco people like to drink sweet green tea with fresh peppermint.

abschnitte.titel: Herbal tea is not real tea
abschnitte.text: **Peppermint tea**, camomile tea or fruit tea are not made from the tea plant. They are called **herbal teas** or **fruit teas**. Strictly speaking, they are tea-like drinks. In Switzerland herbal teas are very popular, often made with herbs from the Alps.

gewusst: After water, tea is one of the most widely drunk drinks in the world.
In East Frisia in Germany, people drink especially large amounts of tea.

teile.einleitung: Whether sun, rain or snow: the weather is with us every day. It describes what the air outside is like at the moment, and it can change quickly.
wichtigste: The weather is the state of the air at a place at a particular time.
Weather includes temperature, wind, clouds, precipitation and air pressure.
Climate, on the other hand, describes the typical weather over many years.
You measure weather with a thermometer, a rain gauge and a weather vane.
The foehn is a warm, dry wind in the Alpine valleys.
MeteoSwiss is the federal weather service.

abschnitte.text: The **weather** is what we experience outside today or tomorrow. It can be sunny in the morning and rain in the afternoon. Weather includes the **temperature**, the **wind**, the **clouds** and the **precipitation**, that is, rain, snow or hail. Air pressure also plays an important part. The weather is driven by the sun, which warms the air and the ground to different degrees.

The two words are often confused. Weather applies to one day and one place. A sentence like “Tomorrow it will rain in Bern” is therefore a statement about the weather. **Climate**, on the other hand, describes what the weather is normally like at a place, measured over many years, usually over 30 years. That it is warmer on average in Ticino than in the Jura is a statement about the climate.

With a **thermometer** you measure the temperature in degrees Celsius. A **rain gauge** is a container that catches the rain. In this way you can see how much water has fallen. The **weather vane** turns with the wind and shows where it is blowing from. With a barometer you measure air pressure. Weather stations measure all this automatically, often round the clock.

A typical wind of Switzerland is the **foehn**. Damp air rises on one side of the Alps, rains out and falls down into the valley on the other side. As it falls, the air becomes warm and dry. The foehn is well known, for example, in the Reuss valley in Uri, in the canton of Glarus and in the Rhine valley. In foehn conditions the view is often especially clear, and the mountains seem very close.

**MeteoSwiss** is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology. It runs measuring stations and weather radars all over Switzerland. From these it produces weather forecasts for the coming days. For thunderstorms, gales or heavy rain it issues **severe weather warnings**, so that people can protect themselves.

gewusst: In a strong foehn it can suddenly turn spring-like warm in an Alpine valley in winter.
Weather arises almost only in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the troposphere.

teile.einleitung: Skiing, tobogganing and winter holidays in the mountains: winter tourism is very important for many Swiss mountain resorts. It began in the Engadine.
wichtigste: Winter tourism in Switzerland began in 1864 in St Moritz.
The first winter guests came from England.
Later skiing and tobogganing became very popular.
St Moritz twice hosted the Winter Olympics.
Many mountain villages today depend heavily on tourism.

abschnitte.text: For a long time, guests came to the Alps only in summer. That changed in **1864** in **St Moritz** in the canton of Graubünden. The hotelier **Johannes Badrutt** bet his English summer guests that it was sunny and pleasant in the Engadine in winter too. The English came back in winter and were thrilled. This is how **winter tourism** began in Switzerland.

The first winter guests amused themselves with tobogganing, ice skating and walks. In St Moritz famous runs were built such as the **Cresta Run** for skeleton and a bobsleigh run. Around 1900 **skiing** appeared and became more and more popular. Later the resorts built ski lifts and cable cars. St Moritz hosted the **Winter Olympics** in 1928 and 1948.

Today winter tourism is very important for many mountain regions, for example in Graubünden, in Valais and in the Bernese Oberland. Hotels, mountain railways, ski schools and restaurants provide many jobs. **Climate change**, however, presents the resorts with challenges: at lower altitudes there is less snow. Many ski areas therefore rely on **artificial snow** or offer more activities without snow.

gewusst: Badrutt is said to have promised the English to pay their travel costs if they did not like it in winter.

teile.einleitung: For decades, very many people in China have been moving from the countryside to the cities to work there. These migrant workers helped to build China's factories and cities, but often live with fewer rights than the city dwellers.
wichtigste: In 2024 the Chinese statistics office counted about 300 million migrant workers.
In Chinese they are called “nongmingong”, literally peasant workers.
The hukou, the household registration, was introduced in 1958 and puts them at a disadvantage in the cities.
Many moved from inland provinces such as Sichuan or Henan to the coastal regions.
Shenzhen, founded in 1980 as a special economic zone, became an important destination.
At the New Year festival millions travel home, and this wave of travel is called Chunyun.

abschnitte.titel: From the village to the factory
abschnitte.text: Since the **economic reforms** from the end of the 1970s, China's industry grew quickly. Workers from provinces in the interior such as **Sichuan**, **Henan** or **Anhui** moved to the industrial centres on the coast, for example the **Pearl River Delta**. There was more work there and higher wages. An important destination was **Shenzhen**, which became a special economic zone in 1980. It grew from a small town into a city of millions with many export factories.

The **hukou** is China's system of household registration. The regulation of **1958** was meant to control the movement of people from the countryside to the cities. Entitlements to school, health care and social benefits depend on the place of registration. Someone who moves from the countryside to the city therefore often has fewer rights there. Since the reforms the system has been gradually relaxed. The term **nongmingong** shows that these people are still officially counted as rural population.

According to the National Bureau of Statistics, there were about **299.7 million** migrant workers in 2024. That is roughly a fifth of China's population. Their average monthly income in 2024 was **4,961 yuan**, which is about 690 US dollars. Many work on building sites, in factories, in restaurants or as couriers.

abschnitte.titel: Going home for the New Year festival
abschnitte.text: At the **Chinese New Year festival**, millions of migrant workers travel to their families in the villages. This wave of travel is called **Chunyun**. Within a few weeks, billions of journeys by train, bus, car and plane take place. It is regarded as the largest yearly movement of people in the world.

Many parents cannot take their children with them to the city, partly because of the hukou. The children then stay with their **grandparents** in the countryside. They are called **left-behind children**, in Chinese liushou ertong. There are tens of millions of them, and some see their parents only once a year. Experts worry about their education and their mental health.

gewusst: During Chunyun, train tickets in China are often sold out very quickly.
Around 1980 Shenzhen was still a small town, and today it is one of the largest cities in China.

teile.einleitung: A desert is an area where it rains very little and so hardly any plants grow. Many people think of endless sand dunes and burning heat. But there are also stone, gravel and even ice deserts.
wichtigste: In a desert very little rain falls, usually less than 250 millimetres a year.
The largest hot desert on Earth is the Sahara in North Africa.
Antarctica too counts as a desert because of its low precipitation.
Only a small part of the deserts is covered with sand.
A spot with water and palm trees in the desert is called an oasis.
The camel often carries loads in the desert.
By day it can become very hot, and at night very cold.

abschnitte.text: A **desert** is an area with very little **precipitation**, often less than 250 millimetres of rain a year. By comparison, in Zurich about four times as much falls each year. Because there is hardly any water, only a few plants grow. Deserts cover about a third of the land area of the Earth.

The **Sahara** in North Africa, at about 9 million square kilometres, is the largest hot desert, and it is more than two hundred times as big as Switzerland. The **Atacama** in Chile is regarded as the driest desert in the world, and in some places it has not rained for years. In Asia lies the cold Gobi Desert. Antarctica also counts as a desert, because hardly any snow falls there.

Only about a fifth of all deserts are **sand deserts** with dunes. Much more common are **stone deserts**, also called hamada, and gravel deserts. The wind shapes dunes that grow over a hundred metres high and can slowly move. By day temperatures often rise above 40 degrees, and at night it can cool to near freezing point, because no clouds hold the heat.

The **camel** can manage for days without water and so carries loads through the desert. The desert fox, the **fennec**, gives off heat through its huge ears. Many animals such as scorpions or jerboas are active at night, when it is cooler. Cacti in America store water in their thick stems, and some seeds wait for years for rain.

An **oasis** is a green island in the desert where groundwater comes to the surface. There date palms grow, and people grow vegetables. Nomadic peoples such as the **Tuareg** in the Sahara have moved about with their herds for centuries. In the past, caravans of camels crossed the desert to trade salt, gold and cloth.

At the edges of some deserts, fertile land turns into desert, which is called **desertification**. The reasons are droughts, climate change, too many grazing animals and the felling of trees. The Sahel zone south of the Sahara is especially affected. With tree planting such as the Great Green Wall in Africa, countries are trying to stop the advance of the desert.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place with water and plants in the middle of the desert.
A hill of sand piled up by the wind.
Water that falls from the sky as rain, snow or hail.
The spread of the desert onto previously fertile land.
People with no fixed home who move about with their animals.

gewusst: The largest desert in the world is not the Sahara but icy Antarctica.
The sand of the Sahara is sometimes blown by the wind as far as Switzerland and then colours the sky and the snow orange.
A thirsty camel can drink over 100 litres of water in a few minutes.

teile.einleitung: Uluru is a huge red rock in the middle of Australia. It rises about 350 metres above the flat land and is one of the best-known landmarks of the country. For the Indigenous people, the Anangu, it is a sacred place.
wichtigste: Uluru lies roughly in the middle of Australia, in the Northern Territory.
It rises about 350 metres above the plain.
European settlers used to call it Ayers Rock.
For Aboriginal people, especially the Anangu, it is sacred.
Since October 2019 it has no longer been allowed to climb the rock.
At sunset it glows a deep red.

abschnitte.text: **Uluru** is an enormous rock in the dry **centre of Australia**. It lies in the south of the **Northern Territory**, in the middle of the **Outback**, far away from the big cities on the coast. The nearest larger town is **Alice Springs**. Uluru rises about **348 metres** above the flat plain. That is more than twice as high as the Prime Tower in Zurich. The path around the rock is about ten kilometres long.

Uluru consists mainly of **arkose**, a sandstone rich in feldspar. Inside, the rock is actually **grey**. On the surface, however, iron in the rock has combined with oxygen, so the rock has **rusted**. That is why it is red. At **sunset**, in the light of the low sun, it glows a deep red and orange. Many visitors come for exactly this reason.

In **1873** a European explorer gave the rock the name **Ayers Rock**, after a politician from South Australia. The Indigenous people, however, had long called it **Uluru**. Today people mostly use this old name again. In 1985 the land was handed back to the Anangu. Since then they have managed the national park together with the authorities.

For the **Aboriginal people**, the Indigenous people of Australia, and especially for the **Anangu**, Uluru is sacred. There are many old **stories** about the rock, and rock paintings can be found on its walls. Out of **respect** for the Anangu, it has no longer been allowed to climb the rock since **October 2019**. Around the rock, however, you may walk and marvel at it.

abschnitte.titel: Kata Tjuta and the national park
abschnitte.text: Not far from Uluru lies **Kata Tjuta**, a group of many round **rock domes**. European settlers used to call them the Olgas. Together with Uluru, Kata Tjuta forms the **Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park**. The park is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, both for its nature and for its importance to the culture of the Anangu.

gewusst: Most of Uluru probably lies underground, much like an iceberg in the sea.
After rare heavy rainfall, waterfalls pour down the walls of Uluru.

teile.einleitung: The Trans-Siberian Railway, or Trans-Sib for short, is the longest railway line in the world. It runs right across Russia from Moscow to Vladivostok on the Pacific. Anyone who travels the whole route is on the way for about a week.
wichtigste: The Trans-Sib runs through the whole of Russia, from Europe to Asia.
It begins in Moscow and ends in Vladivostok on the Pacific.
The line is about 9,300 kilometres long.
Without stops, the journey takes about six to seven days.
The railway runs through Siberia and along Lake Baikal.
Passengers sleep in sleeping cars.

abschnitte.text: The **Trans-Siberian Railway** connects **Moscow**, the capital of Russia, with **Vladivostok** in the far east. The main line is about **9,300 kilometres** long. That is about thirty times as far as from Geneva to Romanshorn. On the way the train stops in many large cities, for example Novosibirsk and Irkutsk. Between Moscow and Vladivostok the time difference is seven hours.

Work on the line began in **1891**, when Russia was still ruled by a **tsar**. Thousands of workers laid rails through forests, marshes and mountains. The section on the shore of Lake Baikal was especially difficult, where many tunnels and bridges were needed. The railway was meant to link the huge east of the country with the west. To this day it is very important for transporting goods.

A large part of the route runs through **Siberia**, a huge area in the north of Asia. It gets very cold there in winter. From the window you see the **taiga** for days on end, a vast forest with **birch trees** and conifers such as larch, spruce and pine. Near Irkutsk the train runs for a long time along the shore of **Lake Baikal**. It is the deepest lake in the world.

Because the journey takes many days, passengers sleep in the **sleeping car**. The compartments have beds that turn into seats during the day. In every carriage there is a kettle with hot water for tea or soup. At the stations you can get off, stretch your legs and buy something to eat. Many people do not travel the route in one go but take breaks in the cities along the way.

Besides the main line there are important **branches**. One runs through Mongolia to **Beijing**, the capital of China. This line is called the **Trans-Mongolian Railway**. Another line runs through Manchuria to China. This makes it possible to travel all the way from Europe to East Asia by train.

gewusst: Lake Baikal is over 1,600 metres deep and holds about a fifth of the Earth's liquid fresh water.
On the journey from Moscow to Vladivostok you have to put your watch forward by seven hours in total.

teile.einleitung: Economic geography is a part of geography. It studies where on Earth people work, produce and trade, and why in just those places. It explains, for example, why banks cluster in Zurich or pharmaceutical firms in Basel.
wichtigste: Economic geography asks where economic activity takes place and why.
The economy is divided into the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.
In Switzerland the great majority of workers are in the tertiary sector, that is, in services.
Location factors decide where firms settle.
The Von Thünen rings explain land use by distance from the market.
Walter Christaller formulated central place theory in 1933.
A cluster is a spatial concentration of related firms.

abschnitte.text: **Economic geography** links geography and economics. It studies where factories, farms, offices and shops are located and how goods and people flow between them. Raw materials, transport routes, climate and population play a part. Its findings help in the planning of cities, roads and industrial areas.

The **primary sector** obtains raw materials, for example in agriculture, forestry and mining. The **secondary sector** processes them in industry and trades, for example into machines or chocolate. The **tertiary sector** covers services such as trade, banks, schools, hospitals and tourism. Jean Fourastié predicted in 1949 in his three-sector hypothesis that the share of services would keep growing, and this is exactly what has happened in Switzerland, where today about three quarters of workers are in the tertiary sector.

Firms choose their location according to **location factors**. **Hard location factors** can be measured, for example transport links, taxes, land prices or skilled workers. **Soft location factors** are harder to measure, for example the leisure value of a region, its image or its cultural offer. Switzerland often scores with stability, good education and a high quality of life.

Johann Heinrich von Thünen described the **Von Thünen rings** in 1826: around a city, land is used differently depending on its distance from the market. **Alfred Weber** developed a theory in 1909 of where a factory has the lowest transport costs. **Walter Christaller** explained in 1933 with central place theory why there are few big cities and many small places. He studied southern Germany for this.

A **cluster** is a spatial concentration of firms that are linked with one another. The firms share skilled workers, suppliers and knowledge and so profit from one another. A well-known example is Silicon Valley in California with many computer firms. In Switzerland, the watch industry in the Jura arc and the pharmaceutical industry around Basel form such clusters.

Zurich is the most important financial centre of Switzerland, and Geneva is the seat of many international organisations. In the Alps people live heavily from **tourism**, and on the Central Plateau there is a lot of industry and agriculture. Because Switzerland has hardly any raw materials, it relies on knowledge, research and high-quality products. Good transport routes such as the Gotthard Base Tunnel connect the economic regions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reason why a firm settles in a particular place.
An area of the economy, for example agriculture, industry or services.
A concentration of firms of the same industry in one place.
A place that offers goods and services also for the surrounding area.

gewusst: Von Thünen developed his theory on his own estate in Mecklenburg and spent years working out yields and costs for it.
About 200 years ago most people in Switzerland worked in agriculture, whereas today only a few per cent do.

teile.einleitung: A thermometer is a device used to measure temperature. We need it for the weather, at the doctor's, in the kitchen and in many factories. In Switzerland it usually shows the temperature in degrees Celsius.
wichtigste: You measure temperature with a **thermometer**.
In Switzerland temperature is measured in **degrees Celsius**.
At 0 degrees Celsius water freezes, and at 100 degrees it boils.
Weather stations measure the air temperature about **2 metres above the ground in the shade**.
There are liquid thermometers and **digital thermometers**.

abschnitte.text: Many simple thermometers have a thin glass tube with a liquid in it, for example coloured alcohol. When it gets warmer, **the liquid expands** and rises in the tube. When it gets colder, it contracts and sinks. On a **scale** you can read how warm it is. **Digital thermometers** measure the temperature with an electronic sensor and show a number.

In Switzerland and most countries, temperature is measured in **degrees Celsius**. The scale is named after the Swedish scientist **Anders Celsius**. At 0 degrees water freezes, and at 100 degrees it boils at sea level. In the USA people mostly use **degrees Fahrenheit**. In science there is also the unit **kelvin**.

For the weather, the **air temperature** is measured. Weather stations measure it about **2 metres above the ground** and in the **shade**. In the sun the thermometer itself would heat up and show too much. That is why it is often kept in a light-coloured, well-ventilated weather screen. In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss runs many such measuring stations.

A **clinical thermometer** shows whether someone has a fever. In the kitchen you use a thermometer to check whether meat is cooked. Many houses have an outdoor thermometer at the window. Fridges, heating systems and cars also constantly measure the temperature so that everything works properly.

gewusst: Older thermometers contained poisonous mercury, and in Switzerland such clinical thermometers are now banned.
On the kelvin scale the zero point lies at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: In many warm parts of the Earth there is no winter and summer as there is with us, but a rainy season and a dry season. In the dry season hardly any rain falls for several months. Plants, animals and people have to adapt to this.
wichtigste: The dry season is the months when hardly any rain falls.
The grass turns yellow and withered, and the ground hard and dusty.
Many waterholes dry up.
Bush fires easily start in the dry grass.
Many animals travel far to find water and grass.
The dry season is followed by the rainy season.

abschnitte.text: The **dry season** is a period of the year when almost no rain falls for several months. It occurs mainly in the **tropics**, for example in the **savannas** of Africa. It stays warm there all year round. The seasons differ mainly in whether it rains or not. The dry season is followed by the **rainy season**, in which it often rains heavily.

Without rain, **the grass dries out**. It turns yellow and brown and rustles in the wind. The ground becomes hard and dusty and cracks. Many trees drop their leaves so that they lose less water. Rivers become narrow, and many **waterholes** dry up in the heat. Only with the rainy season does the landscape turn green again.

Dry grass burns very easily. That is why there are often **bush fires** in the dry season. They can be started by lightning, but often they are also started by people. Many plants of the savanna are adapted to fire. Some trees have thick bark, and the grass quickly shoots up again from the roots. After a fire, fresh green blades often sprout.

In the dry season **food becomes scarce**. That is why many animals travel far to find water and grass. Well known is the great migration of **wildebeest** and **zebras** in East Africa, for example in the Serengeti. Elephants dig for water with their feet and trunks in dry riverbeds. At the last waterholes many different animals then meet.

The dry season is difficult for people too. Without **irrigation**, farmers can hardly grow anything in this time. Many herders move with their herds to places where there is still water. If the rainy season fails or is too short, there can be a **drought**. Then water and food are lacking.

gewusst: The baobab tree stores a lot of water in its thick trunk for the dry season.
There is also a dry season around the Mediterranean, but there it falls in summer.

teile.einleitung: Lake Titicaca lies high in the Andes on the border between Peru and Bolivia. It is the largest freshwater lake in South America and one of the highest large lakes in the world. For the Incas it was a sacred place.
wichtigste: Lake Titicaca is the largest **freshwater lake in South America**.
It lies about **3,810 metres** above sea level.
It covers about **8,300 square kilometres**, more than ten times the size of Lake Geneva.
For the **Incas** the lake was sacred.
The **Uros** live on floating islands made of **reeds**.
Many people at the lake speak **Aymara**.

abschnitte.text: Lake Titicaca lies about **3,810 metres** above sea level, which is higher than most peaks in the Swiss Alps. It is one of the highest lakes on which large ships sail. At about **8,300 square kilometres** it is more than ten times the size of **Lake Geneva**, which covers about 580. The western part belongs to **Peru** and the eastern part to **Bolivia**. At this height the air is **thin** and contains less oxygen, so visitors get tired more quickly.

abschnitte.titel: The sacred lake of the Incas
abschnitte.text: For the **Incas**, Lake Titicaca was sacred. According to a legend, their first ruler rose from the lake. On the **Island of the Sun** in the lake there are still ruins from the time of the Incas today. People lived by the lake long before the Incas, and the old ruined city of Tiwanaku lies very close by.

The **Uros** people have lived for a long time on islands they build themselves in the lake. They pile many layers of **reeds** on top of one another, which creates an island that floats on the water. Because the reeds at the bottom slowly rot, the islands have to be renewed again and again. The Uros also build houses and boats out of reeds. Many **Aymara** people also live around the lake, and they still speak their own language today.

The **Titicaca water frog** lives in Lake Titicaca. It has a great deal of wrinkled skin so that it can take in enough oxygen in the cold water. It is found almost only in the lake and in a few waters around it, and it is seriously endangered. The people at the lake often keep **llamas** and **alpacas**. They use their wool and let them carry loads.

gewusst: The Titicaca water frog spends almost its whole life under water.
Lake Titicaca lies more than 1,300 metres higher than the summit of the Säntis.

teile.einleitung: The United States of America, or USA for short, is a big country in North America. It consists of 50 states and stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Like Switzerland, the USA is a federal state.
wichtigste: The USA consists of 50 states.
The flag has 13 red and white stripes.
Most people speak English.
The money is called the dollar.
The President lives in the White House.
On the west coast lies the Pacific.
The Mississippi flows through the country from north to south.

abschnitte.text: The USA lies between **Canada** in the north and **Mexico** in the south. In the east lies the **Atlantic**, in the west the **Pacific**. Through the middle of the country the **Mississippi** flows from north to south to the Gulf of Mexico. There are deserts, high mountains such as the Rocky Mountains, wide plains and big forests. Alaska in the far north and the islands of Hawaii are also part of it.

The USA consists of **50 states**. Like the cantons in Switzerland, they have their own governments and laws. On the flag there is one star for each state, so 50 stars. The **13 stripes** recall the first 13 colonies, which declared themselves independent in 1776. The capital is **Washington, D.C.**, where the President lives and works in the **White House**.

On **Mount Rushmore** the faces of four presidents are carved into the rock: Washington, Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt and Lincoln. In **Los Angeles** lies **Hollywood**, where many films are made. New York is the largest city in the country, with the Statue of Liberty in the harbour. Many people also visit national parks such as the Grand Canyon or Yellowstone.

Most people speak **English**, and many also speak Spanish. The money is called the **dollar**. In the USA live people whose ancestors immigrated from all over the world. Long before the Europeans, many Indigenous peoples lived here. The USA is one of the largest economic powers in the world.

gewusst: The USA is over 200 times as big as Switzerland.
The Statue of Liberty in New York was a gift from France.

teile.einleitung: The 95 Theses are a list of statements that Martin Luther wrote down in 1517. In them he criticised the Church's trade in indulgences. With the Theses the Reformation began, which greatly changed Christianity in Europe.
wichtigste: Martin Luther published his 95 Theses in 1517.
On 31 October 1517 he sent them to the Archbishop of Mainz.
The main subject was criticism of indulgences.
The Theses were written in Latin but were soon translated into German.
Whether Luther nailed them to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg is disputed.
31 October is now Reformation Day.
Luther was born in Eisleben in 1483 and died there in 1546.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 in **Eisleben**. He became a monk and later a professor of theology at the University of **Wittenberg**. He read the Bible very closely and asked himself how a person can be made right with God. His answer: by God's grace and faith alone, not by money or deeds. Luther died in 1546 in his birthplace, Eisleben.

In the late Middle Ages the Church sold so-called **indulgences**. Whoever paid was supposed to be freed from the punishment for his sins. Luther thought this was wrong. In his Theses he wrote that true **repentance** must come from the heart. You could not buy yourself out of sins with money. With his statements he first wanted to start a discussion among scholars.

Luther wrote the Theses in **Latin**, because that was the language of scholars. On 31 October 1517 he sent them to the Archbishop of Mainz. Soon the Theses were translated into German and multiplied with the still young **printing press**. In this way they spread across the whole of Germany within a few weeks. Many people now discussed Luther's questions.

The story is well known that Luther nailed the Theses with a hammer to the door of the **Castle Church** in Wittenberg. Whether this really happened is **disputed** among historians. Church doors, however, often served at that time as a kind of notice board. Today the Theses stand cast in bronze on the door of the Castle Church.

The year 1517 is regarded as the beginning of the **Reformation**. From the dispute came the Protestant churches, which separated from the Church in Rome. In Switzerland too there were soon reformers, for example **Huldrych Zwingli** in Zurich. 31 October is celebrated as **Reformation Day**. Many Reformed churches in Switzerland celebrate Reformation Sunday on the first Sunday in November.

gewusst: The Theses were originally meant for a debate among scholars, not for the whole people.
In Germany Reformation Day is a public holiday in several federal states.

teile.einleitung: The Sustainable Development Goals, the SDGs for short, are a plan of the United Nations for a better future. By 2030 they are meant to reduce poverty, protect the environment and make a good life possible for all people.
wichtigste: The UN General Assembly adopted the 2030 Agenda in 2015.
It contains 17 goals with a total of 169 targets.
Their predecessors were the eight Millennium Development Goals (2000 to 2015).
The SDGs apply to all countries, including Switzerland.
The guiding principle is: leave no one behind.
SDG 1 is called “No poverty”, SDG 13 “Climate action”.

abschnitte.text: In September **2015** the **UN General Assembly** in New York adopted the **2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development**. At its core are the **17 Sustainable Development Goals**, or **SDGs**. These goals are divided into a total of **169 targets**. They are meant to be achieved by the year 2030. “Sustainable” means acting in such a way that future generations can also live well.

Each goal has a number and a theme. **SDG 1** is called **“No poverty”**, SDG 2 “Zero hunger”, SDG 4 “Quality education”. **SDG 5** deals with **gender equality**, that is, equal rights and opportunities for women and men. **SDG 13** calls for **“Climate action”**. Other goals concern clean water, clean energy, life below water and on land, and peace.

abschnitte.titel: From the Millennium Goals to the SDGs
abschnitte.text: The predecessors of the SDGs were the eight **Millennium Development Goals** for the years 2000 to 2015. They were aimed above all at poorer countries. An important difference: the **SDGs apply to all countries**, including rich ones such as **Switzerland**. Here too they concern, for example, energy use, waste, education and equality. The federal government reports regularly on how Switzerland is getting on with the goals.

Over the whole agenda stands the guiding principle **“Leave no one behind”**. Progress is meant to benefit all people, including the poorest and the disadvantaged. To measure poverty, the **World Bank** sets a line for **extreme poverty**. In **June 2025** it set this at **3.00 dollars a day**. Anyone with less than that counts as extremely poor. Experts assume that many goals will not be fully achieved by 2030.

gewusst: Each of the 17 goals has its own coloured symbol, which you can recognise on posters worldwide.
Governments, experts and millions of people from all over the world took part in drawing up the SDGs through surveys.

teile.einleitung: In a flood, land that is normally dry is covered with water. This usually happens after heavy rain or when a lot of snow melts. Floods can cause great damage, but in the past they were also useful.
wichtigste: Floods often come after heavy rain or snowmelt.
In August 2005 flooding in Switzerland caused damage of around 3 billion francs.
The Nile flood brought the ancient Egyptians fertile mud.
On sealed surfaces, rainwater cannot soak away.
A flash flood is a sudden flood after heavy rain.
People protect themselves by giving rivers more room.

abschnitte.text: A **flood** happens when a stream, river or lake carries more water than its bed can hold. The causes are often days of **heavy rain** or rapid **snowmelt**. On the coast, too, a **storm surge** can flood the land. A **flash flood** is a sudden flood after a heavy thunderstorm. The water rises sharply in a short time, which is especially dangerous in narrow valleys and dried-out stream beds.

abschnitte.titel: Why concrete makes the problem worse
abschnitte.text: On meadows and in forests, rain can **soak** into the ground. On roads, squares and roofs it cannot, and such surfaces are called **sealed**. There the water runs straight off and reaches streams and rivers all at once. The more ground is built over, the faster the waters swell. Straightened rivers also carry the water away quickly.

In **August 2005**, days of rain on the northern side of the Alps led to flooding and landslides. The damage came to around **3 billion francs**. It was one of the most expensive natural events in Switzerland. Today many rivers are being given **more room** again. In such **river restoration** projects, rivers are widened and given **floodplains** where the water can spread out without flooding villages. **Flood retention basins** also help: they fill up in heavy rain and release the water slowly again.

In ancient Egypt the **Nile** burst its banks every year. The flood left **fertile mud** on the fields, and the farmers could harvest rich crops. Elsewhere floods are a great danger. In 2022 an extremely strong **monsoon** led to huge floods in **Pakistan**. Around 33 million people were affected, and over two million lost their homes.

gewusst: The ancient Egyptians set their calendar by the yearly Nile flood.
Part of Pakistan stood under water for so long in 2022 that huge lakes formed.

teile.einleitung: A volcano is a place on the Earth's surface where molten rock comes out from inside the Earth. Over time a mountain often grows from it. The name comes from the Roman god Vulcan.
wichtigste: Deep under a volcano, magma collects in the magma chamber.
The magma rises up through the vent.
The name comes from the Roman god Vulcan.
Many volcanic cones consist of layers of lava and ash.
A shield volcano is broad and flat.
Etna is the highest active volcano in Europe.
A volcano that will never erupt again is called extinct.

abschnitte.text: Deep under a volcano, molten rock, the **magma**, collects in a **magma chamber**. It rises up through a channel, the **vent**. At the top of the volcano lies the **crater**. When the magma reaches the surface, it is called **lava**. With every eruption new lava and ash are deposited, and so the mountain grows.

The word volcano comes from the Roman god **Vulcan**. He was the god of fire and of smiths. The Romans believed that he had his forge under an island in the Mediterranean. This island is still called **Vulcano** today and is itself a volcano.

Many volcanoes are steep cones made of **layers of lava and ash**, and they are called **stratovolcanoes**. One example is **Etna** in Sicily, the highest active volcano in Europe. A **shield volcano**, on the other hand, is **broad and flat** like a shield lying on the ground. It forms from runny lava that flows a long way. The great volcanoes of Hawaii are shield volcanoes.

An **active** volcano can erupt at any time. A **dormant** volcano has been quiet for a long time but could become active again. A volcano that will never erupt again is called **extinct**. In Switzerland there are no active volcanoes. Not far from Schaffhausen, however, there are extinct volcanoes in the Hegau, for example the Hohentwiel.

gewusst: Most volcanoes in the world lie under the sea.
Around the Pacific there are so many volcanoes that people speak of the Pacific Ring of Fire.

teile.einleitung: Victoria Falls is a mighty waterfall in the south of Africa. Here the River Zambezi plunges over an edge into a deep gorge. It lies on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.
wichtigste: Victoria Falls lies in Africa.
The Zambezi plunges down here.
It lies on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe.
It is about 1,700 metres wide and about 100 metres high.
It is named after Queen Victoria.
The African name means “the smoke that thunders”.
It forms the largest continuous curtain of water in the world.

abschnitte.text: At **Victoria Falls** the **Zambezi** plunges into a narrow gorge across a width of about **1,700 metres**. The water falls about **100 metres**. There are higher and also wider waterfalls. But Victoria Falls forms the **largest continuous curtain of water** in the world. That is why it is often regarded as the largest waterfall of all.

The water plunging down whirls up a huge cloud of fine **spray**. You can see it from many kilometres away. The roar can also be heard far off. That is why the falls are called **Mosi-oa-Tunya** in an African language, “the smoke that thunders”. In sunshine a **rainbow** often glows in the mist.

The Scottish explorer **David Livingstone** reached the falls in 1855 as the first European. He named them after the British **Queen Victoria**. The local people, of course, had known the waterfall long before. Today Victoria Falls is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**. A bridge over the gorge connects **Zambia** and **Zimbabwe**.

gewusst: In the rainy season much more water plunges down than in the dry season.
A town in Zambia near the falls is called Livingstone.

teile.einleitung: Venezuela is a country in the north of South America on the Caribbean. It has the largest oil reserves in the world and spectacular landscapes with table mountains and waterfalls. The capital is called Caracas.
wichtigste: The capital of Venezuela is Caracas.
In the north the coast lies on the Caribbean Sea.
The largest river is the Orinoco.
Venezuela has the largest oil reserves in the world.
The name means “Little Venice”.
The freedom fighter Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas.
The high table mountains are called tepuis.

abschnitte.text: Venezuela lies in the north of **South America**, and its coast borders the **Caribbean Sea**. The capital, **Caracas**, lies in a valley near the coast. The name was given by European sailors: on Lake Maracaibo they saw houses on stilts in the water, which reminded them of **Venice**. “Venezuela” therefore means roughly “Little Venice”. The national language is **Spanish**.

The largest river is the **Orinoco**, which flows into the Atlantic in a broad delta. In the south-east the **tepuis** rise up, high table mountains with steep walls and flat tops. On their plateaus live plants that exist nowhere else. From one tepui plunges **Angel Falls**, the highest waterfall in the world. In the west of the country lie spurs of the Andes.

Venezuela has the **largest oil reserves in the world**, much of it in the area along the Orinoco. Oil has been the country's most important source of income for over a hundred years. Because the economy depends so heavily on oil, falling oil prices have a big effect. In recent years Venezuela has gone through a severe economic crisis. Many people have therefore left the country.

**Simón Bolívar** was born in Caracas. At the beginning of the 19th century he led several countries of South America to independence from Spain. In Venezuela he is honoured as a national hero. Many squares and streets bear his name. The country's currency, too, is called the **bolívar**.

gewusst: The water of Angel Falls drops so far that on the way it partly turns into spray.
The state of Bolivia is also named after Simón Bolívar.

teile.einleitung: A value chain shows all the steps that a product goes through, from the raw material to the finished device in the shop. The example of the smartphone shows well how many countries and firms are involved.
wichtigste: The smile curve shows that research and marketing bring a lot of added value, assembly little.
The metal tantalum from the ore coltan is in the tiny capacitors of smartphones.
Contract manufacturers such as Foxconn assemble devices for other brands.
TSMC of Taiwan is the largest contract manufacturer of semiconductor chips.
Tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold count as conflict minerals in the EU.
In Switzerland, due diligence duties on conflict minerals and child labour have applied since 2022.

abschnitte.titel: At the start: the raw materials
abschnitte.text: A smartphone contains many different **raw materials**. The ore **coltan** contains the metals tantalum and niobium. **Tantalum** is needed for very small, powerful capacitors. In many touchscreens, **indium tin oxide** forms a transparent layer that conducts electricity. Indium is a rare metal and mostly arises as a by-product of zinc production.

Some raw materials come from areas with armed conflicts. Mining them there financed armed groups. The EU counts **tin**, **tantalum**, **tungsten** and **gold** as **conflict minerals**. Firms that import them have to meet **due diligence duties** and check where they come from. In Switzerland, similar duties for conflict minerals and **child labour** have applied since 1 January 2022. They were introduced as an indirect counter-proposal to the **Responsible Business Initiative**.

The chips in a smartphone are often made by specialised firms. **TSMC** of Taiwan is the largest contract manufacturer of **semiconductor chips** in the world. It produces to the designs of other firms. The devices are often assembled by **contract manufacturers** such as **Foxconn**. This Taiwanese firm builds many smartphones in China for other brands.

The founder of the computer firm Acer, **Stan Shih**, described the **smile curve**. If you plot the added value along the chain, a smiling shape results. At the start, in **research** and **design**, and at the end, in **marketing** and **sales**, it is high. In the middle, in **manufacturing**, lies the lowest point. A study of 2010 showed that of about 179 US dollars in manufacturing costs for an iPhone 3G, only about 6.50 dollars went to final assembly in China.

Old devices are part of the chain too. A lot of **electronic waste** used to end up in poorer countries. **Agbogbloshie** in Accra, the capital of **Ghana**, became well known. There devices were often taken apart and burned under dangerous conditions in order to obtain metals. In Switzerland you can hand in old electrical devices free of charge in shops, because disposal is already included in the purchase price.

gewusst: A smartphone contains dozens of different chemical elements.
Assembly made up only about 3.6 per cent of the manufacturing costs of the iPhone 3G.

teile.einleitung: The tundra climate is a cold climate in the far north and in high mountains, in which the warmest month is no warmer than 10 °C. The warmth is not enough for trees, so only low plants grow. Frozen ground and swampy summers are typical.
wichtigste: In the Köppen-Geiger system the tundra climate is called ET.
The warmest month averages between 0 and 10 °C.
The 10 °C July isotherm roughly coincides with the polar tree line.
Mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs grow.
The ground below is often permafrost.
In Switzerland similar conditions are found above the tree line.

abschnitte.text: In the **Köppen-Geiger** climate classification, the tundra climate has the code **ET**. In the tundra climate the **warmest month** averages more than **0 °C** but less than **10 °C**. In the northern hemisphere, the **10 °C July isotherm** roughly coincides with the polar **tree line**. An isotherm is a line that connects places with the same temperature. North of it the warmth is no longer enough for trees.

The **growing season** is short and cool. That is why only low plants grow: **mosses**, **lichens** and **dwarf shrubs**. Dwarf shrubs such as the **dwarf birch** stay close to the ground. There it is a little warmer and more sheltered from the wind. In winter a blanket of snow protects them from icy winds.

In tundra regions **permafrost** is widespread. This is ground or rock that stays frozen without a break for at least two years. In summer only the top layer thaws. The frozen ground below does not let the **meltwater** seep away, and because of the cold little evaporates. That is why the ground is often **swampy**. On slopes the thawed, mushy soil slowly slides downhill over the permafrost, which is called **solifluction**.

In the tundra climate often only **little precipitation** falls. Even so, it is usually not regarded as dry, that is, not **arid**. Cold air can take up little water, and the sun supplies little energy for evaporation. That is why even a little precipitation is enough to make the climate **humid**. North of the **Arctic Circle** there is the **polar day** in summer and the **polar night** in winter. Despite constant daylight the summer stays cool, because the sun stands low.

abschnitte.titel: Alpine tundra and where the word comes from
abschnitte.text: In **Switzerland** too there are conditions that resemble the tundra. Above the **tree line**, depending on the region at roughly 1,800 to 2,400 metres, it is too cold for trees. There alpine meadows, dwarf shrubs, mosses and lichens grow, which is called **alpine tundra**. There is also permafrost at high altitudes in the Alps. The word “tundra” came into German via **Russian** and probably originates from Finnish or Sami.

gewusst: The Finnish word “tunturi”, from which “tundra” probably derives, means a treeless mountain or high plateau.
If the permafrost in the Alps thaws, rockfalls and debris flows can become more frequent.

teile.einleitung: A tornado is a violent whirl of air that reaches from a thunderstorm cloud down to the ground. It is small, but it can cause enormous damage. Most tornadoes occur in the USA, but they also happen in Europe and in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Most strong tornadoes form from **supercell thunderstorms**.
You can see them as a **funnel cloud** that reaches the ground.
Their strength is rated by the damage using the **Fujita scale**.
The strongest tornadoes reach **over 400 km/h**.
Over water, such a whirl is called a **waterspout**.
A **cellar** or a room without windows offers protection.

abschnitte.text: Most strong tornadoes form from **supercells**. These are large thunderstorms with a **rotating updraught**. From this rotation a narrow whirl can form that reaches down to the ground. You see it as a **funnel cloud**, a rotating tube of cloud. It becomes visible through water vapour, dust and debris that it sweeps up.

The **Fujita scale**, today mostly in its enhanced form, rates tornadoes by the **damage** they cause. The strongest tornadoes are given level 5. In them, wind speeds of **over 400 km/h** have been measured with radar. That puts them among the fiercest winds on Earth. Most tornadoes are much weaker, however.

A tornado is usually only a few dozen to a few hundred metres wide and often lasts only **minutes**. A **hurricane**, on the other hand, is hundreds of kilometres across and can last for days. Hurricanes form over warm seas, and tornadoes from thunderstorms over land. If a whirl forms over a lake or the sea, it is called a **waterspout**. Waterspouts are occasionally also seen over Swiss lakes.

In a tornado the main dangers are **flying debris** and splintering glass. The best protection is a low-lying room, such as a **cellar**, or an inner room without windows. You should keep away from windows and protect your head. In the USA there are sirens and warnings on the radio and on mobile phones. Many houses there have a special shelter.

gewusst: In the USA there are over a thousand tornadoes every year, more than in any other country.
In Switzerland too there are a few tornadoes almost every year, mostly weak ones.

teile.einleitung: A wadi is a valley in the desert that is dry most of the time. Only after heavy rain does water suddenly flow in it, often as a dangerous flash flood. The word comes from Arabic.
wichtigste: A wadi is a mostly dry river valley in desert regions.
The word comes from Arabic.
After heavy rain, sudden flash floods threaten.
Water flows in it only occasionally.
In the south-west of the USA a wadi is called an arroyo.
At the mouth of a wadi an alluvial fan often forms.
The well-known desert valley Wadi Rum lies in Jordan.

abschnitte.text: The word **wadi** comes from **Arabic** and means valley or river bed. Wadis are found in deserts such as the Sahara or on the Arabian Peninsula. Most of the time the river bed is dry. Only after irregular **heavy rain** does water flow in it. This kind of flow is called **episodic**. In the south-west of the USA such a valley is called an **arroyo**.

The hard, dry desert ground **hardly absorbs any water**. When it rains heavily, the water therefore runs off very fast and collects in the wadi. In a short time a raging **flash flood** can arise, even if it is not raining at all at the spot itself. That is why it is dangerous to **camp** in a wadi. The flood sweeps along sand, gravel and stones.

Where the wadi comes out of the mountains onto the plain, the water loses force. It drops the **rubble** it carries, and an **alluvial fan** forms. In the ground of the wadi the **groundwater** is often closer to the surface than all around. That is why more shrubs and trees grow here. For a long time, people and animals have used wadis as routes and watering places.

Many wadis are bigger than today's rainfall can explain. They formed partly in **damper climate phases**, when more rain fell in the desert. A famous desert valley is **Wadi Rum** in **Jordan**. It is known for its red sandstone rocks and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: A wadi can stay dry for years and then fill with water in a few minutes.
Many place names in Arab countries begin with the word wadi.

teile.einleitung: Urban mining means roughly “mining in the city”. It means that raw materials are recovered from waste, old devices and buildings, instead of being newly taken from the ground. In this way cities themselves become a kind of raw material store.
wichtigste: Urban mining recovers raw materials from waste, devices and buildings.
Such raw materials are called secondary raw materials.
A tonne of old smartphones contains more gold than many ores.
In 2022 about 62 million tonnes of electronic waste were produced worldwide.
In Switzerland you pay an advance recycling fee when you buy a device.
Shops must take back old devices of the same kind free of charge.
Demolition material is turned into recycled concrete, or RC concrete for short.

abschnitte.titel: The city as a raw material store
abschnitte.text: In houses, roads, pipes and devices there are huge amounts of metal, concrete and other materials. In **urban mining** all this is seen as a store from which raw materials can be taken again later. Raw materials from recycling are called **secondary raw materials**, as opposed to the primary raw materials from mining. This protects nature, because fewer new mines are needed. It also often saves energy.

A smartphone contains small amounts of **gold**, silver, copper and other metals. If you work it out for a tonne of old mobile phones, there is more gold in it than in many gold ores. That is why people talk of a “gold mine”. According to the Global E-waste Monitor, about **62 million tonnes of electronic waste** were produced worldwide in 2022. Only part of it is properly collected and recycled.

In Switzerland you pay an **advance recycling fee** when you buy an electrical device. This pays for the later disposal. Shops must **take back** old devices of the kind they sell **free of charge**. For computers, entertainment electronics and telephones, the organisation **Swico** arranges the take-back. A lot is also reused in building: **RC concrete** made from demolition material is increasingly used for new buildings.

Not everything can be easily recovered. **Rare earths** are often built firmly into devices in tiny amounts only, for example in magnets. Getting them out is laborious and expensive. Another idea is **landfill mining**: old rubbish tips are dug up to find the useful materials in them again. It is also important to build buildings and devices so that they can be taken apart easily later.

gewusst: In the drawers of many households lie old mobile phones that nobody needs any more, and with them unused gold.
A large house can later become a source of raw materials for a new house.

teile.einleitung: Wind power is electricity obtained from the force of the wind. It is a renewable energy, because the wind never runs out.
wichtigste: Wind turbines turn the movement of the wind into electricity.
Wind power is renewable and gives off hardly any CO₂ in operation.
China produces the most electricity from wind power (as of 2024).
Wind farms stand on land or in the sea.
In Switzerland there are so far only a few large wind turbines.

abschnitte.text: A modern **wind turbine** usually has three long rotor blades. The wind turns them, and the rotation drives a **generator**. This produces electric current, which flows into the electricity grid. So that as much wind as possible arrives, wind turbines stand on tall towers and in windy places, for example on coasts, on hills or in the sea.

Worldwide, wind power is being greatly expanded. The country that produces the most electricity from wind is **China** (as of 2024). The USA and Germany are also among the big wind power countries. Wind farms in the sea are called **offshore wind farms**. There the wind blows more strongly and more steadily than on land.

In Switzerland, wind power so far supplies only a small part of the electricity. Most of it comes from **hydropower**. The wind farm on **Mont Crosin** in the Bernese Jura is well known. There are also wind turbines on the Gotthard Pass. New installations are often controversial: supporters stress the clean electricity, especially in winter, while opponents worry about the landscape, noise and birds.

gewusst: The rotor blades of large wind turbines can be longer than the width of a football pitch.

teile.einleitung: Uxmal is an ancient Maya ruined city on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is the best-known example of the Puuc style, with richly decorated stone façades. Today Uxmal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Uxmal lies on the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
The city was built by the Maya.
It is the best-known example of the Puuc style.
The Pyramid of the Magician is famous.
Uxmal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Uxmal** lies in the hill country of the **Puuc** in the north of the **Yucatán** Peninsula. The city flourished over a thousand years ago. The best-known buildings include the **Pyramid of the Magician** with its unusual rounded outline, the **Nunnery Quadrangle** and the **Governor's Palace**.
