Since 1996 Uxmal has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

Typical of the **Puuc style** are smooth lower walls with richly decorated façades above them. The decoration consists of many small, precisely cut stones fitted together like a mosaic. Often you can see masks of the rain god **Chaac** with a long, curved nose. In this dry region without rivers, rain was especially important to the Maya. They collected water in underground cisterns.

gewusst: On the Governor's Palace at Uxmal, thousands of individual stones are fitted together into a large pattern.

teile.einleitung: The westerlies are a zone in the middle latitudes in which the wind mostly blows from west to east. They also determine the weather in Switzerland and in the whole of Central Europe.
wichtigste: The westerly zone lies roughly between 40° and 60° latitude.
Switzerland lies at about 46° to 48° north, and so in the westerly zone.
Typical is changeable weather with passing low-pressure systems.
Westerly winds bring mild air from the Atlantic and make winters in Western Europe mild.
In the southern hemisphere the stormy westerlies around 40° south are called the “Roaring Forties”.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current is also called the West Wind Drift.

abschnitte.text: The **westerly zone** lies in the **middle latitudes**, roughly between 40° and 60° north and south. It lies between the **subtropical high-pressure belt** and the **subpolar low-pressure trough**. Its boundaries shift with the seasons. Switzerland lies at about 46° to 48° north, and so in the middle of this zone. That is why our weather often comes from the Atlantic.

In the westerly zone, **low-pressure systems** with their **fronts** keep moving from west to east. They bring clouds, rain and wind. In between come spells of **high pressure** with fine weather. That is why the weather changes often. For weather services such as MeteoSwiss, it is important to observe the lows over the Atlantic closely.

The **Atlantic** stores a lot of heat, partly through the **North Atlantic Current**. The westerlies carry this mild sea air far into Europe. That is why winters in Western Europe are comparatively mild. On west coasts such as in Ireland or Norway there is an **oceanic climate**: the differences in temperature are small, and it rains often. Further east on the continent, winters become colder.

In the southern hemisphere, between 40° and 60° south, there is almost only **ocean**. Without mountains and continents there is no friction, so the westerlies there are stronger and steadier. Sailors call them the **Roaring Forties**. The winds drive an ocean current that circles Antarctica completely: the **Antarctic Circumpolar Current**. It too is called the **West Wind Drift**.

abschnitte.titel: The rain shadow of the Andes
abschnitte.text: When damp westerly winds meet a mountain range, the air rises and rains out. On the other side it arrives dry, which is called a **rain shadow**. This is how it is in **Patagonia**: on the Chilean side of the **Andes** it rains a great deal, while in eastern, Argentine Patagonia it is very dry. Something similar is known on a smaller scale in the Alps too.

gewusst: Further south, sailors call the westerlies the “Furious Fifties” and the “Screaming Sixties”.
Aircraft flying from America to Europe are often faster than in the opposite direction, thanks to a tailwind at height.

teile.einleitung: A U-shaped valley, also called a glacial trough, is a valley that was shaped by a glacier. In cross-section it looks like a U, with a broad valley floor and steep walls. There are many such valleys in the Swiss Alps, and the best-known example is the Lauterbrunnen Valley.
wichtigste: A U-shaped valley has a U-shaped cross-section with steep sides.
It forms when a glacier scours out a valley.
Above the steep trough walls lies the flatter trough shoulder.
Hanging valleys open out high above the valley floor, often with waterfalls.
The Lauterbrunnen Valley in the Bernese Oberland is a textbook example.
The Yosemite Valley in California is also a U-shaped valley.

abschnitte.text: A river usually cuts downwards and forms a **V-shaped valley** with a narrow floor. During the **ice ages**, mighty glaciers filled many such valleys. A **valley glacier** scours out the floor and the sides at the same time with ice and the rock it carries. In this way the valley becomes wider and deeper. A **U-shaped cross-section** is formed, with a broad valley floor and steep walls, the **U-shaped valley**.

The steep slopes of a U-shaped valley are called **trough walls**. Above them there is often a flatter edge in the terrain, the **trough shoulder**. It often shows the height of an older valley floor or of the former glacier surface. In the Alps, **alpine pastures** and villages often lie on such shoulders. On the trough wall you can also see the **trimline**: below it the rock has been smoothed by the ice, and above it it has been weathered jagged by frost.

The great main glacier had more ice and therefore more power than the small **side glaciers**. It therefore scoured out its valley deeper. After the ice melted, the side valleys end high above the main valley, and they are called **hanging valleys**. Their streams plunge as waterfalls over the trough wall. In the **Lauterbrunnen Valley**, numerous streams fall in this way over almost vertical rock walls, for example the **Staubbach Falls**.

Under the pressure of the ice, a glacier can also flow a little **uphill**. In this way it sometimes scours out basins that lie lower than the later valley exit. This is called **glacial overdeepening**. Harder rock, on the other hand, remains standing across the valley as a **rock bar**. In the overdeepened basins behind such thresholds there are often **lakes** or flat plains of gravel today.

U-shaped valleys are found wherever large glaciers once lay. In Switzerland, besides the Lauterbrunnen Valley, for example the **Reuss valley in Uri** and many other Alpine valleys were shaped by ice. In California the **Yosemite Valley** is famous, with granite walls such as **El Capitan** and high waterfalls. The **fjords** in Norway are U-shaped valleys into which the sea flooded after the ice age.

gewusst: On the floor of the Lauterbrunnen Valley, the Staubbach Falls plunge almost 300 metres freely down the rock face.
Fjords are often much deeper than the sea in front of their mouths, because the glaciers overdeepened their basins.

teile.einleitung: Albert Schweitzer was a theologian, doctor, musician and philosopher. In Africa he founded a hospital in the jungle and treated many sick people there. For his work he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Albert Schweitzer was born in 1875 in Kaysersberg in Alsace.
He was a theologian, doctor, musician and philosopher.
In 1913 he founded a hospital in Lambaréné in present-day Gabon.
His guiding idea was “reverence for life”.
He paid for his hospital with organ concerts.
He received the Nobel Peace Prize for the year 1952.
He died in Lambaréné in 1965.

abschnitte.text: Albert Schweitzer was born in **1875** in **Kaysersberg** in **Alsace** and grew up in Günsbach. At that time Alsace belonged to the German Empire, and later to France again. Schweitzer's father was a pastor. Albert studied **theology** and **philosophy** and became a pastor and lecturer himself. He loved music from an early age.

Schweitzer was a well-known **organist**. He played in many churches in Europe. He wrote a big book about **Johann Sebastian Bach**, first in 1905 in French. All his life he studied Bach's organ music. With the income from his **concerts** he later supported his work in Africa.

At the age of **30**, Schweitzer began to study **medicine** as well. He wanted to help as a doctor in Africa. In **1913** he founded a hospital in **Lambaréné** in present-day **Gabon**. Together with his wife **Helene** he treated a great many sick people there. The hospital lay in the middle of the jungle, which is why it is often called the **jungle hospital**.

At the centre of Schweitzer's thinking is the idea of **“reverence for life”**. He meant that we should respect and protect every life, that of humans, animals and plants. For him this was the basis of all **ethics**, that is, of the question of how to act rightly. This idea has impressed many people.

abschnitte.titel: Nobel Prize and the end of his life
abschnitte.text: Schweitzer received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for the year **1952**, although it was awarded in 1953. With the prize money he built a village for people with **leprosy**. He worked in his hospital until a great age. In **1965** he died in Lambaréné at the age of 90. He was buried next to the hospital.

gewusst: The hospital in Lambaréné still exists today.
Many schools and hospitals in Europe bear the name Albert Schweitzer.

teile.einleitung: World trade is the name for the exchange of goods and services between the countries of the Earth. Whether bananas from Ecuador, mobile phones from China or medicines from Basel: much of what we use every day has made a long journey. World trade links the economies of almost all states with one another.
wichtigste: In world trade, countries buy and sell goods and services across their borders.
Goods sent out are called exports, goods brought in are called imports.
The World Trade Organization, the WTO, has its seat in Geneva.
The forerunner of the WTO was the GATT agreement of 1947.
David Ricardo founded the idea of comparative advantage in 1817.
Switzerland belongs to the free trade organisation EFTA.
The largest container port in the world in 2024 was Shanghai.

abschnitte.text: No country can make everything its people need by itself. That is why countries sell goods abroad, which are **exports**, and buy other goods in, which are **imports**. Traded goods include raw materials such as oil, foods such as coffee and industrial goods such as cars. Services such as insurance, tourism or software are also part of it.

Over 2,000 years ago, caravans on the **Silk Road** were already bringing silk and spices from China to the Mediterranean. From the 15th century European sailors crossed the oceans and built trading networks around the world. With steamships and railways, trade became much faster in the 19th century. In 1956 the American Malcom McLean introduced the standardised **container**, which made loading enormously easier.

The British economist **David Ricardo** showed in 1817, with the principle of **comparative advantage**, that trade is worthwhile. His example was England and Portugal, which exchanged cloth and wine. Each country should specialise in what it does best by comparison. In this way more goods are produced in total, and both sides profit.

After the Second World War, many states concluded the **GATT** in 1947, an agreement to reduce customs duties. From it, in 1995, came the **World Trade Organization, the WTO**, with its seat in Geneva. It sets rules for trade and settles disputes between countries. In addition there are **free trade agreements**, in which individual countries lower or abolish customs duties among themselves.

The **trade balance** compares a country's exports and imports. If a country exports goods worth 300 and imports 250 billion francs' worth, it has a surplus of 50 billion. The **terms of trade** describe the ratio of export prices to import prices. If export prices rise, a country can buy more imported goods for its goods.

Switzerland is a small country but earns a great deal of money from exports, especially medicines, chemicals, machines and watches. It has belonged to **EFTA** since 1960, together with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. The most important trading partner is the European Union. Since 2014 a free trade agreement with **China** has been in force, and via the Rhine ports in Basel, goods travel by ship as far as the North Sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: Selling goods or services abroad.
Buying goods or services from abroad.
A charge that has to be paid on goods when they cross a border.
Trade between countries with no or only a few customs duties and obstacles.
A standardised steel box that fits on ships, trains and lorries.

gewusst: The port of Shanghai handled more than 50 million standard containers in 2024.
A large container ship can today carry over 20,000 standard containers at once.
Around four fifths of all goods in world trade are carried across the sea by ship.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht Dürer was one of the most important artists of the German Renaissance. He painted pictures, drew, and created famous woodcuts and engravings. Many of his works show themes from the Bible and the Christian faith.
wichtigste: Dürer was born in Nuremberg in 1471 and died there in 1528.
In 1498 he became famous with the woodcut series “Apocalypse”.
Around 1492 he worked for printers in Basel.
His three master engravings are copper engravings from the years 1513 and 1514.
The “Praying Hands” were a study for an altarpiece.
In 1526 he gave Nuremberg the panels “The Four Apostles”.

abschnitte.text: Albrecht Dürer was born in **Nuremberg** in **1471** and died there in **1528**. At that time the city was a centre of trade and **printing**. Dürer's father was a goldsmith. Albrecht first learned this craft, then became a painter. On his **journeyman's travels** he stayed in **Basel** in 1492 to 1493. Several woodcuts for books are attributed to him there.

Dürer became famous in **1498** with the woodcut series **“Apocalypse”**. It shows scenes from the **Revelation of John**, the last book of the Bible. The 15 large pictures show, among other things, the **four horsemen of the Apocalypse**. Dürer published the series himself as a book. In a **woodcut**, a picture is cut into a wooden block and then printed.

In 1500 Dürer painted a **self-portrait in a fur-trimmed coat**. In it he shows himself strictly from the front, symmetrical and with long hair, as **Christ** was otherwise portrayed. In this way he stressed the dignity of the artist. The brush drawing **“Praying Hands”** of 1508 is also very well known. It was a preliminary study for the Heller Altarpiece in Frankfurt and shows the hands of an apostle.

Dürer's three **master engravings** date from the years 1513 and 1514. They are **copper engravings**: the lines are cut into a copper plate with a burin. One is called **“Knight, Death and the Devil”**. It shows a rider who rides on undeterred past two sinister figures. Another shows **Saint Jerome** peacefully in his study, with a lion and a dog. Jerome translated the Bible into Latin.

Dürer was very interested in the ideas of **Martin Luther**. In **1526** he gave the council of the city of Nuremberg two large panels: **“The Four Apostles”**. They carry quotations from the Bible in Luther's translation. For that reason they are also seen as a profession of faith in the **Reformation**. Today the panels hang in the **Alte Pinakothek** in Munich.

gewusst: Dürer also painted famous nature studies, for example of a young hare.
Dürer was among the first artists to mark their works with a sign of their own, a monogram of A and D.

teile.einleitung: Tourism means that people travel to another place for a time, to go on holiday, to experience something or to get to know something new. For many countries it is an important branch of the economy. It also plays a big role for Switzerland, with its mountains, lakes and cities.
wichtigste: Tourism means travelling and staying overnight in another place, for example on **holiday**.
**France** has received the most foreign visitors for many years.
In 2024 about **100 million** international visitors came to France, followed by **Spain**.
The UN's **World Tourism Organization** has its headquarters in **Madrid**.
In Switzerland modern tourism began in the Alps in the **19th century**.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **tourism** when people leave their usual place of residence for a certain time and stay overnight somewhere else. Many travel on **holiday** to relax, do sport or see cities. Others travel on business or visit relatives. Many jobs are part of tourism: in hotels, restaurants, on railways, in travel agencies and on mountain railways.

**France** has received the most international visitors for many years, about 100 million in 2024. After it comes **Spain**. Many people visit Paris, the beaches on the Mediterranean or famous sights. The **World Tourism Organization** of the United Nations, now called **UN Tourism**, has its headquarters in **Madrid**. It collects data on travel worldwide.

In the **19th century**, mainly wealthy visitors from England came to the Swiss Alps to hike and climb mountains. Large **hotels** and mountain railways were built, and later ski resorts. Well-known destinations today include Zermatt, Lucerne, Interlaken and the Engadin. Many jobs in mountain regions depend on tourism. The organisation **Switzerland Tourism** promotes holidays in Switzerland abroad.

Tourism brings money and work to a region. But it can also cause problems. In very popular places it sometimes gets too crowded, rents rise and nature suffers. This is called **overtourism**. Air travel also puts a strain on the climate. That is why many places are looking for **sustainable tourism** that protects nature and the local people.

gewusst: In 1863 the Englishman Thomas Cook organised one of the first package tours to Switzerland.
The word tourism comes from the French “tour”, meaning a round trip.

teile.einleitung: A world map shows the whole Earth flat on a sheet of paper or a screen. At a glance you can see all the continents, oceans and countries. But because the Earth is a sphere, every world map has to distort reality a little.
wichtigste: A world map shows the whole surface of the Earth flat.
A book with many maps is called an atlas.
On most maps north is at the top.
A sphere cannot be shown flat without distortion.
The way the sphere is transferred onto the flat surface is called a map projection.
A globe shows the Earth as a sphere without distortion.
Lines of longitude and latitude form a grid with which any place can be found.

abschnitte.text: A world map shows the seven continents and the great oceans on a flat surface. There are **political maps**, on which countries and borders are coloured, and **physical maps**, which show mountains, rivers and deserts. A **key** explains what the colours and symbols mean. A book with many such maps is called an **atlas**, named after a giant from Greek legend.

The Earth is a sphere, and a sphere cannot be made flat without stretching or tearing. Try it with an orange peel: it can never be laid completely smooth on the table. That is why every world map distorts sizes, shapes or distances. Only a **globe** shows everything in the right proportion.

The cartographer **Gerhard Mercator** drew a famous world map in 1569 that helped sailors to navigate. On it, countries near the poles look far too big, so Greenland looks almost as big as Africa. In reality Africa is about fourteen times bigger. Other **projections**, such as the Winkel tripel projection, spread the errors more evenly.

abschnitte.titel: Finding your way on the map
abschnitte.text: On most maps **north** is at the top, south at the bottom, east on the right and west on the left. Across the map runs a grid of **lines of latitude** and **lines of longitude**. The equator divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres, and the prime meridian runs through Greenwich near London. With these coordinates any place can be given exactly. Bern, for example, lies at about 47 degrees north.

The ancient Greeks already drew maps of the world as it was then known, around the Mediterranean. America, Australia and Antarctica were missing for a long time, because the Europeans did not know them yet. The oldest surviving globe, the **Erdapfel** of Martin Behaim, was made in 1492 in Nuremberg. Today maps are made very precisely with satellite images.

In many Swiss schools, children work with the **Swiss World Atlas**. The Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo** for short, produces the official national maps of Switzerland. These maps are known worldwide for their accuracy and beautiful relief shading. On the swisstopo map portal you can look at Switzerland online in every detail.

begriffe.erklaerung: A book with many maps.
A spherical model of the Earth.
A method of transferring the round Earth onto a flat map.
An explanation of the colours and symbols on a map.
Shows how much reality is reduced on the map.

gewusst: On many world maps Greenland looks as big as Africa, although Africa is about fourteen times bigger.
In Australia there are world maps with south at the top, and they are just as correct.
The Erdapfel of 1492 does not yet show America, because Columbus only arrived there in the same year.

teile.einleitung: The Volcanic Explosivity Index, or VEI for short, is a scale for the strength of volcanic eruptions. It runs from 0 for calm eruptions to 8 for the most gigantic ones. It was developed in 1982 by Chris Newhall and Stephen Self.
wichtigste: The VEI was developed in 1982 by Chris Newhall and Stephen Self.
The scale runs from 0 to 8.
From VEI 2 upwards, the volume of ejected material grows by a factor of 10 with each step.
VEI 8 needs more than 1,000 km³ of material.
Tambora in 1815 is the only eruption of recorded modern times with VEI 7.
The VEI does not take account of the amount of sulphur gases.

abschnitte.text: The **Volcanic Explosivity Index** was developed in 1982 by the researchers **Chris Newhall** and **Stephen Self**. It rates eruptions on a scale from **0 to 8**. What matters most are the **volume of ejected material**, that is, how much material is thrown out, and the **height of the eruption column**. An eruption with VEI 0 is calm, and the lava simply flows out. The higher the number, the more explosive the eruption.

From **VEI 2** upwards, each step means roughly **ten times more** ejected material. An eruption with VEI 6 is therefore about ten times bigger than one with VEI 5. Such a scale is called **logarithmic**. For the highest step, **VEI 8**, an eruption has to eject more than **1,000 km³** of material. Such giant eruptions last happened many tens of thousands of years ago.

The eruption of **Eyjafjallajökull** in Iceland in 2010 had **VEI 4**. Even so, it paralysed air traffic in Europe. The eruption of **Vesuvius** in the year 79, which buried Pompeii, had **VEI 5**. The eruption of **Tambora** in Indonesia in 1815 is the only one of recorded modern times with **VEI 7**. It also led to the year without a summer in Switzerland in 1816.

abschnitte.titel: What the VEI does not measure
abschnitte.text: The VEI says nothing about the amount of **sulphur gases**. These gases, however, can strongly affect the **climate**. In the upper air they form fine droplets that screen out sunlight. So an eruption with a rather small VEI can cool the weather more than a bigger one. That is why researchers use the VEI together with other measurements.

gewusst: The Yellowstone supervolcano in the USA had eruptions of VEI 8 in the distant past.
The eruption of Pinatubo in 1991 in the Philippines had VEI 6 and measurably cooled the Earth afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Sugar cane is a large grass from which a large part of the world's sugar is obtained. It grows in warm countries and can reach several metres in height.
wichtigste: Sugar cane belongs to the grasses.
It grows in warm countries and can reach several metres in height.
Brazil grows the most sugar cane.
The stalks are pressed to obtain the sweet juice.
Sugar from sugar cane is called cane sugar.
In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet.

abschnitte.text: **Sugar cane** belongs to the **grasses**, like wheat or maize. It has thick, firm **stalks** that can grow **several metres** tall. Inside the stalks there is a sweet juice. Sugar cane needs a lot of warmth, sun and water. That is why it grows only **in warm countries**, mainly in the tropics and subtropics. Originally it comes from the area around New Guinea in South-East Asia.

After the harvest the stalks are **pressed** in big mills. In this way the sweet **juice** is obtained. This is cleaned and boiled down until **sugar crystals** form. Brown sugar from sugar cane is often called **cane sugar**. The pressed fibres, the **bagasse**, are often burned to produce energy for the factory.

The country that grows **the most sugar cane** is **Brazil**. India comes next. In Brazil, sugar cane is used to make not only sugar but also **ethanol**, a **fuel for cars**. Many cars there can run on it or on a mixture of petrol and ethanol. The big plantations are also controversial, however, because nature can be lost to them.

No sugar cane grows in Switzerland, because it is too cold. Here sugar is obtained from **sugar beet**. They grow in fields on the Central Plateau and are harvested in autumn. In the sugar factories in **Aarberg** in the canton of Bern and in **Frauenfeld** in Thurgau, sugar is made from them. White beet sugar and white cane sugar are chemically practically the same.

gewusst: After the harvest, sugar cane can regrow several times from the same rootstock.
In the past sugar was so expensive in Europe that it was called “white gold”.

teile.einleitung: Livestock farming means that people keep farm animals such as cows, sheep, goats or camels. The animals provide milk, meat, wool or leather, and some also help with carrying loads. All over the world, livestock farming looks quite different depending on the landscape and climate.
wichtigste: Livestock farming means keeping farm animals.
In Switzerland many cows go up to the alp in summer.
On the alp the cowherd looks after the cows and makes cheese.
In Argentina the cattle herders are called gauchos.
In New Zealand there are more sheep than people.
Sheep provide milk, meat and wool.
In the desert, camels are kept for carrying loads and for their milk.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are many meadows and pastures but little flat arable land. That is why keeping **dairy cows** is very important. In summer many farmers take their cows up to the **alp** in the mountains. There the **cowherd** looks after the animals and makes **cheese** from the milk. In autumn the decorated cows return to the valley in the **alp descent**.

On the wide grass plains of Argentina, the **pampas**, huge herds of cattle graze. The cattle herders there are called **gauchos**. They ride horses and drive the herds together. Argentina is known for its beef. The gauchos are seen as a symbol of the country.

In **New Zealand** there are clearly more **sheep** than people. The mild, damp climate lets grass grow all year round. Sheep provide **milk**, **meat** and **wool**. The wool is sheared once a year without hurting the animal. It is made into jumpers, socks and blankets.

In deserts and dry regions **camels** are often kept. They can go a long time without water and can carry heavy loads. Their **milk** is an important food for many families. Some herding peoples move as **nomads** with their herds from pasture to pasture. In this way the animals always find enough food.

gewusst: A cow eats a great deal of grass each day, often more than 50 kilograms.
Camels can drink over a hundred litres of water at once.

teile.einleitung: A low-pressure area, or low for short, is an area where the air pressure is lower than in its surroundings. Lows often bring clouds, wind and rain. They are very important for the weather in Switzerland and in the whole of Europe.
wichtigste: In the centre of a low, **the air rises**.
As it rises, the air cools and **clouds and precipitation** form.
In the northern hemisphere the air circles **anticlockwise** around a low.
The technical word for a low is **cyclone**.
The **Icelandic Low** and the **Genoa Low** often shape our weather.

abschnitte.text: In a low, air flows together from all sides and has to **rise**. As it rises, it cools. Cold air can hold less water vapour, so the vapour **condenses** into tiny droplets. This is how clouds form, and there is often **precipitation**. That is why a low usually means dull, wet weather.

The air does not flow straight into the low. Because of the **rotation of the Earth** it is deflected, which is called the **Coriolis force**. In the northern hemisphere the air therefore circles **anticlockwise** around a low, and in the southern hemisphere the other way round. The technical word **cyclone** comes from the Greek word for circle. At height the wind blows almost parallel to the **isobars**, while near the ground **friction** slows the wind and the air flows at an angle into the low.

Over the North Atlantic there is often an **Icelandic Low**. Together with the **Azores High** further south it steers the **westerly winds** towards Europe. These winds bring damp sea air and repeated rain to Switzerland. Many lows travel to us from the west across France. On a weather map you can recognise them by a large L and isobars lying close together.

When cold air from the north meets the Alps, a low often forms in the **lee** of the Alps, which means on the side away from the wind, over the Gulf of Genoa. This **Genoa Low** carries damp Mediterranean air towards the **southern side of the Alps**. In Ticino and other areas south of the Alps it can then rain or snow very heavily. Weather situations like this can lead to flooding.

gewusst: Hurricanes and typhoons are also especially strong low-pressure areas.
With a barometer you can measure the air pressure and so recognise an approaching low.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect makes sure that it is pleasantly warm on Earth. Certain gases in the air hold back part of the heat, rather like the glass roof of a greenhouse. People strengthen this effect when they put more of these gases into the air.
wichtigste: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be about -18 °C on average instead of about 15 °C.
Greenhouse gases hold back heat radiation coming from the ground.
Important greenhouse gases are water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane.
Nitrogen and oxygen are not greenhouse gases.
Joseph Fourier was the first to describe the effect, in 1824.
When people burn coal, oil and gas, they strengthen the greenhouse effect.

abschnitte.text: **Sunlight** passes almost unhindered through the air and warms the ground. The warm ground gives the energy back off as **heat radiation**, also called **infrared**. **Greenhouse gases** can absorb this long-wave radiation. They send part of it back down to the Earth. In this way more heat stays near the Earth's surface.

abschnitte.titel: Without it, it would be icy
abschnitte.text: Without the **natural greenhouse effect**, the average temperature on Earth would be about **-18 °C**. In fact it is about **15 °C**, which is about 33 degrees more. Only this makes liquid water and so much life on Earth possible. The effect gets its name from the **greenhouse**, a building with a glass roof. Heat is also trapped inside it, even though the physics there works a little differently.

The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**. Others are **carbon dioxide (CO2)**, **methane** and **nitrous oxide**. Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of the air, but they are not greenhouse gases. Their molecules consist of two identical atoms, and when they vibrate their **dipole moment** does not change, so they do not absorb heat radiation. Over 100 years, methane has about **30 times the effect** of the same amount of CO2, but it breaks down after about twelve years.

The French mathematician **Joseph Fourier** recognised in **1824** that the Earth would have to be much colder without an atmosphere. From **1859** the Irish physicist **John Tyndall** showed in the laboratory that water vapour and CO2 absorb heat radiation. The Swedish chemist **Svante Arrhenius** calculated in **1896** how much the temperature changes when the CO2 content of the air changes. He later won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, though for other work.

Since industrialisation, people have burned large amounts of **coal, oil and natural gas**. This produces CO2, which gets into the air. Cattle farming, rice fields and rubbish tips also release methane. As a result the greenhouse effect gets stronger, and the Earth warms up. This extra part is called the **human-made greenhouse effect**. In Switzerland you can see its consequences, for example, in the shrinking glaciers.

gewusst: Without the greenhouse effect the Earth would be about 33 degrees colder on average and largely covered in ice.
There is also a greenhouse effect on Venus: its dense CO2 atmosphere makes it the hottest planet in the solar system.

teile.einleitung: Vancouver is a large port city on the west coast of Canada. It lies between the sea and the mountains in the province of British Columbia. In 2010 the Winter Olympics took place here.
wichtigste: Vancouver lies in the province of British Columbia.
The capital of the province is not Vancouver but Victoria.
The city is named after the navigator George Vancouver.
Vancouver has the largest port in Canada.
Stanley Park, with old rainforest, lies on a peninsula.
In 2010 the Winter Olympics took place here.
The climate is mild and rainy.

abschnitte.titel: Between the sea and the mountains
abschnitte.text: **Vancouver** lies in the south-west of Canada on the coast of the **Pacific**. Behind the city the Coast Mountains rise up. Vancouver is the largest city in the province of **British Columbia**. The capital of the province, however, is **Victoria** on the offshore Vancouver Island. The city of Vancouver was founded in 1886.

The city is named after the British navigator **George Vancouver**. At the end of the 18th century he explored this coast. Today Vancouver has the **largest port in Canada**. Many goods are shipped from here to Asia, such as timber, grain and coal. The port is therefore important for the whole economy of the country.

In the middle of the city, on a peninsula, lies **Stanley Park**. There grow the huge old trees of a temperate **rainforest**. A long path leads along the shore around the park. For Canada the climate is **mild and rainy**, because the sea warms the land in winter. Snow rarely falls in the city, but there is plenty in the nearby mountains.

In 2010 Vancouver hosted the **Winter Olympics** and the Paralympics. Some events took place in the ski resort of Whistler in the mountains. Switzerland won several gold medals then, among them through the ski jumper **Simon Ammann**. He won on both hills.

gewusst: In Vancouver you can sometimes walk by the sea and ski in the nearby mountains on the same day.
Simon Ammann had already won on both hills in 2002 in Salt Lake City.

teile.einleitung: Vesuvius is an active volcano in Italy, very close to Naples. It became famous through its eruption in the year 79, which buried the Roman city of Pompeii. Today it is regarded as one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world.
wichtigste: Vesuvius lies near Naples in southern Italy.
In the year 79 it buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Pliny the Younger described this eruption in letters.
The last eruption was in 1944.
The old crater wall Monte Somma partly surrounds the cone.
Very many people live right on its slopes.

abschnitte.text: **Vesuvius** rises on the Gulf of **Naples** in southern Italy and is about 1,300 metres high. It is a **stratovolcano** made of lava and ash. The present-day cone is partly surrounded by an old, semicircular crater wall called **Monte Somma**. Since 1995 the area around the volcano has been a **national park**. Walkers can climb up to the rim of the crater.

In the year 79 Vesuvius erupted violently. Ash, pumice and glowing avalanches buried the Roman cities of **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**. The Roman writer **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from a distance. In two letters to the historian Tacitus he described it in detail. His uncle, **Pliny the Elder**, died in the eruption.

Since the year 79 Vesuvius has erupted many times. A big eruption in 1631 claimed many victims. The **last eruption** was in **1944**, in the middle of the Second World War. Since then the volcano has been quiet. Experts expect, however, that it will erupt again at some point.

At Vesuvius it is not only the volcano itself that is dangerous, but above all its location. **Very many people** live right on its slopes and in the big city of Naples. That is why researchers constantly **monitor** the volcano with measuring instruments. For an emergency there are plans for how people would be brought out of the danger zone.

gewusst: The ash preserved Pompeii so well that you can still see wall paintings, streets and bread ovens today.
Especially violent eruptions with a high column of ash are called “Plinian”, after Pliny the Younger.
